Simulations with 8-64 antennas confirm gains of 1.9-3.7 dB over pseudo-inverse RZF, with GIM-MMSE eliminating essentially all PAPC violations up to 20% per-antenna budget imbalance. The framework applies directly to fully-digital massive MIMO. Cell-free and hybrid analog-digital arrays are promising extensions.

Signal Processing.title: DNN-Driven Proactive UAV Trajectory and Beam Steering for Blockage-Resilient Communications
Signal Processing.summary: This paper proposes Autonomous UAV Communication (AutUAVCom), a proactive communication system that jointly adapts the flight trajectory and RF beam steering to minimize UAV energy consumption while satisfying secrecy and reliability requirements for rescue teams operating in dynamic, cluttered, and GPS-denied environments. Unlike existing modelbased proactive approaches, AutUAVCom employs a deep neural network-based Tracking and Prediction (T&P) module that combines onboard sensing with spatiotemporal and body-orientation information to track users, localize blocking objects, and predict future trajectories and potential beam blockages. Building on the T&P module, we formulate a constrained optimization problem and develop a two-step iterative numerical approach. Monte Carlo simulations show that, relative to a reactive system, AutUAVCom achieves 10% and 19% gains in energy efficiency and channel secrecy, respectively, while reducing the outage probability by 85%, under a mean blockage arrival interval of 120 seconds and a mean blockage duration of 20 seconds.

Signal Processing.title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
Signal Processing.summary: Recent experimental demonstrations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have attracted significant attention for their ability to establish information-theoretically secure encryption keys for next-generation communication systems. As practical deployment accelerates, the realization of compact, scalable, and high-throughput discrete-variable (DV) QKD systems has become increasingly important. While advances in photonic integration are enabling low-size, low-weight, and low-power QKD hardware, the security and performance of these systems rely heavily on efficient post-processing techniques to generate identical, secure keys. This tutorial presents a comprehensive algorithm-level review of practical post-processing techniques for DV-QKD, with particular emphasis on information reconciliation methods based on Cascade, Winnow, low-density parity-check (LDPC), and polar codes. We also analyze the theoretical asymptotic and finite-size secret key rates (SKRs) of DV-QKD and benchmark these bounds against the practical SKRs achieved using actual post-processing algorithms. Furthermore, we present a server-client model to implement the entire QKD post-processing pipeline. The performance is evaluated in terms of QBER and SKR across various system parameters, considering the complete post-processing pipeline, including sifting, information reconciliation, privacy amplification, and authentication. This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.
Signal Processing.comment: Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society

Signal Processing.title: Evaluation of a Multi-Link Machine Learning Approach for Rainfall Detection Using Satellite Microwave Links
Signal Processing.summary: The impacts of climate change have increased the need for reliable real-time rainfall monitoring systems. This study investigates rainfall detection using a network of opportunistic sensors based on satellite microwave links (SMLs) combined with machine learning (ML) classifiers. Two models, a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN), were trained on aggregated SML data, including information from neighboring links. The results demonstrate that leveraging information from multiple links substantially enhances the detection of both wet and dry periods compared to single-link approaches. Moreover, the RF model consistently provides a more stable and reliable trade-off than CNN, improving rainfall detection and reducing misclassifications overall, with particularly strong performance during harsh weather conditions. The study spanned up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.

Signal Processing.title: AirFM-DDA: Air-Interface Foundation Model in the Delay-Doppler-Angle Domain for AI-Native 6G
Signal Processing.summary: The success of large foundation models is catalyzing a new paradigm for AI-native 6G network design: wireless foundation models for physical-layer design. However, existing models often operate on channel state information (CSI) in the spatial-temporal-frequency (STF) domain, where multipath components are superimposed and structurally entangled. This hinders the learning of a universal channel representation. Their reliance on global attention also incurs prohibitive overhead. In this paper, we propose AirFM-DDA, an Air-interface Foundation Model in the Delay-Doppler-Angle (DDA) domain. AirFM-DDA reparameterizes CSI into the DDA domain to resolve multipath components along physically meaningful axes and employs window-based attention with frame-structure-aware positional encoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate transferability across scenarios, tasks, datasets, and antenna configurations. For channel prediction and estimation, AirFM-DDA generalizes zero-shot to unseen cities, achieving average normalized mean-square error (NMSE) gains of 4.9-8.5 dB over the strongest baselines. With only 10% labeled data, it achieves average gains of 12.0 percentage points in Top-1 accuracy for beam prediction and 3.4 percentage points in F1 score for line-of-sight (LoS) identification. It further transfers across simulated datasets and adapts to measured data and different antenna arrays. Compared with global attention, window-based attention reduces training and inference costs by nearly an order of magnitude.
Signal Processing.comment: 18 pages

Signal Processing.title: Quantum-Enhanced Classical Communications for DPMZM-based NG-PON2 Systems
Signal Processing.summary: This paper presents a framework for integrating quantum detection techniques into a Dual-Parallel Mach-Zehnder Modulator (DPMZM)-based Next Generation Passive Optical Network 2 (NG-PON2) communication system. We present a system model for the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system and characterize its signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), demonstrating its superiority over conventional MZM-based systems. We analyze the performance of various quantum modulation techniques, including binary phase-shift keying, quadrature phase-shift keying, and M-ary quadrature amplitude modulation. A comprehensive analytical framework is developed to evaluate the SNR, BER, and mutual information for both classical and quantum detection schemes within the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system. Our simulation results show that quantum detection significantly outperforms classical detection, and the DPMZM architecture further enhances the performance over the baseline MZM architecture by improving the effective modulation efficiency and receiver sensitivity.

Signal Processing.title: DeepRT-Cal: Learning to Calibrate Ray-Traced Twin Channel Statistics with Low-Fidelity Environmental Geometry
Signal Processing.summary: Sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems increasingly rely on digital twin channels (DTCs) to represent and interact with physical radio environments. Ray tracing (RT) is naturally suited to DTC construction because it provides deterministic and physically interpretable channel predictions. However, high-fidelity three-dimensional environment models are expensive to obtain, whereas geometric inaccuracies in low-fidelity models can alter the detected multipath components (MPCs) and consequently distort received-power and delay-domain twin channel statistics. Building on the DeepRT ray-tracing framework, this paper proposes DeepRT-Cal, a geometry-aware cross-fidelity calibration framework that predicts high-fidelity twin channel statistics from low-fidelity geometry and RT features.The network encodes global link descriptors, masked low-fidelity MPC tokens, propagation-corridor geometry, and link-centered environmental objects. During training, detailed geometry is introduced as privileged information with structured masking, while deployment requires only low-fidelity geometry and low-fidelity RT information. A link-conditioned cross-attention module retrieves the environmental context relevant to each Tx--Rx link. The prediction heads estimate high-fidelity twin channel statistics, including total received power, RMS delay spread, mean excess delay, and a normalized power-weighted power-delay profile (PDP). Outdoor evaluation shows that, in an non-line of sight (NLoS) region, the method reduces power MAE from 16.80 to 3.88 dB and RMS delay-spread MAE from 304.89 to 98.19 ns. In a LoS-dominated region, power prediction improves, while RMS delay-spread accuracy remains comparable to direct RT.
Signal Processing.comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables

Signal Processing.title: Capacity of Multi-Layer Manhattan-Grid UAV Corridors Served by Terrestrial 5G NR Networks
Signal Processing.summary: Advanced air mobility (AAM) is expected to organize unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) traffic into corridors at multiple altitudes. In this paper, we study the downlink (DL) and uplink (UL) capacity of a multi-layer Manhattan-grid corridor mesh served by a terrestrial fifth-generation (5G) new radio (NR) macro network. The corridor spacing and the numbers of layers, UAVs, and base stations are configurable. We combine the 3GPP aerial channel and antenna models, correlated UAV mobility, and frequency-selective fading with an NR physical-layer abstraction that includes channel aging and link adaptation. Results show that UAVs above 90 m experience a DL signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) about 17 dB below that of ground users, and that a dense macro network with $10^\circ$ downtilt leaves 17-29% of corridor positions without DL service under full-buffer load, regardless of corridor spacing. On a common layout, the carrier frequency (700 MHz, 3.5 GHz, or 7.2 GHz) changes the UAV SINR by less than 0.5 dB, since the corridor links are strongly interference-limited. The UL is the bottleneck: at 85% satisfaction, a 20 MHz carrier supports only about 3.4-4.1 UAVs/km$^2$ with 4 Mb/s of UL video per UAV.
Signal Processing.comment: Under Review

Signal Processing.title: FoundaRF: A Physics-Informed Foundation Model Framework for Radio-Frequency Passive Components
Signal Processing.summary: Designing RF/mmWave passive components is a time-consuming process that relies heavily on expert knowledge and iterative EM simulations. Although recent ML surrogate models have shown great promise in accelerating passive design, they remain task-specific and lack generalization. This paper presents FoundaRF, a foundation model framework that unifies passive layout modeling across diverse layout structures and technologies. It combines a self-supervised encoder with adaptive layout processing and physics-aware decoders to enable few-shot transfer. Experiments across four semiconductor technologies show strong generalization to unseen structures, outperforming baselines with up to a 3.3x reduction in prediction error, reducing labeled-data requirements by up to fourfold, and substantially shortening design turnaround. FoundaRF establishes a scalable and data-efficient solution for RF/mmWave passive design automation.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)

Signal Processing.title: Learning Latent Fields in Multiobject Tracking
Signal Processing.summary: Multiobject tracking using measurements from arrays of wireless sensors is a key task in applications ranging from autonomous navigation to public safety. Many existing methods compress raw complex-valued signals into detections or intensity maps during preprocessing, thereby discarding potentially relevant information about the objects and the propagation environment. We propose a Bayesian framework for multiobject tracking that relates object states to raw complex-valued signals via a physics-based superpositional model. The model combines a physics-based array manifold, such as radar steering vectors or the replica vectors of matched-field processing, with a latent field. This latent field is a family of context-dependent signal-power distributions that captures the effects of the objects and the propagation environment and is shared across objects and time. It is parameterized by a conditional normalizing flow, which is trained during runtime without labeled data by maximizing an evidence lower bound (ELBO) derived from the Bayesian model. Learning and inference are thus coupled in a sequential framework. We evaluate the method in simulation and in real-world radio and acoustic experiments, with spatial scales ranging from meters to kilometers, and show that it outperforms detection-based methods.
Signal Processing.comment: Minor wording changes to the abstract; technical content unchanged

Signal Processing.title: GeoJeV: Unified Spatial Probability for Training-Free Efficient Evidence Acquisition in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
Signal Processing.summary: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.

Signal Processing.title: Stochastic High-Resolution Parameter-Based Channel Modeling for Sub-Terahertz Outdoor Device-to-Device Propagation at 145 GHz
Signal Processing.summary: Since device-to-device (D2D) systems operating in the sub-THz regime are of interest for a variety of 6G applications, modeling their propagation channels is therefore essential. This paper presents high-resolution parameter estimation (HRPE) of specular multipath components (MPCs) as well as diffuse multipath components (DMCs) from an extensive measurement campaign. The extracted MPCs and DMCs are then clustered, and statistical models for both intra- and inter-cluster statistics are established. Among other insights, we find a large number (typically 10-50) of clusters; both the powers and densities of MPCs within each cluster show significant variations. DMC occurs both when associated with discrete MPCs and standalone. The paper provides a complete model that can generate double-directional impulse responses, and a MATLAB program implementing it is made available. Extensive verifications of "derived" (not directly modeled) parameters are provided as well.
Signal Processing.comment: Currently under submitted and under revision in the IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications

Signal Processing.title: Sparse Network Inference under Imperfect Detection and its Application to Ecological Networks
Signal Processing.summary: Recovering latent structure from count data has received considerable attention in network inference, particularly when one seeks both cross-group interactions and within-group similarity patterns in bipartite networks, which are widely used in ecology research. Such networks are often sparse and prone to imperfect detection. Existing models mainly focus on interaction recovery, while the induced similarity graphs are much less studied. Moreover, existing models for under-counted data place sparsity, if at all, on the detection model rather than on these graphs. To address these issues, we propose a nonnegative low-rank factorization framework that jointly estimates detection probabilities and promotes sparse within- and cross-group graphs through $\ell_{1/2}$ regularization. For the resulting nonconvex, nonsmooth problem, we develop an ADMM-based algorithm with adaptive penalization, and establish asymptotic feasibility and KKT stationarity of cluster points under stated assumptions. We also give sufficient conditions for exact recovery of within- and cross-group graphs. On synthetic data with up to 20% missing entries, the method recovers the graphs and detection probabilities with competitive accuracy. Across three ecological datasets, it matches the baseline held-out predictions while estimating detection probabilities and within- and cross-group graphs.
Signal Processing.comment: 16 pages, 2 figures

Signal Processing.title: An Ultra-Low-Noise Tunable TIA in 45nm Silicon Photonics for Electro-Optical Ultrasound Data Acquisition
Signal Processing.summary: This paper presents the design and experimental characterization of a 32-channel, WDM-compatible electronic-photonic receiver array fabricated in the GlobalFoundries 45nm monolithic silicon photonics process. Optimized for miniaturized, millimeter-scale electro-optical ultrasound data acquisition probes for broadband photo-acoustic imaging (PAI), the chip utilizes integrated micro-ring resonator (MRR) demultiplexers and photodiode (PD) arrays to decode multi-wavelength acoustic signals outside the body. This work focuses specifically on the comprehensive characterization of the receiver front-end, evaluating both the optical WDM filter bank and the transimpedance amplifier (TIA) performance. Monolithic co-integration minimizes critical photodiode-to-TIA interface parasitics. The TIA incorporates a DC-offset cancellation loop that compensates for photodiode-induced offset currents while providing tunable low-frequency cutoff control over a range of 30 kHz to 1.5 MHz. This tunability enables effective suppression of flicker noise and improves overall signal integrity. The front-end achieves the peak transimpedance gain of 144 dB$Ω$ while maintaining an ultra-low input-referred noise current density of $1\text{ pA}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, demonstrating a highly scalable architecture for high-sensitivity intravascular and endobronchial imaging.

Signal Processing.title: Energy-Aware Vertically Layered Pinching-Antenna System Design with Probabilistic LoS Availability
Signal Processing.summary: This paper investigates a vertically layered pinching antenna (PA) system, in which dielectric waveguides deployed at different heights provide additional vertical spatial degrees of freedom for line-of-sight (LoS)-favorable PA placement. We consider a practical energy model that captures in-waveguide attenuation, base station-to-feed-point optical-fiber loss, and PA repositioning energy, along with a statistical LoS-availability model that depends on elevation and distance. We then jointly optimize the transmit beamforming, PA positions, time allocation, and transmission rates to maximize the expected successfully delivered frame-effective sum rate under per-user outage and quality-of-service constraints. To avoid enumerating the exponentially many LoS states, we derive a certified conditional-moment outage envelope for outage-guaranteed rate selection and a differentiable safe approximation of the chance constraints to facilitate tractable optimization. Building on these results, a block coordinate descent algorithm with a penalty-aided majorization-minimization procedure attains a high-quality suboptimal solution. Simulation results confirm the gains of vertical layering and reveal a fundamental energy-LoS tradeoff: LoS-favorable PA placement generally enhances both performance and reliability, although it incurs higher attenuation, path loss, and energy costs.

Signal Processing.title: Sensing-Based Communication: A Non-Orthogonal Passive Reflection Framework for ISAC
Signal Processing.summary: While integrating uplink without disrupting the primary downlink remains a critical challenge for existing reflective communication systems, this paper proposes a non-orthogonal passive integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) mechanism termed Sensing-based Communication. Originating from and validated within an optical retro-reflective system, this mechanism possesses an underlying wave-agnostic architecture with the potential to be generalized across other physical modalities. It leverages incident downlink signals for parasitic modulation via passive tags. By relying solely on fundamental on-off keying (OOK) reflection, the tag unifies the reflective sensing channel and the uplink communication channel, and simultaneously achieves both sensing and duplex communication. Consequently, our approach introduces uplink capability without sacrificing the downlink data rate or consuming additional spectrum resources. At the receiver, we design a joint decoding architecture combining cross-correlation computation and successive interference cancelation (SIC) to fully exploit the degrees of freedom in broadband signals for multi-user interference suppression. We derive closed-form expressions for the interference and bit error rate (BER) assuming zero-mean Gaussian signals. Using an experimental testbed, we validate the pivotal theoretical finding, the scaling relationship of SINR with signal bandwidth and cross-correlation time--where linear regression yields a strong goodness-of-fit with $R^2 = 0.9688$. Furthermore, evaluations under noise-like orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) waveforms exhibit high consistency between theoretical derivations and simulation data ($R^2 = 0.9372$, mean absolute percentage error, $\text{MAPE} = 14\%$), confirming the model's accuracy and waveform generalizability.

Signal Processing.title: Two-Timescale Receive Combining for Fronthaul-Constrained Uplink XL-MIMO with Visibility Regions
Signal Processing.summary: Extremely large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) arrays are hard to deploy in virtualized radio access networks, because the fronthaul data rate grows with the number of antennas when the radio unit forwards every antenna sample. We propose a two-timescale receiver that allocates the per-user combining ranks under the fronthaul stream budget from the channel statistics. The radio unit applies the long-timescale transform, after which the distributed unit applies a minimum mean-squared-error receiver in the reduced dimension. For disjoint visibility regions, we prove that the reduced-dimension receiver decouples across users. We characterize the sum-rate loss to second order and show that the greedy allocation, which we call saturating capture, minimizes its leading term. In simulations, the allocation gains over a uniform-rank baseline, matches a budget-trimmed threshold rule at a small number of users and exceeds it as the array and the user count grow. The gain grows with the heterogeneity of the per-user eigenvalue profiles and vanishes for identical profiles. Under out-of-cell interference offset by at least half a window width, the gain survives with clean covariances, which window-restricted estimation keeps for disjoint windows.
Signal Processing.comment: The manuscript was submitted to IEEE, and is currently under review

Signal Processing.title: Bayes-Optimal Quantum Computational Sensing via Convex Spectral Design
Signal Processing.summary: Quantum computational sensing performs task-specific inference directly through coherent sensing dynamics, avoiding an intermediate estimation step. Existing designs, however, typically optimize quantum control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance can depend strongly on initialization. This contribution formulates binary phase classification directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) restricts this response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, while the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program for the globally Bayes-optimal sensor response. Fejér--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The same formulation extends naturally to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty. Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign also lowers error under phase uncertainty.

Signal Processing.title: Real-Time Trans-Oceanic Fiber Sensing via Convergence of Long-Reach OFDR, High-Speed Optical Networking, and RDMA-Capable Edge-GPUs
Signal Processing.summary: We demonstrate real-time network-integrated bi-directional fiber sensing over a 4400-km subsea cable. Streaming and fusing two OFDR instruments via RDMA over a live transoceanic 130Gbaud coherent link and GPU edge-compute enabling parallel capture of multiple spatial resolutions from ~10m to ~100m.
Signal Processing.comment: 3 pages, 2 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategic Competition and Convergence in LLM Leaderboards
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Leaderboards are a popular way to compare large language model (LLM) capabilities and can influence how model developers invest resources. We ask when competition on leaderboards leads developers to produce models with similar capability profiles, which we call monoculture, or similar performance levels. We study this by formulating leaderboard competition as a game in which model developers invest resources across capabilities to maximize their win rate. We show that similar production functions can induce similar capability profiles, while comparative advantage can sustain distinct capability profiles. We then study convergence in performance levels and show that diminishing returns can lead to an increasingly crowded competitive frontier. Using data from LM Arena and OpenRouter, we find that developers improve more in categories where they lag competitors, while still retaining category-specific advantages. At the same time, we find that the frontier of models becomes increasingly crowded, alongside increasingly diversified model usage patterns. Our results suggest that increasing competition does not need to produce interchangeable models, but can instead sustain competitive models with distinct strengths.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds.
  For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt Σ)$, where $Σ$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_B})$, where $Σ_S$ and $Σ_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations.
  We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Optimal Regret for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Artificial Shoppers and Attention Competition
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. Second, we identify an alignment paradox: some consumers can become worse off than without AI even though their best option remains recommended and becomes cheaper. Salience can induce a switch to a lower-quality product whose quality loss exceeds the saving relative to the original purchase. The assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for consumers' realized welfare. Third, assistance can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus with the high- and middle-quality pair; delegation can do so with the high- and low-quality pair. Fourth, among AI designs, the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair wherever all compared pricing equilibria exist. Yet this preferred design can yield lower platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus than the no-AI optimum.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Effective Horizons for Prophet Inequalities with Discounted I.I.D. Rewards
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study prophet inequalities for $n$ i.i.d. base rewards subject to multiplicative discounts across $S$ phases. For equal-length phases and a common discount factor $\widetildeγ$, we characterize the optimal competitive ratio of single-quantile policies as $n\to\infty$ with $S$ and $\widetildeγ$ fixed. The resulting sharp guarantee describes the dependence on the phase parameters: it recovers $1-1/e$ without discounting and approaches $1/2$ in the worst-case regime. We also establish a distribution-free comparison that bounds the discounted prophet by a fractional i.i.d. maximum with effective horizon $B$, the sum of the discount weights across all observations. The comparison yields acceptance probability $1/B$, determined only by the phase profile. This calibration attains the canonical optimum even among single-quantile policies that may choose their acceptance probability using the known base distribution. The comparison also gives guarantees for heterogeneous discounts and unequal phase lengths. A complementary optimal-stopping upper bound establishes the same limiting optimum of $1/2$ for arbitrary stopping rules in the canonical model. Finally, the same effective-horizon calibration sets acceptance probability $1-\widetildeγ$ under infinite-horizon geometric discounting. This explicit quantile rule attains Boshuizen's (1994) known optimal worst-case ratio $1/(1+\widetildeγ)$ without solving a Bellman equation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations: A Separation at 1-1/e and a 0.6767 Guarantee for I.I.D. Weights
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give $(1-1/e)$-competitive algorithms for matroid prophet-secretary and prophet-secretary with XOS valuation functions. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits. For every matroid, we give a randomized $(1-1/e+\varepsilon_0)$-competitive algorithm, where $\varepsilon_0=10^{-6}$. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes $O(N^4)$ such queries in expectation and $O(N^4\log(N+2))$ in the worst case, where $N$ is the number of elements.
  We further consider the i.i.d. version of this problem and provide a $0.6767$ competitive ratio for every matroid with i.i.d.\ nonnegative weights from a known distribution. This guarantee even holds in fixed arrival order (a.k.a. i.i.d. matriod prophet inequalities), even when the algorithm learns the order only as the elements arrive.
  For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that $1-1/e$ is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than $1-1/e$, even when the buyers' valuations are i.i.d., every additive clause has coefficients in $\{0,1\}$, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: An Inspection Game for Monitor Design Against GNSS Timing Attacks in Synchronous Islanding
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Phasor measurement units (PMUs) take their time from GNSS, so a spoofer that slowly drags a receiver clock rotates the reported phase without touching the power waveform. The threat is acute in synchronous islanding, where a controller keeps an islanded generator in phase with the grid, using one PMU on each side of an open breaker, so that the two can be reconnected at any moment: a differential clock bias of about $0.56$\,ms can make the controller hold the generator $10^\circ$ out of phase while it reports perfect synchronism. We cast the defense as a zero-sum inspection game. The defender, as inspector, chooses its timing monitors and audits the clocks periodically; the attacker, as inspectee, drags the two clocks to an unsafe bias by the next audit; the payoff is the evidence, the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the probability laws of the defender's record under attack and under normal operation. Our central result is that the evidence equals the cost of the cheapest innocent explanation of the attacked record. This single identity predicts which monitors work, turns the attacker's best response into a strictly convex quadratic program, and turns the defender's design into a convex program with a saddle point. Pairing explanations, which bound the evidence from above, with test statistics, which bound it from below, certifies audit periods in which every successful attack leaves at least a threshold of evidence. On a 50\,Hz island, these evidence-based periods, at the matched-test threshold, are up to 8.4 times as long as those of a rule that checks each monitor separately, and the case study favors placing the better oscillator on the utility side of the breaker.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Infinite lexicographic products of positional objectives
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This paper contributes to the study of positional determinacy of infinite duration games played on potentially infinite graphs with neutral transitions. Recently, [Ohlmann, TheoretiCS 2023] established that positionality of prefix-independent objectives is preserved by finite lexicographic products. We propose two different notions of infinite lexicographic products indexed by arbitrary ordinals, and extend Ohlmann's result by proving that they also preserve positionality. In the context of one-player positionality, this extends positional determinacy results of [Grädel and Walukiewicz, Logical Methods in Computer Science 2006] to edge-labelled games and arbitrarily many priorities for both Max-Parity and Min-Parity. Moreover, we show that the Max-Parity objectives over countable ordinals are complete for the infinite levels of the difference hierarchy over $Σ^0_2$ and that Min-Parity is complete for the class $Σ^0_3$. We obtain therefore positional languages that are complete for all those levels, as well as new insights about closure under unions and neutral letters.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Attaining Optimal Values under Sure Constraints
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: A game may have, for each target below its value, a finite controller meeting that target, yet no finite controller attaining the value itself. We study finite stochastic games with a hard specification that must hold on every supported execution, including paths of probability zero. Max uses a pure finite controller; Min may use any pure public-history strategy. We distinguish three numerical questions: can a supplied target be met, can the unspecified optimum be attained, and what is one exact value? For explicit hard and Boolean soft Streett conditions, the strict and non-strict supplied-threshold problems are coNP-complete, attainment of the unsupplied supremum is $\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete, and one exact reduced fraction is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete under polynomial metric reductions. The proofs preserve both the value and its finite attainability when fixing a single opponent, and encode adaptive queries without computing unknown subgame values. The same construction yields matching value-comparison and exact-output lower bounds for ordinary stochastic Streett games with unrestricted randomized history strategies. We also bound the memory needed for optimal finite implementations for arbitrary Muller hard conditions and rational rewards in $[0,1]$ determined by infinitely recurring states. One controller is sure from the entire original sure region and attains at every finitely attained start, with no attainment premise on the other states. For $n$ states in that region it uses $2^{O(n\log(n+1))}Q(1+\log R)$ modes, where $Q$ is the product of the least common denominators of full original chance rows sourced in that sure region and $R$ clears all reward values. Its joint dependence on $Q$ and $R$ is worst-case sharp at each fixed $n\ge6$ when $Q,R\ge2$. Optimal dependence on arena size and efficient general synthesis are not resolved here.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 61 pages, 6 figures. Complete proofs included. Corresponding author: Takuto Yamauchi

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 33 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Fair Selection of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common resource. Such problems typically admit a continuum of equilibria, so any implementation must \emph{select} one. This selection is not neutral: it decides how the cost of the shared constraint is distributed among the agents, a decision often expected to be fair. The variational GNE (v-GNE), which charges all agents a uniform shadow price, is the conventional choice and is frequently advocated as fair. Through the lens of \emph{comparability} from social choice theory, we show that the GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability of costs, whereas the v-GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability, one of the stronger notions. We then introduce the fair GNE (f-GNE), which selects an equilibrium by explicitly optimizing a fairness metric matched to the comparability at hand, and give constructive routes to compute it for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games. An electric-vehicle charging game serves as a running example throughout this self-contained tutorial.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Book chapter, 25 pages, 4 figures. To appear in Socio-Inspired and Socially Aware Control for Complex Systems, Springer

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: As Easy as Rank One: Optimal Algorithms for Matroid Secretary and Single-Sample Matroid Prophet
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We resolve the matroid secretary conjecture in its strong form and the single-sample matroid prophet inequality problem, achieving competitive ratios $e$ and $2$, respectively. Both ratios are optimal, even for rank-one matroids.
  For matroid secretary, our ordinal algorithm accepts the elements of the canonical optimum independently, each with probability $1/e$. It needs only the number of elements in advance and uses an expected polynomial number of independence queries on arrived elements. For single-sample matroid prophet inequalities, our algorithm uses one sample per independent value distribution and $O(n^2)$ independence queries on a known $n$-element matroid. It works for every arrival order fixed independently of the samples, values, and algorithmic randomness. The selected elements and their values have exactly the joint distribution obtained by independently retaining each element--value pair in the canonical optimum of a fresh product draw with probability $1/2$.
  Our main algorithms maintain a reference state whose greedy solution contains every accepted element. Its updates, made even after rejections, preserve exact distributional invariants. A short reversible-update argument gives a $4$-probability-competitive secretary algorithm, already resolving the original conjecture; a related invariant gives the optimal single-sample prophet inequality. For secretary, we characterize the distributions achievable by ordinal algorithms through a finite polytope. A continuous-time formulation then lets us design an accepted-set distribution achieving the optimal ratio $e$ and realize it efficiently. We also obtain guarantees for matroid intersections.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: This paper merges and extends arXiv:2609.14555, arXiv:2609.19118, and arXiv:2609.30421

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Robust Analysis of First-Price Auctions with Large Supply
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
This paper performs a robust analysis of welfare (i.e., the price of anarchy) in multi-unit first-price auctions with independent private values and unit-demand bidders. We employ a smoothness framework (see \citealp{ST-13}) to analyze the price of anarchy when supply is large.
  The main barrier to analysis in this framework is a worst-case bid distribution that establishes a lower bound on the price of anarchy of $1- \frac{1}{e}$. We show that such worst-case distributions cannot arise in equilibrium when agents' values satisfy a mild density lower bound condition. This characterization leads to novel asymptotic lower bounds. In particular, the price of anarchy for $ε$-approximate equilibrium as the number of units goes to infinity is at least $1-Θ\left(ε\log \left(\frac{1}ε\right)\right)$.
  Our analysis relies on a key structural property of equilibrium bid distributions: for a welfare analysis in any multi-unit first-price auction, it is without loss to analyze (approximate) equilibria with no atoms. In addition to this, we establish continuity and monotonicity properties of Bayes-Nash equilibria. We believe these results are of independent interest.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Is Recursive Self-Improvement Safe?
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The phrase recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to the idea of an AI system designing and creating another, better AI system, which in turn designs and creates an even better one, and so on. While the idea has a long history, it has always been an abstract, futuristic idea -- until recently. Today's frontier AI has attained a set of abilities, including in programming, mathematics, research, tool use, and working coherently over extended periods of time, that make RSI seem plausible. AI companies are starting to pursue it, but many of the involved people are also expressing concerns, asking whether humanity should really set this in motion and under what conditions. I will discuss the situation, argue that we do not even have clear frameworks for thinking about the likely outcomes of RSI, and do a quick game-theoretic analysis of how to choose whether to initiate RSI when another party is making the same choice.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: To appear in IEEE Intelligent Systems

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer.
  We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering.
  The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Proportionality in Elections under Feasibility Constraints and Ranked Ballots: The Solid Coalition Refinement Rule
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study elections with ranked ballots and general feasibility constraints, which indicate which sets of candidates are allowed as outcomes. We introduce the first proportionality axiom for this general setting and show that it extends the established notions from specific models that fit our general framework. We extend the Solid Coalition Refinement (SCR) rule to general constraints and prove that it satisfies our axiom exactly for matroid constraints. Although the naive implementation of SCR involves a step that is computationally intractable for weak orders, we show that in practical cases it can be implemented in polynomial time or efficiently in FPT time. We also illustrate limitations of this rule for approval ballots and provide its first empirical evaluation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Cooperate to Compete: Strategic Data Generation and Incentivization Framework for Coopetitive Cross-Silo Federated Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In data-sensitive domains such as finance, cross-silo federated learning (CFL) allows organizations to collaboratively train AI models without sharing raw data. However, many practical CFL deployments are coopetitive, where organizations cooperate during model training while competing in downstream markets. In such settings, training contributions can improve the global model yet inadvertently strengthen rivals, eroding one's competitive advantage. This dilemma is amplified by non-IID data, which leads to asymmetric learning gains and undermines sustained participation. While existing work reward organizations based on marginal training contributions, they fail to account for the implicit costs of strengthening competitors. In this paper, we introduce CoCoGen+, a coopetition-compatible data generation and incentivization framework that jointly models data heterogeneity and inter-organizational competition while endogenizing GenAI-based synthetic data generation as a strategic decision. Specifically, CoCoGen+ formulates each training round as a weighted potential game, where organizations strategically decide how much data to generate by balancing learning gains against computational costs and utility losses caused by competition. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the continuous Nash equilibrium under the adopted model and develop a provably convergent scalar bisection algorithm. We further analyze how bilateral payoff redistribution modifies residual competition and data-generation incentives, and empirically evaluate the social welfare and individual utilities of the resulting allocations. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 validate the feasibility of CoCoGen+. The results show how heterogeneity, competition intensity, and incentives shape organizational strategies and social welfare, while CoCoGen+ achieves higher social welfare than competition-aware baselines.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Competition-aware Federated Learning, Strategic data generation approaches, A payoff-redistribution based incentive mechanism, Potential game, Social welfare

Computational Complexity.title: Beyond the $n/2$ Threshold: Quantum Query Complexity for Computing Hamming Weight and Symmetric Functions
Computational Complexity.summary: The oracle-interrogation algorithm [van Dam, FOCS '98] computes every $n$-bit Boolean function with bounded error using $n/2+O(\sqrt n)$ quantum queries. In contrast, parity can be computed exactly using $\lceil n/2\rceil$ queries, but whether an additive overhead beyond $n/2$ is necessary for a single Boolean output has remained open. In this work, we construct an explicit family of symmetric Boolean functions requiring $n/2+Ω(n^{1/3})$ quantum queries at a fixed positive constant error. We also give an algorithm that recovers the exact Hamming weight using $n/2+O(n^{1/3})$ quantum queries with bounded error, and therefore computes every symmetric Boolean function within the same query bound. Together, these results determine the optimal additive order for Hamming weight recovery and for the worst case over symmetric Boolean functions at sufficiently small constant error.

Computational Complexity.title: A proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture
Computational Complexity.summary: Aaronson and Ambainis conjectured that every bounded polynomial of low degree on the discrete cube has an influential variable. They showed that the conjecture implies that the acceptance probability of every quantum algorithm making $T$ queries can be approximated on most inputs by a classical algorithm making $\mathrm{poly}(T)$ queries. We prove their conjecture: every function $f\colon\{-1,1\}^n\to[-1,1]$ of degree at most $d\ge1$ has a variable of influence at least $c\,\operatorname{Var}(f)^{5/2}/d^{6}$, where $c>0$ is an absolute constant. In the original formulation, for polynomials of degree at most $d$ with values in $[0,1]$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ and variance at least $\varepsilon$, this gives a variable of influence at least $(\varepsilon/d)^{7}$. The proof is elementary, with steps inspired by works of others. Thus, as Aaronson and Ambainis anticipated, superpolynomial quantum speedups in the query model require structure, such as a promise on the inputs.
Computational Complexity.comment: 60 pages. Lean formalization and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/physical-superintelligence/aaronson-ambainis

Computational Complexity.title: The k-Clique hypothesis is dead, for good
Computational Complexity.summary: We present an algorithm that solves the $k$-Clique problem for any large enough $k$ and any $n$-vertex graph in $n^{\left(\fracω{3}-c\right)k}$ time, where $ω\geq 2$ is the matrix multiplication exponent and $c>0$ is a positive constant independent of both $ω$ and $k$. This refutes the long-standing $k$-Clique conjecture, regardless of the value of the matrix multiplication constant, even if $ω=2$. In fact, our algorithm solves the more general problem of counting weighted $k$-Cliques.

Computational Complexity.title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
Computational Complexity.summary:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory.
  In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation.
  Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.

Computational Complexity.title: Metric Dimension Parameterized by Bag-Connected Treewidth and Bag-Connected Pathwidth
Computational Complexity.summary: The metric dimension of a graph is the minimum size of a set of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices of the graph. We prove that \MetricDimension{} is NP-complete on planar graphs of treewidth and bag-connected treewidth exactly three. The graphs in our construction have no induced cycle longer than four and have (prefix-connected) pathwidth at most four. In particular, the problem admits no XP algorithm parameterized by bag-connected treewidth unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$. This answers questions of Bonnet and Purohit and of Bousquet, Deschamps, and Parreau. We prove that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by bag-connected pathwidth.

Computational Complexity.title: Tensor value and the 9/4 bound for matrix multiplication
Computational Complexity.summary: We give an exposition of OpenAI's recent result that the exponent of matrix multiplication is at most 9/4 valid over every field. Our main tool is a fractional symmetrized variant of the tensor value introduced by Coppersmith and Winograd, used in place of spectral points (tensor characters) in the original proof. We prove a superadditivity inequality for a power of this value on partially direct sums, whose summands share one tensor factor and occupy independent subspaces in the other two. Together with the degenerations of polynomial multiplication tensors from the OpenAI proof, this inequality yields the bound.

Computational Complexity.title: Optimizing Computational-Statistical Runtime for Wasserstein Distance Estimation
Computational Complexity.summary: Squared Wasserstein distance is a frequently used tool to measure discrepancy between probability distributions. This distance is typically computed between empirical measures of size $n$ from two underlying random samples. Unfortunately, even in lower dimensional Euclidean space problems $\left( d \in \{2,3\} \right)$, algorithms for Wasserstein distance computation with approximate or exact precision guarantees scale poorly in the runtime as a function of $n$ and the desired precision. In response, we consider the computational-statistical runtime, where the goal is to estimate from samples the Wasserstein distance between potentially smooth measures up to $ε$-additive error in expectation with respect to the sampling; we allow $O(1)$ computational cost for collecting a sample. Towards this, we develop a Sample-Sketch-Solve paradigm where we introduce a regular cartesian grid sketch of the samples. We show that (especially under $α$-Hölder smooth distributions) this can compress the data without increasing asymptotic error, and also regularizes the structure which enables faster exact algorithms. Ultimately, we approximate $W_2^2(P,Q)$ within $ε$ error in $ε^{-\max(2,\frac{d+1+o(1)}{1+α})}$ time for $0 < α< 1$ Hölder smooth distributions $P,Q$ on $(0,1)^{d}$; an optimal $Θ(ε^{-2})$ for $α> 1/2$ when $d=2$ and nearly optimal as $α\to 1$ when $d = 3$.

Computational Complexity.title: What remains of the planar induced minor conjectures?
Computational Complexity.summary:
Dallard, Milanič, and Štorgel, and independently Gartland and Lokshtanov, conjectured that for every planar graph $H$, Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring are polynomial-time solvable in $H$-induced-minor-free graphs. As a structural explanation, Gartland and Lokshtanov further conjectured that such graphs admit balanced separators dominated by a constant number of vertices. Bonnet and Chang recently refuted the independent-set part of the algorithmic conjecture, by showing that Maximum Independent Set is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in graphs excluding the $5\times5$ grid as an induced minor.
  We revisit both conjectures. We show that the graphs used by Bonnet and Chang exclude much simpler planar graphs, including several $16$-vertex trees, and we introduce a second, independent family of hard instances. We also prove that $3$-Coloring is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in both settings, thus refuting the algorithmic conjecture in full, even in its quasipolynomial version, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{QP}$. On the structural side, we identify planar graphs $H$ for which the structural conjecture holds, while the algorithmic one fails. Thus, constantly dominated balanced separators cannot by themselves explain the tractability of Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring.

Computational Complexity.title: On Positive Computation
Computational Complexity.summary: We introduce new notions of reducibility for monotone classes and show that a monotone version of Circuit Satisfiability and the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem are complete for $mNP$, even under positive reductions (which are not the same as monotone reductions). If this holds for all (monotone) $mNP$-complete problems - that they are also so complete for $mNP$ -, then $P\neq NP$. We introduce positive models of relativized computation and show that the separation $posP\subsetneq mNP$ does not relativize, even when oracles are restricted to monotone sets. Yet, there is a (weak) diagonalization proof that $posP\subsetneq mNP$.

Computational Complexity.title: A Dichotomy for Complex Boolean Holant with Binary Disequality
Computational Complexity.summary: We classify Boolean Holant problems with a supplied binary disequality signature and an arbitrary fixed finite set of algebraic complex-valued signatures. Each problem is polynomial-time computable or $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard, and the tractability criterion is decidable. The proof combines arity reduction with the growth of the available binary transfer group and uses stable pairs to recover the structure of higher-arity signatures. We also prove a dichotomy for the disequality-edge model when the signature set contains an endpoint-nondegenerate irreducible eight-vertex signature, resolving the corresponding arity-four cases in the main proof.
Computational Complexity.comment: 242 pages; proof and exposition revised, corrections made, Lean repository linked

Computational Complexity.title: A Full Complexity Dichotomy for Complex-Valued Boolean Holant Problems
Computational Complexity.summary: A Boolean Holant problem evaluates a graph partition function specified by local signatures at its vertices. We prove a complexity dichotomy for arbitrary finite sets of algebraic complex-valued signatures on general graphs: an explicit, decidable criterion characterizes the polynomial-time cases, and every remaining case is $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. The proof resolves the all-even case by constructing signatures with nonzero endpoints and all remaining support on the central layer, then classifying them according to half their arity. Binary transfer groups and matching-product reconstruction provide the main tools in the small- and large-height cases, respectively.
Computational Complexity.comment: 98 pages; proof and exposition revised, Lean repository linked

Computational Complexity.title: From Block Orthogonality to Decidability in Complex-Weighted Counting CSP
Computational Complexity.summary:
In a landmark JACM paper recognized with the 2021 Gödel Prize, Cai and Chen established a complexity dichotomy for counting CSPs over arbitrary finite domains with algebraic complex weights. Their tractability criterion consists of three conditions on the infinite family of functions obtained from CSP instances by summing out some variables: the Block Orthogonality and Type Partition conditions, and a Mal'tsev polymorphism condition on support and row-equivalence relations. They left open whether this criterion is decidable from the finite set of constraint functions. We resolve this question by giving a total exact algorithm for every $q$-element domain ($q\ge 1$), with algebraic weights encoded exactly. We also prove that the Block Orthogonality condition implies the other two conditions, reducing the tractability criterion to a single structural property. We obtain similar decidability and structural results for Lin's tractability criterion for $\#\mathrm{CSP}^{d}$, where each variable occurs a multiple of $d$ times.
  Our method first shows that every failure of Block Orthogonality can be witnessed by a generated function of arity at most $q^2+1$. At each such arity, we reduce checking infinitely many generated functions to finitely many exact algebraic tests, using tensor products and a pinned extension of Young's all-instance isomorphism theorem. For the structural implication, we use powers of generated functions to control complex cancellation and construct functions whose supports encode row equivalence. These constructions yield the Type Partition and Mal'tsev polymorphism conditions.
Computational Complexity.comment: 68 pages; revised proof and exposition, including a correction; Lean repository linked

Computational Complexity.title: Bounded Relative Boundary Implies Narrow DNF Approximation
Computational Complexity.summary: We prove Friedgut's conjecture (J. Amer. Math. Soc. 12 (1999)) that every increasing family in the $p$-biased discrete cube with bounded relative boundary can be approximated arbitrarily well by one whose minimal elements have size bounded independently of the dimension and the bias. For $0<p\le 1/2$, every increasing Boolean function with total resampling influence at most $K$ is $\varepsilon$-close under $μ_p^n$ to a monotone DNF of width $\exp(O((K+1)^2/\varepsilon^2))$, from which the full conjecture follows for all $p\in(0,1)$. We build on Hatami's pseudo-junta theorem (Ann. of Math. 176 (2012)), whose approximator need not be increasing. Our randomized shifts produce an increasing approximator that is measurable with respect to a controlled refinement of Hatami's adaptive partition. Retaining only short positive certificates yields the desired narrow DNF.
Computational Complexity.comment: 13 pages; proof and exposition revised, Lean repository linked

Computational Complexity.title: Hardness of Unique Shortest Vectors and Bounded Distance Decoding
Computational Complexity.summary:
We prove randomized NP-hardness of the unique shortest vector problem (uSVP) at every constant uniqueness factor greater than one, and of bounded distance decoding (BDD) at every fixed positive fraction less than one half of the minimum distance, in both their threshold decision and search versions. Both results hold in every fixed $\ell_p$ norm with $1\le p<\infty$. Previous Euclidean NP-hardness results for the search versions reached uniqueness factors tending to one and decoding radii greater than the minimum distance divided by $\sqrt2$.
  For linear codes over every fixed finite field and each fixed ${0<ρ\le1/2}$, the decision version of BDD with radius strictly less than $ρ$ times the minimum distance is equivalent under deterministic polynomial-time reductions to satisfiability for circuits promised to have at most one satisfying input. It is therefore NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions. Earlier hardness for decoding general codes applied beyond half the minimum distance.
  For every fixed $p>2$ and for $p=\infty$, there is a constant $ε>0$ such that, under randomized polynomial-time reductions, uSVP in the $\ell_p$ norm is NP-hard at uniqueness factor $n^ε$, and BDD in the $\ell_p$ norm is NP-hard at radius $λ_1/n^ε$, where $n$ is the lattice rank and $λ_1$ is its minimum distance.

Computational Complexity.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Bounds for $β$-TSP
Computational Complexity.summary: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) asks for a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. Its approximability depends on the edge lengths: unrestricted instances admit no constant-factor approximation unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, metric instances admit Christofides' $3/2$-approximation, and fixed-dimensional Euclidean instances admit a PTAS. We study $β$-TSP, where the edge lengths satisfy $ \ell_{uw}\leqβ(\ell_{uv}+\ell_{vw}) \qquad \forall\,u,v,w\in V\ \text{pairwise distinct}, \quad β\in\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]. $ The condition arises naturally in various settings, for example, when metric travel times are combined with positive service times at the vertices. The previous best approximation algorithm, due to Böckenhauer et al., ranges from $1$ at $β=1/2$ to $3/2$ as $β$ approaches $1$. We obtain a strictly better guarantee for every $1/2<β<1$ by combining two simple constructions whose guarantees counterbalance each other. We also improve the best known approximation hardness bound for every $1/2<β<1$.

Computational Complexity.title: Precedence Constraint Scheduling on a Fixed Number of Machines
Computational Complexity.summary:
We give a deterministic exact algorithm for $P_m\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ for every fixed $m\ge3$. The algorithm constructs an optimum schedule in $$
  O(L)+m^{O(m^2)}\, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, {\log n} $$ elementary RAM operations, where $n \ge 2$ is the number of jobs and $L$ is the binary input length. Its word size is $O(m^2 \log n)$ bits. An implementation with a fixed number of tapes uses $O(L)+m^{O(m^2)} \, n^{12m^2+26m+2} \, \log^3 n$ steps. For three machines the respective polynomial degrees are $94$ and $188$, apart from the displayed logarithmic factors.

Computational Complexity.title: A note on a problem in communication complexity
Computational Complexity.summary: We study bounded-error randomization and majority operators in structural communication complexity. We give a communication-complexity formulation of Tarui's theorem and identify the bounded-error closure of weakly unbounded-error communication with a distributional perturbation of logarithmic margin complexity. Retaining the Boolean guarantee in Tarui's probabilistic polynomials yields the stronger inclusion $\mathsf{PH}^{\mathrm{cc}} \subseteq \mathsf{ZP}\mathbin{\cdot} \mathsf{PP}^{\mathrm{cc}} \subseteq \mathsf{BP}\mathbin{\cdot} \mathsf{PP}^{\mathrm{cc}}$. We also define a majority operator satisfying $\mathsf{PP}\mathbin{\cdot} \mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{cc}} = \mathsf{PP}^{\mathrm{cc}}$ and use Sasaki's majority formula to prove that $\mathord{\oplus}\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{cc}} \subseteq \mathsf{PP}\mathbin{\cdot} \mathsf{PP}^{\mathrm{cc}}$. For the inner-product function modulo two, both the outer index and each inner protocol have logarithmic cost. Together with Forster's lower bound, this gives an explicit witness to the non-idempotence of the majority operator and to $\mathsf{PP}\mathbin{\cdot} \mathsf{PP}^{\mathrm{cc}} \not\subseteq \mathsf{UPP}^{\mathrm{cc}}$. Both the bounded-error closure and the two-level majority class are contained in $\mathsf{PSPACE}^{\mathrm{cc}}$.

Computational Complexity.title: Path Isolation and Reachability in Surface-Embedded Graphs with Restricted Cycle and Cut Structure
Computational Complexity.summary:
We study the reachability problem in directed surface-embedded graphs under two structural restrictions, using isolating weight assignments.
  First, we consider graphs whose underlying undirected embeddings contain at most polynomially many simple surface non-separating cycles. We develop a polynomially bounded, logspace-computable skew-symmetric edge-weight assignment with nonzero circulation around every simple cycle. This yields an unambiguous logspace (UL) upper bound for directed reachability. The construction also gives an SPL upper bound for bipartite perfect matching in the corresponding undirected graph class.
  Second, for $g$-genus directed graphs admitting a balanced hierarchical genus decomposition with $O(\log n)$ crossing edges at every partition, we obtain an unambiguous $O(\log g \cdot \log n)$-space bound for reachability. Our approach combines path-isolating weights for lower-genus subgraphs using polynomially bounded FKS hashing refinements at successive merging levels.

Computational Complexity.title: Two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard
Computational Complexity.summary: Given a fixed straight-line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two-colouring of its edges that minimizes monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP-complete, even for points in general position with integer coordinates. Thus exact minimization is NP-hard, resolving the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. We reduce from MaxCut on permutation graphs by representing source vertices with classes of geometric edges, whose crossings encode source adjacencies. The target complete graph also contains every other edge between its points, and their freely chosen colours can affect the encoded cost. To control these interactions, we construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use program points to turn this reference into colour preferences on other edges. The optimum differs from a computable baseline plus the amplified minimum number of uncut source edges by an error small enough to distinguish consecutive source values. The reduction is deterministic, with polynomially many points and polynomial coordinate bit length.
Computational Complexity.comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Updated author information, presentation and declarations. Proof code and reproducible computations: https://github.com/Myyura/two-colour-crossing-complete-geometric-graphs

Computational Complexity.title: On derandomizing the line-point low-degree test
Computational Complexity.summary:
We investigate the derandomized version of the classical line-point low-degree test in the high-error regime in the bivariate setting and reveal some unexpected behavior. The classical line-point low-degree test takes an $m$-variate function $f$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, queries it along a random line and accepts if the restriction of the function to this line is a low-degree polynomial.
  The high-error version of (the analysis of) this test asserts that if $f$ has at least $ε$ expected local agreement with a degree-$k$ univariate polynomial on a random line, then in fact $f$ is non-trivially close to some degree-$k$ $m$-variate polynomial even as $ε$ approaches $0$ (provided $q$ is sufficiently large compared to $k$ and $1/ε$). The derandomized version of the problem asks if the same holds when the line is not chosen uniformly over all possible lines but rather from a small set.In this paper we explore the bivariate case ($m=2$). We show, somewhat surprisingly, that there exists a function $f\colon \mathbb{F}_q^2 \to \mathbb{F}_q$ and a set of lines $\mathcal{L}$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ of size nearly $q^{3/2}$ such that on every line in $\mathcal{L}$, $f$ has agreement $\approx 1/2$ on average with some univariate polynomial of degree $k=\sqrt{q}/2$ and yet $f$ is $1 - O(q^{-1/2})$ far from every polynomial of degree $O(k)$. On the positive side, we show that once the field size $q$ is at least $k^2/(ε)^{O(1)}$ such examples disappear and we can get sets of lines of size $O(q/ε^{O(1)})$ on which the low-degree test has a high-error analysis.
  On the way to our positive result, we show a new high-degree version of the classical two-direction Polishchuk--Spielman divisibility lemma.
Computational Complexity.comment: Abstract shortened due to arxiv requirements

Computational Complexity.title: Deterministic factorization of constant depth circuits from whitebox PIT
Computational Complexity.summary:
We show that over the field of rational numbers, there is a deterministic algorithm for factorization of constant depth circuits that makes calls to a (whitebox or blackbox) PIT algorithm for such circuits. The time complexity of the algorithm (and hence the number of calls to the PIT oracle) is polynomially bounded in the size and degree of the input circuit. Our reduction to PIT is fairly simple and general and applies as it is to other natural classes of algebraic circuits like formulas and algebraic branching programs.
  Prior to this work, the known deterministic factorization algorithms for constant depth circuits crucially relied on \emph{blackbox} PIT [Bhattacharjee et al.]. Our main technical ingredient is an efficient, deterministic algorithm that, when given access to sufficiently high degree truncations of \emph{all} the power series roots of a constant depth circuit, uses oracle calls to any (whitebox or blackbox) PIT algorithm for these circuits, and partitions the roots into the sets of conjugates; thereby identifying the irreducible factors.
  For our proof, we rely on a root recombination criterion using logarithmic derivatives [Sasaki et al., Bostan et al., Lecerf] and show that this criterion can be efficiently and deterministically implemented for power series roots of constant depth circuits using access to any PIT oracle. On the way, we discuss an algorithm that may be of independent interest: it takes as input a matrix whose entries are multivariate constant depth circuits over a field $\mathbb{F}$, requires oracle access to any PIT algorithm for these circuits and outputs a basis for the $\mathbb{F}$-kernel of this matrix in polynomial time.

Computational Complexity.title: Reconfiguration of Time-Bounded Descriptions
Computational Complexity.summary: Time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity measures a string by the length of its shortest program that prints it within a deadline. An adjunction-universal machine (Bauwens, Kozachinskiy, and Shen, arXiv, 2025) is a Turing machine that simulates every Turing machine $M$ on every input $z$ with polynomial overhead when given a code of $M$, computable from $M$ in polynomial time, followed by $z$ unchanged.
