However, this threshold is typically selected empirically, with limited theoretical guidance. This paper establishes a connection between threshold-based event encoding and discretized learning systems and identifies a dimensionless ratio governing information retention. From this connection, we derive an information-sufficiency boundary using normal-condition data and formulate a data-driven criterion that selects the sparsest threshold retaining a prescribed fraction of peak discriminative information. The framework is illustrated using event cameras and evaluated on power-system fault classification. Results show that the proposed design identifies sparse operating thresholds while exposing the tradeoff between information retention, event activity, and classification performance.

Systems and Control.title: Beyond Accuracy: Physics-Informed Evaluation of ANN-based Power Flow Solvers under System Shift
Systems and Control.summary: Recent advances in artificial deep learning-based power flow (PF) solvers have primarily focused on improving estimation accuracy, while their physical feasibility and operational reliability under realistic system variations remain insufficiently evaluated. This paper proposes a physics-informed evaluation framework for deep learning-based PF solvers under topology and load distribution shifts. Beyond conventional voltage-domain errors, the framework incorporates KCL gaps, branch-flow gaps, KVL residuals, continuous feasibility scores, and strict, practical, and relaxed PF feasibility rates. Four case studies are designed to investigate topology shifts, mixed topology training, load distribution shifts, and combined topology distribution shifts. Eight ANN architectures, including graph input models, load-only baselines, and physics-informed neural networks, are evaluated under consistent settings. The results demonstrate that low estimation errors do not necessarily correspond to physically feasible or operationally reliable PF solutions, particularly under combined system shifts. The proposed framework establishes an initial foundation and analysis for the development and verification of trustworthy deep learning-based PF solvers, providing support for their reliable deployment in future AI-enabled power system analysis.

Systems and Control.title: Intelligent Carbon Emission-aware Radio Unit Activation Control in Dense Heterogeneous Energy 6G Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Base stations account for a dominant share of energy consumption and operational carbon emissions in radio access networks. In O-RAN deployments with heterogeneous energy sources, however, minimizing energy consumption alone does not necessarily minimize carbon emissions. In this work, we investigate carbon-aware DRL for RU sleep control. Under the adopted source-matched operational accounting model, renewable-matched RUs are assigned zero direct operational emissions, whereas non-renewable-supplied RUs incur operational emissions. The problem is formulated as a Markov decision process and evaluated using two carbon-aware reward formulations and a conventional energy--QoS reward baseline. We implement and compare TD3, PPO, and a heuristic method under realistic mobility and 3GPP channel models across multiple renewable-matched RU layouts and traffic loads. Simulation results show that TD3 learns more energy-efficient activation policies than PPO, achieving approximately 3%--6% lower energy consumption in representative scenarios. TD3 also achieves 8%--12% lower operational emissions than PPO in scenarios with a low proportion of renewable-matched RUs and up to a 20% reduction relative to the heuristic baseline under moderate renewable availability and high traffic load. Moreover, the joint energy,carbon and QoS reward achieves approximately 12%--28% lower operational emissions than the energy and QoS reward, while maintaining comparable energy consumption.

Systems and Control.title: PA-SaR: Perception-Aware Learning, Control, and Coordination for Multi-Robot Search and Rescue
Systems and Control.summary: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.

Systems and Control.title: Koopman Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
Systems and Control.summary: We propose a Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm for controlling nonlinear robotic systems with unknown dynamics. The K-MBRL learns a control policy by minimizing an approximate policy objective that combines the analytical immediate cost with an estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step predicted state. To this end, we develop a stochastic Koopman operator-based learning method to approximate the unknown nonlinear dynamics in a linear representation, while a critic function estimates the remaining future cost. This formulation offers two key advantages. First, the linear Koopman dynamics simplify the model-dependent policy gradient computation to a constant matrix product, enabling computationally efficient policy improvement. Second, one-step model propagation mitigates the accumulation of prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts while retaining long-term cost information through the critic. The learned policy enables real-time control through feedforward evaluation without online optimization. We establish policy learning convergence guarantees under standard stochastic approximation assumptions. Simulations on HalfCheetah and quadruped four-legged locomotion tasks demonstrate strong sample efficiency and improved performance compared with classical model-free and model-based reinforcement learning baselines. A pendulum swing-up task is used to assess policy gradient approximation accuracy and conduct ablation studies on the learning mechanism and key hyperparameters. The proposed K-MBRL is further validated on a physical quadruped robot performing a challenging sequence of maneuvers: rising to an upright posture supported by two rounded rear feet, maintaining balance during bipedal walking, and safely returning to the ground, as shown in Fig.1.

Systems and Control.title: Data-driven Linear Quadratic Integral Control: A Convex Formulation and Policy Gradient Approach
Systems and Control.summary: This paper studies the data-driven synthesis of linear quadratic integral (LQI) controllers for continuous-time systems. The objective is to achieve optimal state-feedback control with integral action for reference tracking using only measured data. To this end, we derive a data-driven closed-loop parameterization of the augmented dynamics that incorporates the integral state while relying solely on input-state-output measurements of the underlying system. Based on this parameterization, a data-driven convex optimization problem is formulated whose solution yields the optimal linear quadratic regulator (LQR) feedback gain for the augmented system without explicit knowledge of the system matrices. In addition, a projected policy gradient flow, which is a preconditioned version of the model-based policy gradient flow, is derived to compute the optimal controller within the space of stabilizing gains. The proposed approach enables data-driven optimal tracking control while avoiding explicit state augmentation in the data collection phase. For time-varying gains, as they arise in an online implementation, the direct, incremental, and feedforward realizations of the LQI controller are compared, and the equilibrium required for feedforward is obtained from the same data. The method is illustrated on a distributed generation unit (DGU) in a DC microgrid, including an online implementation with closed-loop data under load changes, and by a Monte Carlo study on random systems with noisy data.

Systems and Control.title: Adaptive Reparametrized Time for Score-Based Diffusion Sampling
Systems and Control.summary: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.
Systems and Control.comment: 37 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables. Accepted for publication in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR)

Systems and Control.title: Stability of DC Microgrids with Nested Nonlinear Control Frameworks: The Fast Communication Scenario
Systems and Control.summary: As modern power systems continue to evolve into multi-agent, converter-dominated systems that demand reliable, stable, and optimal control architectures within an expandable framework, this paper investigates scalable stability guarantees of a promising nonlinear communication-reliant control framework for DC microgrids. Particularly, relying on nested control loops, inner decentralized (primary) and outer distributed (secondary), the control configurations are designed to simultaneously achieve proportional current sharing and voltage containment within pre-specified limits, at the converged steady state. By enforcing sufficient time-scale separation at the border between the control loops, the system admits a singular perturbation formulation, allowing global exponential stability (G.E.S.) to be established via Lyapunov arguments. Although the theoretical G.E.S. certificate is structurally scalable, the stability guarantees depend on a sufficiently large permanent leakage, introduced in the primary controller. Thus, this paper emphasizes the importance of appropriate practical tuning guidelines for establishing suitable system configurations under which the DC microgrid is practically scalable and its equilibrium is G.E.S.. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through case studies on a low-voltage DC microgrid under load variations and topological changes, followed by a small-signal stability analysis

Systems and Control.title: Discrete-Time Stochastic Control Beyond i.i.d. Noise
Systems and Control.summary: We study discrete-time stochastic control problems where the noise driving the state dynamics is a stationary infinite-order chain rather than an i.i.d. sequence. We formulate the problem as a controlled Markov process by enlarging the state space to include the posterior distribution of the noise given the state-action history. Assuming that the sensitivity of the noise transition kernel to past noise values decays exponentially, we show that the expected total variation distance between the full-history and finite-memory noise filters decays at rate $\sqrt{N}ρ^{\sqrt{N}}$. We use this result to construct finite-memory control models and establish explicit near-optimality bounds for their policies. Finally, under suitable ergodicity conditions, we show that Q-learning converges to the optimal solution of the approximate model, so the same performance bounds apply to the learned policies.

Systems and Control.title: Industrial Load Modeling and Optimization for Market-Based Interaction with Power Systems
Systems and Control.summary: The transition toward a renewable-dominated power system increases the flexibility needed to balance net-load variations. Industrial loads account for over 40% of the world's electricity consumption and can shift large amounts of demand through automated production scheduling. However, making industrial processes a dependable flexibility resource for power systems remains challenging because industrial process constraints are non-convex, equipment parameters are often private, and device-level models of thousands of facilities are too detailed for aggregator and power-system optimization. This dissertation builds computationally efficient methods for modeling and optimizing industrial flexibility for power-system interaction. Specifically, this dissertation uses smart meters as the external measurement interface and maps industrial process constraints into a concise flexibility space for power-system operation. The resulting chain of mechanism modeling, parameter identification, constraint dimension reduction, and optimal decision-making makes industrial-load participation computationally tractable while retaining precise process models for final execution.
Systems and Control.comment: PhD thesis, Tsinghua University, June 2026, 176 pages

Systems and Control.title: Predictive Neuromorphic Control of a Scanning Mirror System: An Event-Centric Framework
Systems and Control.summary: Organizing control around events can reduce sensing and actuation demands while directly linking control decisions to the occurrence and timing of desired system behaviors. This paper proposes a novel event-centric model predictive control (MPC) framework that unifies event sensing, event prediction, and event regulation. Events define the feedback information, prediction horizon, and event-timing objectives, placing them at the center of predictive control design. The framework is developed for a scanning mirror system equipped with a baseline neuromorphic controller composed of spiking neurons that supports sparse actuation. The control objective is to achieve prescribed zero-crossing times and a desired scanning range while minimizing the mechanical energy transferred between the actuator and the mirror. A sampling-based algorithm is presented to obtain suboptimal solutions of the event-centric MPC optimization problem without requiring an explicit event-to-event prediction model. By grounding predictive optimization in events, the proposed framework opens a new direction for MPC design and its integration with neuromorphic control.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages, submitted to ECC27, this work is the first, foundational work that proposes Event-Centric Model Predictive Control (EC-MPC), a framework that combines model predictive control and neuromorphic control. Philosophy: predicting events but not trajectories; regulation without calibration

Systems and Control.title: Safe and Scalable Minimax Adaptive Control of Positive Systems
Systems and Control.summary: This paper studies minimax adaptive control of positive linear systems with fixed unknown dynamics and nonnegative disturbances. We reformulate the problem by compressing the historical data into a vector and a positivity-induced consistency set containing the models compatible with the observations. Together with the physical state, these quantities form a sufficient information state and yield an exact reformulation as a standard minimax dynamic game. We allow the admissible input set to adapt to the current consistency set, ensuring positivity for every remaining feasible model. As inconsistent models are eliminated, the input set can expand, allowing less cautious control actions. For finite model sets, we derive an explicit solution to the Bellman inequality and construct a safe and stabilizing certainty-equivalence controller with robustness guarantees. The framework also accommodates structured classes of continuum model uncertainty whose consistency sets admit fixed, finite-dimensional representations, enabling scalable information-state updates.

Systems and Control.title: Distributionally Robust Indirect-Feedback Stochastic MPC with Gelbrich Ambiguity Sets
Systems and Control.summary: Stochastic model predictive control uses disturbance statistics to set safety margins. Errors in these statistics can invalidate the safety guarantees. This paper therefore describes the uncertainty in the disturbance mean and covariance by a prescribed Gelbrich ambiguity set. This contains distributions of any shape whose moments are close in the Gelbrich distance to the nominal values, including distributions with unbounded support. For linear time-invariant systems with additive disturbances, we build on the indirect feedback paradigm, propagate this moment uncertainty along the error dynamics, and obtain a closed-form constraint tightening that is computed offline. Robustness enters as a single additive term that grows with the size of the ambiguity set, so the online problem remains a quadratic program. Recursive feasibility and closed-loop satisfaction of conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) constraints hold for every disturbance distribution in the set. We illustrate the method on a linearized planar quadrotor.
Systems and Control.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the 2027 European Control Conference (ECC)

Systems and Control.title: Excitable Behaviours of a First-Order High-Pass Neuron Model
Systems and Control.summary: With the rise of neuromorphic technologies, simple and tunable neuron models are needed to analyse and design spiking systems. However, the simplest neuron models, e.g., Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) models, usually fail to capture the excitable behaviours of biological neurons. This could be a significant limitation, as excitability enables reliable spike timing under parametric uncertainties. Recently, a minimal excitable model, the so-called High-Pass Model (HPM), was introduced in neuroengineering. It simply consists of a static sigmoid with a high-pass filter in positive feedback. Given its novelty, it is still unclear how easily the HPM can be tuned, and how much of the excitable behaviours of a biophysical neuron it can reproduce. To address these questions, we investigate the tunability of a first-order HPM sub- and supra-rheobase, i.e., below and above the onset of the tonic spiking regime (where the neuron spikes periodically), and compare its behaviours with those of a simple Hodgkin-Huxley-type Conductance-Based Model (CBM). Below rheobase, both models fire spikes in response to transient inputs, including post-inhibitory rebound spikes. Above rheobase, an affine reparametrization of the input of the HPM suffices to fit its frequency-current curve to that of a CBM. The two models mostly differ near their respective rheobases, where the first-order HPM lacks bistability and spike latency. We suggest that modifying the frequency-selective element of the HPM may be sufficient to overcome this limitation. These results highlight the potential of the HPM as a fundamental computational primitive in neuromorphic, spike-based technologies.

Systems and Control.title: Delay-Certified Readiness Barriers for Overactuated Multirotor Allocation Without Lipschitz Constants
Systems and Control.summary: Overactuated multirotors can produce the same wrench with many rotor-speed combinations, some of which leave the vehicle unable to change its wrench quickly, e.g., to reject a gust. Readiness barriers keep this ability, the readiness, above a floor, but only in continuous time; with sampled commands and varying speed-controller delays, the available robustness bound covers less than one millisecond. We remove this limit by exploiting the structure of the problem: each rotor responds monotonically and in closed form to its own torque, so the speeds reachable under uncertain switching times lie in a cheaply computed box, and the lowest readiness over that box sits at a corner known in advance. This yields a Lipschitz-free test that a command keeps the readiness above its floor until the next sample, plus a fallback torque that keeps the vehicle on a certified plan. In hexarotor simulations with 2--40~ms delays and $\pm2$~ms jitter, the filter never violated the floor. At $10\pm2$~ms, it matched a delay-compensating predictor within the design envelope and cost 2--30\% more tracking error beyond it, where the predictor alone violated the floor in 2 to 16 of 16 missions. A tuned robust predictor was also safe with synchronous switching, but not with per-rotor jitter.
Systems and Control.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Systems and Control.title: An extended Perron-Frobenius operator filter for nonlinear state estimation
Systems and Control.summary: We propose an extended Perron--Frobenius Operator Filter (PFOF) for nonlinear state estimation. The method learns the Perron--Frobenius operator, an infinite-dimensional linear operator fully preserving properties of a nonlinear dynamical system, using the extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (eDMD). This enables us to explicitly account for non-Gaussian distributions exhibited by the nonlinear system within a linear-operator representation, while retaining the freedom to choose basis functions in eDMD. Through two numerical examples, we show that the extended PFOF achieves high computational efficiency and high estimation accuracy by exploiting the flexibility in the choice of basis functions in eDMD.
Systems and Control.comment: Submitted to Nonlinear Theory and Its Applications, IEICE (NOLTA), 9 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables

Systems and Control.title: Safety and Connectivity Certificates for Finite-Time Formation Transitions
Systems and Control.summary: Finite-time formation transitions are useful for coordinating multi-agent systems in time-critical missions, but convergence to a prescribed formation in finite time does not guarantee collision avoidance or communication connectivity during the transition. Existing approaches address finite-time coordination and safety-constrained formation control, yet explicit connections between disagreement during transitions, formation geometry, and coupling-gain selection need to be developed for certifying safe maneuvers. This paper develops a disagreement-based framework for certifying transient safety and connectivity during finite-time tracking of arbitrary prescribed formation trajectories. Local feedback guarantees exact finite-time tracking with a graph-independent settling-time bound, while a graph-dependent disagreement bound is used to derive sufficient geometric conditions for collision avoidance and connectivity preservation. These conditions further yield an offline coupling-gain selection rule based on the available geometric clearance. Numerical simulations illustrate the trade-off between convergence rate and control effort as the coupling gain increases. They also demonstrate the effectiveness and conservatism of the proposed certificates.

Systems and Control.title: Online Adaptive Clustering in Robust Distributed Model Predictive Control
Systems and Control.summary: This paper proposes a dynamic clustering framework for tube-based model predictive control (MPC) of coupled multi-agent systems. Agents within a cluster coordinate their dynamics explicitly, while couplings from agents outside the cluster are treated as bounded disturbances. For each admissible cluster, we construct a state-dependent mismatch measure from a robust upper bound on its predicted closed-loop cost and an optimistic, partition-independent lower bound. Combining this mismatch with a communication penalty enables online selection of the clustering topology, ranging from centralized to fully decentralized operation. The resulting switching controller is shown to preserve recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction, and to render the closed-loop system practically asymptotically stable. Furthermore, the mismatch provides an upper bound on the finite-horizon performance difference with respect to centralized MPC. An eight-agent spring--damper example illustrates how the controller adapts cooperation while maintaining performance close to centralized MPC with reduced communication.

Systems and Control.title: The Role of Insurance in Power-System Risk Management: A Critical Review
Systems and Control.summary: Modern power systems are becoming more renewable-rich, digitalized, and interconnected, making risk propagation and economic consequences increasingly complex. Physical mitigation remains the primary means of risk control, but technical and economic limits leave residual risk. Insurance can complement these measures by transferring associated economic losses and influencing power-system decisions through risk-responsive terms. Despite growing interest, the literature remains fragmented across power-system engineering, actuarial science, and risk finance. This review develops an integrated physical-financial perspective for reviewing insurance in power systems. It examines how power system risks generate residual economic losses and the conditions under which these losses can be insured and transferred. It then develops an actuarial framework for insured-loss assessment and pricing. Insurance-aware decision-making is synthesized through four coupling levels describing how financial protection interacts with power-system decisions. Further progress is constrained by weak physical-financial loss validation, incomplete representation of systemic and evolving portfolio risk, and limited empirical and actuarial grounding of insurance-decision feedback. Research priorities include stronger physical-financial data linkage, forward-looking portfolio assessment, multi-timescale decision feedback, and empirical validation. Addressing these priorities would help move power-system insurance from fragmented applications toward a more coherent approach to residual-risk management in future power systems.

Systems and Control.title: Towards Mode-Balanced Intersection Control: Hierarchical Coordination of Signal Timings, AV Trajectories, and Cyclist Speed Advice
Systems and Control.summary: Connected and automated vehicles (AVs) enable traffic signals and vehicle trajectories to be optimised jointly, but existing co-optimisation frameworks overlook cyclists, even though they share the same intersections. We propose a hierarchical framework that optimises traffic signal timings, AV trajectories, and cyclist speed advice to reduce travel times for both motorised vehicles and cyclists. The upper level jointly optimises signal timings and cyclist speed advice, while the lower level optimises AV trajectories and also updates cyclist speed advice obtained from the higher level at a higher frequency based on the resulting signal plan. The framework is evaluated in simulation under multiple demand profiles and optimisation parameter settings. Compared with optimized vehicle trajectories with fixed-time signal control, the proposed framework reduces mean travel times by 13.6\% for AVs and 12.3\% for cyclists. Adding cyclist speed advice further reduces mean cyclist waiting time by about 80\% relative to the same framework without speed advice. These results demonstrate substantial benefits for both modes of transport.

Systems and Control.title: Towards Design of Efficient Neuromorphic Controllers
Systems and Control.summary: One of the major sources of inspiration for neuromorphic engineering is the central nervous system, which is orders of magnitude more efficient than classical digital clock-based computers. Neuromorphic control aims at recreating this efficiency in control systems, combined with (formal) stability and performance guarantees. In our previous work [1], we have established formal guarantees for the emulation of static output feedback controllers implemented using integrate-and-fire neurons. In this paper, we investigate the ``efficiency'' of the resulting controllers in terms of sparse spiking activity. By changing the network structure of our original implementation, foregoing the unit gain assumption made in our previous work, we will establish that the chosen architecture of the spiking controller significantly affects its sparsity and discuss the implications of these observations for the efficient implementation of spiking controllers.

Systems and Control.title: Learn-To-Propagate: Distributionally Robust Motion Planning for Nonlinear Uncertain Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.

Systems and Control.title: Optimal Last-Iterate Bounds for Nonexpansive Stochastic Approximation
Systems and Control.summary: We establish last-iterate mean-square residual bounds for nonexpansive stochastic approximation (SA), or stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann (KM) iterations. In particular, we consider fixed-point mappings that are nonexpansive with respect to the Euclidean norm, and focus on polynomially decaying stepsizes. We study three conditions on the conditional second moment of the noise, and obtain bounds that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in each case. When it scales linearly with the squared residual, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1-ε})$ for any $ε>0$. In this case, for all considered stepsizes, our bounds match those of the noiseless KM iteration. When it is bounded by a constant, the best rate is $O(\log^2 k/\sqrt{k})$. When it scales affinely with the squared norm of the iterate, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1/2-ε})$, and the mean-square residual can diverge if the stepsizes are not square-summable. Thus, unlike for contractive SA, square-summable stepsizes are necessary for nonexpansive SA. We demonstrate how various algorithms with cocoercive maps, such as stochastic gradient descent, linear SA, and learning in cocoercive games, fit into our framework, and how the different noise conditions arise in each of them.

Systems and Control.title: Event-based analysis of neuromorphic feedback systems
Systems and Control.summary: This article investigates the existence and stability of periodic behavior arising in the feedback interconnection of neuromorphic systems, which evolve according to continuous dynamics but interact only through discrete events. Exploiting the event-driven nature of this interaction, each system is modeled by an operator that maps the history of events to the delay of its response. Building on the fading-memory properties of these operators, the article develops a small-gain result establishing the existence, uniqueness, and robustness of periodic one-to-one rhythms.

Systems and Control.title: Explicit MPC for the constrained zonotope case with low-rank matrix updates
Systems and Control.summary: Solving the explicit Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem requires enumerating all critical regions and their associated feedback laws, a task that scales exponentially with the system dimension and the prediction horizon, as well. When the problem's constraints are boxes or zonotopes, the feasible domain admits a compact constrained-zonotope representation. Building on this insight, we exploit the geometric properties of the equivalent constrained-zonotope reformulation to accelerate the computation of the explicit solution. Specifically, we formulate the multi-parametric problem in the lifted generator space and solve it using second-order optimality conditions, employ low-rank matrix updates to reduce computation time, and introduce an analytic enumeration of candidate active sets that yields the explicit solution in tree form.

Systems and Control.title: Neuromodulation Through Intrinsic Noise
Systems and Control.summary: Neuromodulation, the modulation of excitability through the regulation of neuronal parameters, is a key tool in neuromorphic control design. This paper investigates how spiking excitability can be modulated by intrinsic noise. Focusing on a simplified memristive neuron model, we show that intrinsic noise plays distinct functional roles depending on the feedback pathways: Intrinsic noise in the fast excitatory feedback shapes the nature of excitability and modulates the sensitivity of the neuron to external/internal stimuli, whereas that in the slow inhibitory feedback provides internal stimuli that can trigger stochastic spiking. We expect these findings to guide the design of neuromorphic systems that harness intrinsic noise to exploit beneficial stochastic phenomena, such as stochastic resonance.

Systems and Control.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
Systems and Control.summary: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

Systems and Control.title: Formal Synthesis of Robust Koopman-Model Predictive Control: A Case Study in AC-DC Power Conversion
Systems and Control.summary: This letter proposes a formal synthesis of Robust Koopman-Model Predictive Control (RK-MPC), a novel data-driven approach to formal synthesis of systems with nonlinear dynamics. We formulate a novel optimization problem for RK-MPC by incorporating specifications described by Signal Temporal Logic and prove its closed-loop performance. Effectiveness of the proposed RK-MPC is evaluated by applying it to the reliable design of an AC-DC power converter.

Systems and Control.title: Continuous-Time Modeling of Destination-Constrained Dynamic Systems via Doob's $h$-Transform
Systems and Control.summary: Existing work on modeling destination-constrained dynamic systems has mainly focused on discrete-time formulations with linear destination constraints or Gaussian destination distributions. Since practical systems are more naturally modeled in continuous time and often subject to nonlinear/non-Gaussian constraints/distributions, this paper proposes a unified measure-transformation framework for continuous-time modeling of systems subject to deterministic or distributional constraints on a nonlinear function of the terminal state. The framework starts from an unconstrained Itô stochastic differential equation, typically derived from physical laws to describe the system's forward evolution without destination information, and takes its induced path measure as unconstrained measure. Doob's $h$-transform is employed to transform this measure into a constrained path measure incorporating destination information through an injected drift. The resulting system is proved to satisfy the constraints while preserving the laws of the unconstrained state process conditioned on the destination information. The transition density is derived, and the path measure of the distributionally constrained system is proved to uniquely minimize Kullback--Leibler divergence from the unconstrained path measure among those satisfying the same distributional constraint. Its injected drift is further shown to converge pointwise to that of the deterministically constrained system as the destination distribution shrinks to the prespecified value. For linear time-varying unconstrained systems, a simplified form of the constrained systems is derived in terms of the conditional expectation of the terminal state, leading to the development of trajectory-generation algorithms. Numerical simulations evaluate the proposed framework under both types of destination constraints.

Systems and Control.title: Input-to-State Safety and Small-Gain Theorems for Large-Scale Nonlinear Systems
Systems and Control.summary: This paper studies the safety verification problem for a general class of large-scale systems characterized by multiple safety indicator functions. Each safety indicator function satisfies a trajectory-based input-to-state safety (ISSf) estimate that provides a lower bound on its value along system trajectories in terms of the initial state, external inputs, and the other safety indicator functions, whose influence is quantified by continuous and nondecreasing gain functions. Within this framework, we establish a safety-oriented small-gain theorem and its corresponding corollaries that enable compositional and scalable safety verification of the interconnected system, provided that the interconnection gain functions satisfy a small-gain condition on the negative real axis. This condition concerns only the neighborhood of the safety boundary, thereby facilitating the application of our results to safety verification of multi-agent systems under distributed control. Our proof combines small-gain techniques with the lower-bound structure of ISSf estimates and develops an inductive comparison argument that establishes the ISSf property for the overall system throughout the maximal interval of existence. As an application, we establish robust safety for the natural distributed "half-spring" controller, theoretically supporting the computationally efficient and inspiring approach to safety-critical control of multi-agent systems in the presence of obstacles and external disturbances.

Systems and Control.title: Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Battery-Assisted Grid-Import Smoothing in AI Data Centers
Systems and Control.summary: Rapid AI data-center power fluctuations challenge grid integration. Sustained grid-import smoothing requires allocating limited battery power and energy under uncertain demand. We formulate risk-aware BESS scheduling that coordinates advance reserve commitments and demand-responsive dispatch, accounting for operating costs, grid-ramp penalties, and their conditional value-at-risk. We develop battery scheduling decision-focused learning (BS-DFL) with a constraint-aware neural optimization layer trained directly from this objective without optimal-solution labels. The trained layer is then frozen to guide demand-predictor learning through scheduling costs and ramping risk, enabling solver-free rolling-horizon scheduling. In a 10,000-minute simulation using loads derived from measured AI workloads, BS-DFL reduces mean absolute minute-to-minute grid-import changes by 71.70% and total scheduling cost by 18.01% relative to an MSE-trained predictor coupled with a mixed-integer linear programming solver, with an average decision time of 18.77 ms.

Systems and Control.title: Aeroelastically Constrained Optimal Path Planning of a Fixed-Wing Airborne Wind Energy System
Systems and Control.summary: Multi-megawatt fixed-wing airborne wind energy systems (AWES) use an aircraft with large, slender wings that deform over the pumping cycle. To harvest maximum energy, the cycle is usually designed by means of dedicated reference trajectory optimization routines. It is well known that such routines rely heavily on the system model and that close alignment between the model and the physical system is required for the results to hold in practice. Nevertheless, the wing is usually treated as rigid and structural limits are respected indirectly through upper bounding of states and inputs. In this work, we directly enforce bounds on the elastic deflection and twist of the wing in the power-maximizing periodic optimal control problem. To that end, we model the wing by root-clamped modes, loaded by strip-theory aerodynamics and by the gravitational and inertial loads of the manoeuvring aircraft. To keep the problem tractable, the modal dynamics are replaced by their quasi-static equilibrium, which enters every discretization interval as algebraic constraints. For a multi-megawatt reference aircraft, the elastic twist near the wing tips reaches $1.03^\circ$ along the optimal rigid-wing trajectory. With a twist limit of $0.6^\circ$, the optimal trajectory delivers $31\,\%$ less mean power than the rigid-wing one, mainly through a lower tether tension during reel-out. Rigid-wing trajectory optimization can thus overestimate the power that the wing limits permit. Forward simulations that retain the modal dynamics demonstrate that the quasi-static deflection and twist deviate from the dynamic ones by less than $2\,\%$ of their limits. This work shows that elastic deformation can be accounted for in the trajectory optimization and that, depending on the wing limits, it can strongly reduce the achievable power.

Systems and Control.title: Priority-Aware Firm and Flexible Capacity Quantification for Large-Load Interconnection
Systems and Control.summary: We study how to unlock existing transmission capacity to accelerate large-load interconnection under differentiated quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. We establish an efficient framework to quantify firm and flexible hosting capacities and assess marginal values of grid upgrades. Specifically, we define multiple flexible capacity tiers with differentiated QoS limits and design a two-layer priority rule to allocate curtailment among tiers. We then formulate a mixed-integer chance-constrained model to jointly quantify firm and flexible capacities under QoS and priority constraints. To improve computational efficiency, we derive an equivalent aggregate formulation that eliminates individual curtailment variables and priority binaries without changing the feasible capacity set. Numerical results show the computational advantage of aggregation. Multi-tier flexible capacity increases total admitted capacity by 45.0\% over the firm-only hosting capacity.

Systems and Control.title: Efficient control of multi-agent robust MDPs through tensor trees
Systems and Control.summary: This paper introduces a tensor-based framework for controller synthesis of stochastic multi-agent systems under temporal logic specifications that couple the agents, such as one agent reaching its goal only after another agent has reached its own. The agents are modeled as robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs), whose transition probabilities are only known to lie in an ambiguity set, for instance due to abstraction errors, learned models, or uncertain parameters. We show that the decoupled nature of the ambiguity sets allows one to decompose the computation of a lower bound on the satisfaction probabilities into per-agent factors, so that only the per-agent ambiguity sets need to be stored. This leads to improved memory complexity compared to monolithic approaches. We compare our approach with state-of-the-art approaches based on approximate simulation relations and with interval MDP abstractions. On a four-agent ordered reach-avoid benchmark, our approach certifies a lower bound twice as high as the simulation relation- based approach with 20 times less memory, and needs about 200 times less memory than the interval MDP abstraction, even at a resolution with about a million times more joint cells.

Systems and Control.title: Discounted MPC and infinite-horizon optimal control under plant-model mismatch: Stability and suboptimality
Systems and Control.summary: We study the robustness to plant-model mismatch of nonlinear systems in closed loop with (discounted) optimal controllers designed for a nominal model, with quadratic stage costs across finite and infinite horizons. By combining Lyapunov analysis with a unifying relaxed dynamic programming framework, we establish conditions that guarantee robust stability alongside improved suboptimality bounds compared to existing literature. A key step in our analysis is proving that stability counteracts time-accumulated error growth due to plant-model mismatch, yielding robustness bounds that hold uniformly across all prediction horizons.

Systems and Control.title: Toward Pseudorange-Based PNT with Starlink: A Mock Fused LEO GNSS Implementation
Systems and Control.summary:
We present experimental results from Starlink for pseudorange-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), emulating a system that fuses a primary communications mission with a secondary low-Earth orbit (LEO) PNT mission. Legacy global navigation satellite system (GNSS) constellations faceinherent vulnerabilities and signal limitations, prompting growing interest in
  broadband LEO constellations---such as SpaceX's Starlink---for resilient PNT. However, opportunistic use of stand-alone Starlink signals fails to achieve
  GNSS-competitive accuracy due to frame timing irregularities and reliance on uncorrected poor-quality publicly available ephemeris data. To overcome these limitations, we present a mock
  implementation of a fused LEO GNSS architecture. Our method extracts time-of-arrival observables from live Starlink Ku-band downlinks and pairs them with high-fidelity, beam-specific orbit and clock models distributed as if provided natively by the constellation operator. In a field campaign, and despite constraints imposed by consumer-grade receiver hardware, the method
  yields 95% error bounds of 2.33 m horizontally (semi-major axis), 3.37 m vertically, and 11.19 ns in timing, with the actual solution errors falling well within these bounds.

Systems and Control.title: Safe Approximate Nonlinear Model Predictive Control Without Expert Demonstrations
Systems and Control.summary: Repeated online optimization makes nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) computationally demanding for real-time applications. Neural approximations reduce this cost but often require large datasets of expert NMPC solutions. We introduce Sequential Approximate MPC (Seq-AMPC), a label-free recurrent framework that generates complete control sequences along predicted trajectories using parameters shared across the prediction horizon. The policy is trained directly through known dynamics with losses for control cost, constraint satisfaction, and a cost-decrease condition aligned with a feasible-backup safety filter. Building on this filter, we introduce a stage-cost-dependent acceptance tolerance that preserves recursive feasibility, constraint satisfaction, and asymptotic convergence under nominal MPC assumptions, independently of neural approximation error. We further derive Hoeffding-based finite-sample bounds for the expected fraction of applied proposals and closed-loop cost discrepancy relative to NMPC. We evaluate Seq-AMPC on a quadcopter, chain of masses, obstacle-avoidance vehicle, and robotic manipulator, comparing recurrent and feedforward policies under label-free and imitation training. Across four benchmarks, training takes 0.2-1.7 GPU hours per policy without expert control labels. The filtered controller applies 97.2-99.1% of neural proposals and achieves mean closed-loop cost ratios within 0.3% of NMPC on jointly completed episodes. Tests with suboptimal feasible initial plans further demonstrate the benefit of neural replanning.

Systems and Control.title: Metamorphic testing of learned AC optimal power flow surrogates reveals representation dependence
Systems and Control.summary: Evaluating a learned AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF) surrogate on one grid serialization cannot show whether its accuracy depends on that encoding. We test this dependence with thirteen metamorphic relations, each specifying when a transformation is valid and how to compare its outputs. Our audit covers 17 model and pipeline configurations: two released trained checkpoints and 15 random-weight architecture or mechanism controls. Every configuration violates at least six relations, even at reporting tolerances ten times tighter or looser. For GridSFM-Open v1.1, source inspection and intermediate-tensor interventions point to an indexing bug and three noncanonical or numerically unstable preprocessing choices; a repaired checkpoint remains untested. In a separate case500 training experiment, augmentation lowers transformed-view error in three of four models and median discrepancy and constraint-violation P95 in all four. These benefits depend on the training protocol: some relations worsen, and every evaluated prediction remains AC infeasible. A GPU/CPU eigensolver mismatch accounts for most of the large raw-Laplacian-baseline gain. We recommend reporting representation consistency alongside accuracy, feasibility, and cost. These results establish neither deployment readiness nor universal invariance.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshops on (i) Trustworthy AI Evaluation, (ii) AI Foundations for Power Grids, (iii) Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning, (iv) Sim2Science, and (v) Representations for the Physical Sciences

Systems and Control.title: An Accurate Modulation-Assisted Method for Phasor Estimation Under Decaying DC Offsets
Systems and Control.summary: Decaying DC (DDC) offsets severely compromise the accurate estimation of current phasors immediately following power grid fault occurrence. Consequently, conventional full-cycle discrete Fourier transform (FCDFT) algorithms experience decaying oscillatory magnitude errors, potentially causing distance relays to malfunction. This paper introduces a modulation-assisted technique designed to precisely eliminate the DDC components from fault current signals. By multiplying the fault signal with a high-frequency carrier and applying consecutive sliding Fourier projections, the proposed method effectively isolates the DDC signal while entirely rejecting higher-order harmonic interference. It utilizes a direct algebraic solution derived from a robust forward-difference operation across just three sequential projections to estimate and extract the DDC parameters. Furthermore, the algorithm seamlessly processes both single and multiple DDC components by dynamically tracking them as one equivalent first-order mode. Extensive evaluations are conducted to validate the proposed method accuracy. The proposed algorithm limits the maximum overshoot (MO) to 0.62% (0.59% for $k \geq 8$) for the evaluated DDC cases, and to 2.47% (0.95% at 20 dB for $k = 8$) under noisy conditions.

Systems and Control.title: Incremental Input-to-State Stabilization of Partially Unknown Control-Affine Systems within Prescribed Safe Sets
Systems and Control.summary: Incremental input-to-state stability ($δ$-ISS) guarantees that the trajectories of a system converge towards one another, up to a gain on the difference of their inputs. Some existing learning-based designs that combine incremental stability with safety achieve only incremental input-to-state practical stability, whose non-vanishing offset can make the guarantee conservative. We consider control-affine systems with a known, full-row-rank input matrix and an unknown drift learned using Gaussian process regression. The prescribed safe set is a superlevel set of a smooth function satisfying a radial condition that ensures a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^n$ and it need not contain any equilibrium of the uncontrolled system. Using this transformation, we design a smooth feedback law and derive sufficient conditions that, under the stated learning assumptions, guarantee with high probability both forward invariance of a compact subset of the safe set and $δ$-ISS on that subset. The incremental estimate uses the distance induced by the transformation and contains no practical offset. Simulations on a Van der Pol oscillator and a Lotka-Volterra system illustrate the proposed approach.

Systems and Control.title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight
Systems and Control.summary: Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic. The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change. This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms. Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and (3) the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass. The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, October 2026

Systems and Control.title: Data-Driven Robust Dynamic Wireless Charging Lane Planning with Tunable Profit--Risk Trade-off and Modified User Equilibrium
Systems and Control.summary: Dynamic wireless charging (DWC) has attracted increasing attention as a complement to conventional plug-in charging for electric vehicles (EVs). However, existing planning methods for dynamic wireless charging lanes (DWCLs) overlook realistic EV routing and charging behavior and lack explicit out-of-sample risk control under traffic-demand and renewable-energy uncertainties. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a data-driven two-stage robust planning framework that coordinates DWCL deployment with the operation of coupled traffic--power networks (CTPNs). A data-driven uncertainty set is constructed from joint historical scenarios to preserve spatio-temporal correlations without imposing parametric distributional assumptions. A modified user-equilibrium (MUE) model is proposed to capture realistic EV routing and charging behavior by incorporating state-of-charge (SoC) dynamics and endogenous charging decisions. The resulting two-stage robust model with mixed-integer recourse is reformulated as an equivalent single-stage scenario-approach problem and solved using a customized nested column-and-constraint generation algorithm. An \textit{a posteriori} feasibility guarantee is established to quantify out-of-sample risk. Based on this guarantee, the scenario set is iteratively enriched to meet a prescribed risk tolerance. Case studies on a 69-node power distribution network and a 24-node traffic network demonstrate that the proposed MUE model prevents overinvestment in DWCLs, while the proposed risk-quantification procedure enables a tunable profit--risk trade-off.

Systems and Control.title: Impact of Reduced-Order Modelling on Sum-of-Squares Region-of-Attraction Certification for Grid-Forming and Grid-Following Converters
Systems and Control.summary: With the increasing penetration of power-electronic equipment, the transient stability of grid-forming (GFM) and grid-following (GFL) converters is increasingly characterized through the region of attraction (ROA) of the post-fault equilibrium. Sum-of-squares (SOS) programming yields certified inner approximations of the ROA, yet its computational cost grows rapidly with system order. Reduced-order models are therefore widely used to reduce computational cost and, more importantly, to enable analytical investigation. However, ROA analyses based on these models often assume that reproducing the converter's transient response, or retaining more dynamics in the correct time-frame, is sufficient to preserve the ROA of the full-order system. Using time-domain ODE simulations as a reference, the SOS-based ROA of each reduced-order GFM and GFL model is assessed against both its own simulated ROA and that of the corresponding full-order model, thereby separating SOS-induced conservativeness from model-order-induced ROA distortion. The results indicate that increasing reduced-order model complexity does not necessarily improve SOS-based ROA fidelity. In the cases examined, more complex reduced-order models yield lower SOS coverage of the full-order reference ROA, despite closer ODE-boundary agreement in some regions. Model selection should therefore consider both full-order ROA fidelity and certified coverage of the practical operating range, rather than model complexity alone.

Systems and Control.title: Complete Decentralization of Wave Equation Control on a Compact Domain
Systems and Control.summary: A feedback control policy is completely decentralized if the actuation signal at each location in space can be computed based only on state information from that location. For systems equipped with large numbers of spatially distributed sensors and actuators, completely decentralized controllers are desirable since they can be implemented in a communication and computation efficient manner, but generally perform worse than centralized counterparts. However, through a case study of Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) design for wave dynamics on a compact spatial domain, we show that careful design of system parameters to satisfy certain conditions causes a decentralized control policy to perform as well as any centralized policy. We then propose a spatially filtered $H_2$ norm to show that satisfying these conditions does not inherently degrade achievable closed-loop system performance, enabling simultaneous realization of both desirable performance and communication/computation efficiency via system-control co-design. Additional robustness analysis characterizes a range of system parameters such that the system interconnected with a decentralized controller maintains stability and near-optimal performance. Although our framework is derived for spatially continuous dynamics, we demonstrate that this theory can be leveraged to derive results for decentralization in finite-dimensional settings through a damped mass-spring example.
Systems and Control.comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, submitted to SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization

Systems and Control.title: Residual-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Network KKL Observers with Input-to-State Stability Guarantees
Systems and Control.summary: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) Kazantzis--Kravaris--Luenberger (KKL) observers require an approximate solution to a KKL partial differential equation (PDE) and an approximate inverse of this solution. Either approximation can leave a nonzero estimation bias even without measurement noise. In this paper, we remove both errors from the implemented observer by construction. We build an encoder containing an explicitly invertible neural map. Its closed-form inverse provides the internal state reconstruction used to evaluate the learned KKL residual and correct the latent dynamics. This construction makes the synchronization manifold exactly invariant for every value of the network weights. Based on contraction of the residual-corrected observer dynamics, we prove an input-to-state stability (ISS) result for the implemented error dynamics with respect to measurement noise. A direct consequence is that the estimation error converges exponentially to zero in the noise-free setting. We provide two numerical examples, the Van der Pol oscillator and the chaotic Lorenz system, in which the residual-corrected observers achieve exact noise-free convergence and improved error responses compared with released PINN--KKL baselines.

Systems and Control.title: The Phantom of Davis-Wielandt Shell: A Unified Perspective for Graphical Stability Analysis of MIMO LTI Systems
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents a unified perspective based on Davis-Wielandt (DW) shell of linear subspaces for graphical stability analysis of multi-input and multi-output linear time-invariant feedback systems. Connections between DW shells and various graphical representations, as well as gain and phase measures, are established through an intuitive geometric perspective. We establish a strict DW separation theorem which characterizes subspace separation and provides a basis for comparing the implications and relative conservatism of graphical separation conditions. In particular, we introduce the rotated scaled relative graph ($θ$-SRG) and show that its separation is equivalent to DW shell separation and is therefore the least conservative among all the graphical conditions considered. We derive pointwise and boundary stability conditions for bi-component feedback interconnections and establish a weak DW separation result that relaxes the strict separation requirement at open-loop poles. We also discuss applications to robust stability analysis and provide a numerical example illustrating how DW shells serve as a more reliable robustness indicator.

Systems and Control.title: A Global Routing Method for Electronic Circuit Design Integrating Flow Matching and Constrained A*
Systems and Control.summary: Global routing is a fundamental issue in the design of electronic circuits, as it directly relates to the efficiency, reliability, and compactness of the overall layout of integrated systems. As the demand for higher functionality and reliability within a limited chip area increases, the importance of routing as a design consideration has never been greater. Efficient global routing optimization techniques are therefore required to connect all pins with minimal wirelength (WL), while avoiding congestion and interference across multiple nets within the design space. As the number of nets to be routed increases, global routing inherently suffers from a combinatorial explosion in the design space, making it increasingly difficult to obtain feasible solutions. In this paper, we focus on solving constrained global routing problems based on a heuristic A*-based framework. Based on this concept, a hybrid approach is proposed by integrating constrained A* with flow matching (FM). The method utilizes FM to construct a global cost map that captures routing tendencies across the design space, which is then used to guide the constrained A* search process. This enables efficient exploration of the solution space while satisfying routing constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable WL and via usage to baseline methods while maintaining constraint satisfaction across a wide range of scenarios. Notably, the framework shows strong capability in solving complex routing instances that are difficult to handle using conventional approaches. Additionally, the method shows robust generalization performance across different problem sizes and net configurations.

Systems and Control.title: Benign Geometry and Distributional Robustness of $\mathcal{H}_2$ Synthesis
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we study standard and distributionally robust $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis problem of a stabilizing state-feedback controller for discrete-time linear time-invariant systems. Without requiring a nonsingular disturbance controllability Gramian or a positive-definite control penalty, we establish that stationarity of a stabilizing gain in standard $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis is equivalent to global optimality and derive an exact Pythagorean identity for the performance difference. We then generalize the $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis problem by considering i.i.d. disturbances with zero mean and uniformly bounded second moments, and extend the stationarity-optimality equivalence to the corresponding distributionally robust $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis. Moreover, we show that every standard $\mathcal{H}_2$-optimal gain is simultaneously optimal for every such distributionally robust problem. Finally, we specialize the framework to Frobenius, Kullback--Leibler, and Wasserstein-2 ambiguity sets and obtain explicit characterizations of their worst-case covariances, which, in turn, provide performance certificates for a common optimal controller.

Systems and Control.title: An Inductively Assisted N :1 Switched-Capacitor Ladder Converter
Systems and Control.summary: This paper proposes an inductively assisted N:1 switched-capacitor ladder buck (D-SCLB) converter that replaces the output-side switch in the bottom half-bridge of an N:1 SCLB with a small inductor placed in parallel with the ladder capacitors during the demagnetization phase. The flying capacitors share the load current delivery, lowering the average inductor current to (1-M)Iout and enabling continuous regulation with M=D/(N-1+D). A closed-form output-impedance model, valid for arbitrary N under both optimal and uniform switch sizing, is derived and compared against SC, SCLB, FCMC, and DPSC topologies. For a 4:1 48V-to-PoL design, the D-SCLB reduces the average inductor current by up to 20% and improves the equivalent output impedance by up to 30% relative to the SCLB. Two hardware prototypes on a low-cost two-layer PCB achieve a peak efficiency of 96.2%, with the D-SCLB using 49% smaller inductor volume than the SCLB at comparable efficiency. Model predictions agree with measurements to within 1.5% under heavy load.

Systems and Control.title: Policy Library CBF: Finite-Horizon Safety at Runtime via Parallel Rollouts
Systems and Control.summary: Safety-critical autonomy in unstructured environments poses significant challenges for online safety certification under evolving constraints, particularly when a single backup policy is not effective across operating conditions. We propose the Policy Library Control Barrier Function (PL-CBF), a runtime safety filter that evaluates a library of fallback policies via parallel finite-horizon rollouts. Among policies with constraint-satisfying rollouts and feasible CBF constraints, PL-CBF selects the policy maximizing the volume of its admissible control set and solves a single quadratic program to minimally modify the nominal input within that constrained input set. Using a finite-horizon language metric over closed-loop behaviors, we characterize when a finite policy library contains a constraint-satisfying rollout. Five simulation studies cover indoor robot navigation with a double-integrator model (4 states), highway driving under abrupt friction changes with a nonlinear vehicle model (8 states), and quadrotor flight control among dynamic obstacles (12 states), demonstrating improved safety performance compared with the evaluated baselines while maintaining millisecond-scale mean computation times. Hardware experiments on a mobile robot among moving pedestrians and a custom-built quadrotor among dynamic obstacles demonstrate real-time operation of PL-CBF.

Systems and Control.title: U.S. Data Center Growth Through 2030: A Critical Review of Grid Adequacy and Transmission Expansion Planning
Systems and Control.summary: The growth of large data centers raises questions about both supply adequacy and the suitability of load representations used in connection studies. This paper critically reviews the U.S. demand, generation, and transmission outlook through 2030 and examines the implications for transmission expansion planning (TEP). Comparison of public forecasts highlights distinctions among annual average demand, peak demand, and grid connection capacity. National generating-capacity totals cannot establish a dependable surplus because resource availability, regional adequacy, transmission constraints, and project timing determine supply capability. Recent grid events and published dynamic studies demonstrate that faults can trigger substantial data-center transfers to backup supply, followed by delayed or coordinated demand recovery. These behaviors require appropriate representation within the conventional planning framework, alongside assessment of the requested maximum grid import. The selected literature reveals limited integration of validated data-center dynamic models into the technical screening and economic comparison of expansion alternatives. The review identifies the need to establish whether fault response and recovery change feasible connection capacity, required reinforcement, or the preferred transmission investment.

Systems and Control.title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
Systems and Control.summary: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.

Systems and Control.title: A Three-Stage Unsupervised Online Physics-Informed Neural Network for Microgrid Optimal Power Flow
Systems and Control.summary: Optimal allocation of generators is a key challenge in power systems to achieve economical dispatch while satisfying operational constraints. Conventional optimization techniques can be computationally expensive, limiting their applicability in real-time environments, and neural networks often require offline retraining under new operating conditions. This paper proposes a three-stage unsupervised online physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for optimal power flow (OPF). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework satisfies load demand and system constraints while achieving a $43,665 lower operating cost than fmincon-based optimization under the same operating conditions. The training process analysis further demonstrate the framework's ability to adapt its parameters online to variations in load demand and renewable generation in real time.

Systems and Control.title: On-Device Robotic Planning: Eliminating Inference Redundancy for Efficient Decision-Making
Systems and Control.summary: Reasoning-based robotic policies using large language and vision-language models achieve strong semantic planning capabilities but mostly suffer from a high inference latency that limits practical real-time deployment. In this work, we observe that robotic reasoning workloads contain substantial temporal redundancy, where consecutive observations frequently produce identical actions and subgoals. Based on this insight, we present REIS, a human cognition inspired robotic decision-making framework that minimizes unnecessary reasoning while preserving semantic adaptability. REIS combines lightweight scene gating, KV-steered affordance routing, and deliberative reasoning to accelerate robotic control under embodied constraints. Experiments on ALFRED, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that REIS significantly suppresses reasoning overhead while maintaining competitive task performance

Systems and Control.title: Human-on-the-Loop Distributed Control of Grid-Interactive Buildings for Demand Response Participation
Systems and Control.summary: This paper proposes a human-on-the-loop distributed consensus control approach for demand-side management across multiple buildings. Specifically, a novel framework is introduced in which a human acts as the non-autonomous leader in consensus control of cooperative buildings participating in demand response programs. In this system, the facility manager in the facility building serves as the leader, determining the participation level of cooperative buildings in demand response events while simultaneously considering occupants' comfort. Cooperative buildings align their responses with the facility management building, despite lacking direct access to the facility manager's decisions, and this raises two coupled challenges: The manager's actions act as an unknown input to the leader, and the consensus protocol requires a state that cannot be measured. Because the input is unknown, the necessary observer should be an unknown-input observer to guarantee the performance, and the observer-matching condition required by conventional linear designs does not hold for this system. A human-on-the-loop leader-follower consensus protocol is introduced to manage energy use and balance thermal comfort, together with a nonlinear unknown-input sliding-mode observer that reconstructs the local consensus error in finite time without requiring the mentioned condition. Under exact measurements, continuous-time dynamics, and an admissible initial state, a componentwise certificate guarantees bounded tracking and bounds on ramp rate, comfort, and power when the leader power and the ambient temperature remain within prescribed limits. Simulation results validate the approach, demonstrating its ability to achieve consensus, maintain system performance, and enhance the adaptability of power grid operations under various demand response scenarios.

Systems and Control.title: Optimizing Bidding Curves for Renewable Energy in Two-Settlement Electricity Markets
Systems and Control.summary: Coordination of day-ahead and real-time electricity markets is imperative for cost-effective electricity supply and also to provide efficient incentives for the energy transition. Although stochastic market designs feature the least-cost coordination, they are incompatible with current deterministic markets. This paper proposes a new approach for compatible coordination in two-settlement markets based on benchmark bidding curves for variable renewable energy. These curves are optimized based on a bilevel optimization problem, anticipating per-scenario responses of deterministic market-clearing problems and ultimately minimizing the expected cost across day-ahead and real-time markets. Although the general bilevel model is challenging to solve, we theoretically prove that a single-segment bidding curve with a zero bidding price is sufficient to achieve system optimality if the marginal cost of variable renewable energy is zero, thus addressing the computational challenge. In practice, variable renewable energy producers can be allowed to bid multi-segment curves with non-zero prices. We test the bilevel framework for both single- and multiple-segment bidding curves under the assumption of fixed bidding prices.
