Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Competition Versus Complexity in Multiple-Selection Prophet Inequalities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Competition complexity formalizes a compelling intuition: rather than refining the mechanism, how much additional competition is sufficient for a simple mechanism to compete with an optimal one? We begin the study of this question in multi-unit pricing for welfare maximization using prophet inequalities. An online decision-maker observes $m \geq k$ nonnegative values drawn independently from a known distribution, may select up to $k$ of them, and aims to maximize the expected sum of selected values. The benchmark is a prophet who observes a sequence of length $n \geq k$ and selects the $k$ largest values. We focus on the widely adopted class of single-threshold algorithms and fully characterize their $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity. Notably, our results reveal a sharp competition-induced phase transition: in the absence of competition, single-threshold algorithms are fundamentally limited to a $1-1/\sqrt{2kπ}$ fraction of the prophet value, whereas even a $1\%$ multiplicative increase beyond $n$ observations suffices to achieve a $1-\exp(-Θ(k))$ fraction. Another notable result happens when $k=1$: we show that the $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity is exactly $\ln(1/\varepsilon)$, fully resolving an open question by Brustle et al. [Math. Oper. Res. 2024]. Our analysis is based on infinite-dimensional linear programming and duality arguments.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Complexity of Computing a Competitive Equilibrium in Fisher Markets with Chores
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the complexity of computing competitive equilibria in Fisher markets with divisible chores and positive rational disutility coefficients and earning requirements. For linear disutilities, we prove that exact equilibrium computation is CLS-complete. In particular, the problem remains CLS-hard even when the earning requirements are binary in $1$ and $2^k$, where $k$ is an integer. We prove hardness by encoding the first-order conditions of a box-constrained quadratic program in equilibrium prices and earning flows, using a compact minimum-cost flow construction. For convex constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) disutilities, exact equilibrium prices may be irrational. We formulate the problem of finite-precision equilibrium price computation, in which we seek rational prices with a certified market clearing error at most a given rational tolerance encoded in binary. We prove that this problem is CLS-complete for every fixed rational exponent $ρ>1$. To prove this hardness, we encode a quartic polynomial through the fourth-order expansion of the CES price potential function corresponding to the Eisenberg-Gale (EG) dual program, and show that every sufficiently accurate approximate equilibrium of the constructed market lies near uniform prices. Additionally, we also identify a tractable special case of chores Fisher markets. In particular, we provide a strongly polynomial algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in linear markets whose disutility matrix has rank at most two and earning requirements are arbitrary positive rationals. For $n$ agents and $m$ chores, the algorithm uses $O(nm(n+m))$ rational arithmetic operations and comparisons, with polynomial intermediate encoding length.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Large-Market Discipline in Combinatorial Double Auctions: No Recombination, Bundle Selection, and Complementarities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Licences can forbid assembling bundles from several sellers or splitting them among buyers, a restriction we call No Recombination. We study its welfare cost in a double auction as the number of traders on each side of the market grows. We ask whether that cost vanishes as a share of welfare, as the gain from misreporting does with a single good. With two goods and Gaussian shocks, consider the prices that would prevail under free recombination. As the market grows, the loss as a share of optimal welfare vanishes if and only if expected demand for the two-good bundle equals expected supply of whole bundles at those prices. Otherwise the loss persists. In our market, sellers can never gain by misreporting. With two goods, buyers who commit to bidding their values plus fixed margins misreport in symmetric equilibria by amounts that vanish as the market grows. Under these conditions, in large markets No Recombination outweighs strategic bidding as a source of loss.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 107 pages, including a 55-page online appendix

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Complexity of Strong Popularity in Hedonic Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
In a hedonic game, agents are partitioned into coalitions and have preferences over the coalitions they may join. A partition is called strongly popular if it strictly beats every other partition in a majority vote among the agents.
  We study the complexity of determining the existence of strongly popular partitions in two fundamental classes of hedonic games: additively separable and fractional hedonic games (ASHGs and FHGs), where agents' utilities are determined, respectively, by the sum and average of their valuations for the members of their coalitions.
  We prove that this problem is PCW-complete for ASHGs and for FHGs even with non-negative valuations, where PCW is a subclass of $Σ^P_2$ associated with unambiguous problems (which have at most one witness), recently introduced by Gilboa et al. (2025). These are the first natural complete problems for PCW, in the sense that their formulations do not involve arbitrary Boolean circuits. Our results resolve open problems posed by Brandt and Bullinger (JAIR 2022) and Bullinger and Gilboa (IJCAI 2025). The two reductions employ substantially different techniques, reflecting both the distinct utility models and the stringent non-negativity constraint in FHGs.
  Furthermore, in contrast with FHGs, we show that in ASHGs restricting valuations to be non-negative makes the problem polynomial-time solvable.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: This version includes additional results: Theorems 1.2 and 1.3. A preliminary version of Theorem 1.1 in this paper appeared as part of earlier versions of arXiv:2510.19084, when the two works formed a single manuscript

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Welfare in Envy-free Contracts: When Agents Have Sparse Interests
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study welfare maximization under envy-free contracts, where a principal assigns tasks and offers success-contingent payments to heterogeneous agents with hidden effort. For unit-demand agents, we establish a sharp complexity boundary: the problem is polynomial-time solvable when each agent is interested in at most two tasks, but NP-hard with at most three interests. Our algorithm analyzes tree-structured dependencies among forced assignments and reduces optimization to maximum-weight independent set in a perfect graph. When agents may receive multiple tasks, no polynomial-time constant-factor approximation exists unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. Finally, with homogeneous success probabilities and rewards, we establish a welfare- and revenue-preserving equivalence between unit-demand contract design and envy-free pricing. This yields polynomial-time welfare maximization without restricting interests, while revenue maximization remains NP-hard.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Power of Menus in Dynamic Pricing: Optimal Regret and Equivalence Results
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study dynamic pricing where a seller repeatedly interacts with a strategic, non-myopic buyer who has a fixed private valuation and discounts future utility. Prior work focused exclusively on posted-price mechanisms, where the seller gives a take-it-or-leave-it offer. For our first result, under geometric discounting $γ_t = γ^{t-1}$, we show that menu mechanisms consisting of allocation-payment contracts achieve $O(T_γ)$ regret, where $T_γ$ is the buyer's effective discounted time horizon. We also establish a $Ω(T_γ)$ lower bound, demonstrating the bound is tight. Considering the geometric discounting buyer with a constant discount factor, our bound is $O(1)$, while prior bounds using posted-price mechanisms incur an unavoidable $Ω(\log\log T)$ factor in regret. Our second contribution is more conceptual in nature. The problem of dynamic pricing sits at the intersection of two paradigms: learning with strategic agents in computer science / machine learning and revelation-principle-based mechanism design in economics, yet their relationship has remained unclear. We establish an equivalence between these two classes of mechanisms in our single-buyer setting: any adaptive indirect menu mechanism can be converted into an incentive-compatible direct mechanism with no less revenue, and conversely, any such direct mechanism can be implemented by an adaptive indirect menu mechanism with no less revenue. Consequently, the two classes achieve identical optimal regret. The adaptive, data-driven algorithms of online learning and explicit type elicitation from direct revelation type mechanisms are two languages towards solving the same problem.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Welfare, Improvability, and Variance: A Principal-Agent Approach to Optimal Benchmark Item Aggregation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: AI benchmarks have well-documented limitations, with prior work examining contamination, saturation, and construct underspecification. Aggregation has received far less attention: benchmarks are typically summarized by uniformly averaging item-level scores, implicitly treating every test item as equally valuable. We model benchmarking as a multitask principal-agent game and show that the welfare loss from a benchmark is determined jointly by three item-level primitives: alignment with normative welfare priorities, marginal improvability, and performance variance. We translate the theory into an audit framework that ranks items along each of these three axes, and apply it to OLMES items using WORKBank for welfare, the EvoLM 4B suite for improvability, and the PolyPythias 410M panel for variance. The framework surfaces items that are Pareto-inferior within OLMES subject to a pro-worker welfare operationalization. All code is available at https://github.com/stair-lab/principal-agent-benchmarks.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS'26 Evaluations & Datasets Track

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Distributed Learning of $α$-Potential Functions in Strategic Multi-agent Systems
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the problem of computing the tightest \(α\)-potential approximation of a general-sum game over continuous action spaces, within a prescribed class of potential functions and when each player has access only to its own utility function. The difficulty is twofold: the approximation error involves a worst-case search over an infinite set of unilateral deviations, and the required utility information is distributed across players.
  For a linear-in-parameters potential class, we use an exact finite-tuple reformulation that separates the problem into a global outer search over deviation tuples and distributed convex inner problems. We develop a primal--dual inner oracle tailored to this structure and establish a uniform one-sided accuracy guarantee. This oracle can be combined with global outer search to obtain an end-to-end guarantee on the outer optimization error. We also develop a projected zeroth-order outer method as a computationally lighter alternative for higher-dimensional problems. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy--computation tradeoff between the two outer-search methods and show that the proposed optimization framework can improve upon analytical \(α\)-potential constructions.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Finite-Sample and Communication-Efficient Networked Information Aggregation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Building on SODA 2026 work Kearns et al. (2026), we study learning in directed acyclic graphs in which each agent observes only a subset of the input coordinates and may use the predictions of its parents as additional features. In the finite-sample protocol, the message sent along each edge is the agent's prediction vector on a shared sample, so the communication cost is linear in the sample size $m$. In this paper we study this model under communication constraints.
  First, we revisit the finite-sample analysis of the full-message protocol. We identify a gap in the finite-sample proof of Kearns et al. (2026) and develop a different argument that establishes a finite-sample population-risk guarantee along paths satisfying deterministic $M$-coverage.
  Second, we introduce a shared-sketch protocol in which each agent sends a $k$-dimensional linear sketch of its prediction vector instead of the full $m$-dimensional message, where $k\ll m$. We analyze this protocol through a reduction to least squares on the compressed sample together with an oblivious subspace embedding argument. The resulting bound separates statistics from communication: the statistical term is still governed by the original sample size $m$, while the additional error due to compression is controlled by the sketch dimension $k$. For Gaussian sketches, we obtain an explicit high-probability population-risk bound, showing that row subsampling is not the only possible communication-statistics tradeoff for networked information aggregation.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Computational Complexity.title: Proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture: An Exposition
Computational Complexity.summary:
We give an exposition of a recent proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which states that every degree-$d$ polynomial $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0,1]$ has a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$. This implies that quantum query algorithms for decision problems can be efficiently simulated classically on most inputs. It also yields a near-equivalence between the status of the $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ problem in the random oracle and unrelativized worlds.
  We organize the proof around four main steps and discuss how each connects to the literature on the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. To bring out the key ideas, we do not optimize parameters, and our presentation yields weaker exponents than the original.
  $\textbf{Authors' note.}$ The proof was discovered by David Turturean using a research system developed at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), in combination with a non-public Anthropic model. The proof was then shared with the authors, who worked to understand it and prepare this exposition. Anthropic's public models were used in this process.
  The authors did not receive financial compensation from Anthropic or PSI. This article is not intended for publication at a conference or in a journal.

Computational Complexity.title: Closing the Complexity Gap for Wheeler Graph Recognition on $d$-NFAs
Computational Complexity.summary: Wheeler graph recognition asks whether a directed graph whose arcs are labeled by symbols from a totally ordered alphabet admits a Wheeler order, a total order on its vertices compatible with the labels of arcs and the order of their tails. A $d$-NFA is a nondeterministic finite automaton in which at most $d$ transitions with any given label leave each state. For Wheeler graph recognition on $d$-NFAs, Alanko et al. gave a polynomial-time algorithm for $d \leq 2$, whereas Gibney and Thankachan proved NP-completeness for every fixed $d \geq 5$. The computational complexity for $d = 3$ and $d = 4$ remained open. We resolve both open cases by extending the reduction of Gibney and Thankachan with a new encoding of clauses of Not-All-Equal 3-SAT. Specifically, we prove that recognition is NP-complete even for directed acyclic graphs over an ordered binary alphabet with a unique source reaching every vertex and total out-degree at most three at every vertex. Consequently, Wheeler graph recognition on $d$-NFAs is NP-complete for every fixed $d \geq 3$.

Computational Complexity.title: Amortized Cell-Probe Lower Bounds for Dynamic Boolean Problems
Computational Complexity.summary:
We prove the first unconditional amortized $Ω\big((\log N/\log\log N)^2\big)$ cell-probe lower bound for a Boolean dynamic problem. For insert-only multiphase Disjointness with $N$ query sets over $[N]$ and word size $w=Θ(\log N)$, a fixed distribution of interleaved insertions and queries forces this expected average cost per operation, excluding preprocessing. The bound allows sufficiently small constant error for each query of every fixed legal sequence and imposes no restriction on individual operation costs. It transfers to incremental directed reachability, incremental subgraph connectivity, and fully dynamic triangle detection.
  We also prove $t_q=Ω\big((\log N/\log(t_uw))^2\big)$ for amortized insertion time $1\le t_u=N^{o(1)}$ and expected query time $t_q$, when the number of insertions before the final query is not announced in advance. We reach the quadratic-logarithmic scale with bounded error by combining interleaving with the 2.5-round communication framework [Ko26a, Ko26b] and controlling errors among accepted simulations.

Computational Complexity.title: A note on exact external information complexity
Computational Complexity.summary: We study the prior-free zero-error private-coin external information complexity $B(f)$ of finite two-party functions, with correctness on every input. An elementary rectangle/entropy argument gives $B(\mathsf{AND})=\log_2 3$. A complete classification of Boolean $3\times3$ matrices leaves, up to input permutations and output complementation, only the two-overlapping-rectangles function $F$ without an exact value. An entropy potential and a finite rational protocol give $2.1212661667060486842\ldots\le B(F)<2.130998318$. We also determine its deterministic external information and zero-error communication costs. A separate product-prior certificate and internal-information additivity yield $R_0^{\mathrm{pub}}(F^{\times t})\ge2.021991187178562\ldots\,t$, strictly exceeding the fractional-cover rate $2t$.

Computational Complexity.title: On the Complexity of Extending Prescribed Linear Forests to Hamiltonian Cycles in Hypercubes
Computational Complexity.summary: Let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube, and let $P\subseteq E(Q_n)$ be a set of prescribed edges. It is known that, for $n\ge 2$, every such set $P$ with $|P|\leq 2n-3$ whose edges form a linear forest is contained in a Hamiltonian cycle of $Q_n$. This bound is sharp for general linear forests. The computational complexity of deciding whether a prescribed edge set of a hypercube can be extended to a Hamiltonian cycle was posed as an open question by Dvořák [SIAM J. Discrete Math. 19 (2005) 135--144]. We prove that the problem is NP-complete even when the prescribed edges form a spanning linear forest with no isolated vertices. We give a polynomial-time reduction from a restricted 3-SAT problem, using local spanning path-forest gadgets for variables and clauses that are uniformly embedded in the hypercube. The same reduction therefore establishes NP-hardness of two versions of Hamiltonian-cycle extension problems for general prescribed edge sets.

Computational Complexity.title: Hitting sets From Derivations: Waring Rank and Noncommutative ABPs
Computational Complexity.summary:
We give an explicit hitting set of size $\operatorname{poly}(n,d,r)$ for the class of $n$-variate degree-$d$ polynomials whose partial derivative space is bounded by $r$, over any field $\mathbb{F}$ of characteristic zero (or large enough). In particular, this yields a polynomial sized hitting set for the class of depth-$3$ powering circuits.
  The proof extends to the setting of noncommutative ABPs and provides a polynomial sized hitting set (of matrices) for the class of noncommututive polynomials that can be computed by polynomial sized noncommutative ABPs (this was also one of the results reported by Open AI~\cite{OpenAI26} in their release on 6 Oct 2026).
  The main technical insight is the construction of a ``formal derivation'' and properties of the associated Wronskian with respect to this derivation, which was previously studied by Moura \cite{Moura_2004} in a very different context. The proofs in this paper are elementary and completely self-contained.
  AI disclosure: A subset of the stewards obtained a weaker statement (hitting sets for polynomials with bounded partial derivative space) during conversations \cite{astra_proof} with OpenAI GPT-6 Astra. Extensions of this idea to the broader class of noncommutative ABPs were obtained by the other stewards (via further conversations with Astra), prior to OpenAI's dump on 6 Oct 2026.
  The proofs presented in this writeup is a rewriting (in the authors' words) of the proofs for both settings obtained by the models in a form that we believe is understandable to researchers. Although the proof is technically identical to OpenAI's release, we believe this exposition is self-contained, simpler, and more valuable to the community. The absurdity of the situation is not lost on us.

Computational Complexity.title: Linear Objective Problems: A Complexity Framework for Bilevel Optimization
Computational Complexity.summary:
Many bilevel and robust optimization problems are complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, but such results are usually proven one problem at a time with problem-specific reductions. A recurring obstacle is that the lower level must select an optimal solution rather than merely a feasible one, whereas standard reductions preserve only whether a solution exists, not which solutions are optimal. We introduce linear objective problems (LOP), a framework for optimization problems whose solutions are explicit subsets of a ground set and whose objective is linear in these elements. We define tight solution-embedding reductions, which map the optimal solutions of one problem element by element onto the optimal solutions of another, without having to recognize optimal solutions, which is coNP-hard in general. This gives a notion of LOP-completeness, with Satisfiability as the canonical complete problem, even with unit weights.
  We show that many classical problems are LOP-complete, including Vertex Cover, Dominating Set, TSP, Knapsack, and Steiner Tree, and we introduce a duality that transfers LOP-completeness between minimization and maximization problems. As our main application, we prove a meta-theorem for min-max regret optimization under interval uncertainty: for every LOP-complete problem, the min-max regret version is $Σ_2^p$-complete. Instead of a separate proof for each nominal problem, it suffices to show that the nominal problem is LOP-complete. This recovers known results for the interval min-max regret versions of Knapsack and Maximum Benefit Set Cover and yields completeness for over 50 further problems.

Computational Complexity.title: Complexity of Strong Popularity in Hedonic Games
Computational Complexity.summary:
In a hedonic game, agents are partitioned into coalitions and have preferences over the coalitions they may join. A partition is called strongly popular if it strictly beats every other partition in a majority vote among the agents.
  We study the complexity of determining the existence of strongly popular partitions in two fundamental classes of hedonic games: additively separable and fractional hedonic games (ASHGs and FHGs), where agents' utilities are determined, respectively, by the sum and average of their valuations for the members of their coalitions.
  We prove that this problem is PCW-complete for ASHGs and for FHGs even with non-negative valuations, where PCW is a subclass of $Σ^P_2$ associated with unambiguous problems (which have at most one witness), recently introduced by Gilboa et al. (2025). These are the first natural complete problems for PCW, in the sense that their formulations do not involve arbitrary Boolean circuits. Our results resolve open problems posed by Brandt and Bullinger (JAIR 2022) and Bullinger and Gilboa (IJCAI 2025). The two reductions employ substantially different techniques, reflecting both the distinct utility models and the stringent non-negativity constraint in FHGs.
  Furthermore, in contrast with FHGs, we show that in ASHGs restricting valuations to be non-negative makes the problem polynomial-time solvable.
Computational Complexity.comment: This version includes additional results: Theorems 1.2 and 1.3. A preliminary version of Theorem 1.1 in this paper appeared as part of earlier versions of arXiv:2510.19084, when the two works formed a single manuscript

Computational Complexity.title: Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models
Computational Complexity.summary: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $Σ_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, while being derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs. Overall, our results help expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations, while clarifying the fundamental role of feature interactions in shaping their complexity.

Computational Complexity.title: Parameterized Complexity of Stationarity Testing for Piecewise-Affine Functions and Shallow CNN Losses
Computational Complexity.summary:
We study the parameterized complexity of testing approximate first-order stationarity at a prescribed point for continuous piecewise-affine (PA) functions, a basic task in nonsmooth optimization. PA functions form a canonical model for nonsmooth stationarity testing and capture the local polyhedral geometry that appears in ReLU-type training losses. Recent work of Tian and So (2025) shows that testing approximate stationarity notions for PA functions is computationally intractable in the worst case, and identifies fixed-dimensional tractability as an open direction. We address this direction from the viewpoint of parameterized complexity, with the ambient dimension $d$ as the parameter.
  In this paper, we give XP algorithms in fixed dimension for the tractable sides, and prove W[1]-hardness for the complementary sides. Moreover, lower bounds under the parameterized $k$-Clique hypothesis rule out deterministic algorithms running in time $ρ(d)s^{o(d)}$ for any computable function $ρ$, where $s$ denotes the total binary encoding length of the instance. As a further consequence, our results yield the corresponding parameterized complexity picture for testing local minimality of continuous PA functions. We also extend our hardness results to a family of shallow ReLU CNN training losses, tested in the trainable weight space. Thus, the same parameterized-complexity picture also appears for simple CNN training losses.
  Notably, our lower bounds assume that $k$-Clique on $N$-vertex graphs admits no deterministic $ρ(k)N^{o(k)}$-time algorithm for any computable function $ρ$. The recent refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) (OpenAI, 2026) and the stronger fine-grained $k$-Clique hypothesis (Vassilevska Williams and Zamir, 2026) do not contradict this assumption.
Computational Complexity.comment: 2:46 Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 29 pages. This revision states the conditional lower bounds directly under the parameterized k-Clique hypothesis, which is not contradicted by the recent refutations of ETH and the stronger fine-grained k-Clique hypothesis

Computational Complexity.title: Block Sensitivity and Certificate Complexity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions
Computational Complexity.summary: We investigate block sensitivity and certificate complexity of monomial rotation-symmetric Boolean functions, obtaining exact formulas and structural classifications for several families. For odd-degree monomial rotation-symmetric functions, the equality $s(f)=n$ established in our earlier work yields $bs(f)=C(f)=n$. For quadratic monomial rotation-symmetric functions, we determine both measures completely and prove that block sensitivity equals certificate complexity. For consecutive quartic monomials, we determine sensitivity, block sensitivity, and certificate complexity in every residue class of the number of variables. Our principal result is an exact global block-sensitivity formula for consecutive monomials of every even degree $d\ge4$. Writing $n=q(d+2)+ρ$, where $0\leρ<d+2$ and $q\ge\max\{2,d/2-1\}$, we prove \[ bs(F_{d,n})=n-\min\left\{\left\lceil\fracρ{2}\right\rceil,d+2-ρ\right\}. \] We also establish the corresponding sensitivity formula by a self-contained argument, yielding arbitrarily large gaps between sensitivity and block sensitivity as the degree varies. For certificate complexity, we obtain exact pointwise formulas for structured run-and-gap configurations and establish additional global equalities, including $C(F_{6,8q+5})=bs(F_{6,8q+5})=8q+2$ for $q\ge2$. Our methods combine cyclic run decomposition, parity arguments, explicit sensitive-block constructions, and constant-subcube certificates. The exact global certificate complexity for arbitrary even degrees remains open.

Computational Complexity.title: Sensitivity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions via Binary Necklaces
Computational Complexity.summary: Rotation symmetric Boolean functions are important structured families in the theory of Boolean functions, where cyclic invariance permits compact algebraic descriptions while retaining nontrivial local behavior. We investigate their sensitivity through binary necklaces and monomial orbit sums. In the necklace quotient of the Boolean cube, ordinary adjacency does not record the number of coordinate flips: we give a directed flip-multiplicity formula involving stabilizers and distance-two near-periods, and derive exact local sensitivity formulas when the number of variables is an odd prime. For monomial rotation symmetric functions we determine sensitivity for all odd degrees and for quadratic orbit sums. For the consecutive-monomial family of every even degree $d\ge4$, we prove a run-cluster inequality and obtain the eventual exact formula $s(F_{d,n})=n-\min\{r,d+2-r\}$, where $n\equiv r\pmod{d+2}$, under the stated length hypothesis. The consecutive quartic case follows explicitly. We also evaluate sensitivity for cyclic run-threshold functions. Our results provide exact combinatorial and complexity-theoretic information about cyclic Boolean functions and clarify how cyclic symmetry governs local sensitivity.

Multimedia.title: YTShorts-92K: An Interpretable Multimodal Dataset of YouTube Shorts
Multimedia.summary: Short-form video has become one of the dominant formats of online content, yet large-scale datasets enabling the analysis of what makes these videos successful remain limited. Existing resources often focus on post-publication popularity signals or rely on non-interpretable representations such as high-dimensional embeddings. Here, we introduce YTShorts-92K, a dataset of 92,654 YouTube Shorts collected from 345 creators and spanning 12 manually defined content categories. Each video is enriched with an interpretable multimodal feature set covering metadata, textual information, visual characteristics from frames and thumbnails, and cross-modal consistency measures. We describe the collection methodology, data cleaning process, and feature extraction pipeline, followed by descriptive analyses of the diversity of creators, topics, and extracted features. This dataset offers a reusable resource for studying short-form video content, online attention, and multimodal content analysis.
Multimedia.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables

Multimedia.title: When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary
Multimedia.summary: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
Multimedia.comment: Technical report, work in progress

Multimedia.title: TIB: Sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck for Multimodal Attribution beyond Alignment Assumption
Multimedia.summary: Multimodal (e.g. vision-language, in this work) attribution aims to interpret the models without access to ground-truth explanatory supervision. Existing multimodal attribution methods typically rely on paired modalities as proxy supervision, implicitly assuming that image-text pairs are semantically aligned. Information bottleneck (IB)-based attribution methods follow this general paradigm and instantiate it through a global sufficiency-compression objective. In realistic multimodal datasets, however, this assumption is frequently violated due to partial semantic misalignment and unreliable cross-modal correspondences. Through theoretical analysis, we show that, under such misalignment, information-bottleneck-based attribution objectives exhibit a structural limitation: by assuming equal reliability across all proxy supervision signals, they induce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations. To address this issue, we propose TIB, a sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck framework that adaptively modulates attribution strength according to cross-modal reliability, without assuming semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while also validating the identified failure mode.
Multimedia.comment: Accpeted to NeurIPS2026

Multimedia.title: PhysElite: How Far Are LLMs from Solving Olympiad-Level Physics Problems?
Multimedia.summary: Understanding how (multimodal) large language models perform on physics problems requires benchmarks that reflect the difficulty and breadth of expert-level physical reasoning. Existing physics benchmarks remain limited in the following two important ways: (1) short of high-difficulty datasets, and (2) lack of comprehensive coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and step-by-step solution processes. As a result, model performance on current datasets may not be fully representative of their ability to solve complex physics problems. To address these issues, we present PhysElite, a large-scale bilingual multimodal benchmark for Olympiad-level physics reasoning. PhysElite contains 11,586 Olympiad-tier problems. For each problem, we provide corresponding visual diagrams, step-by-step bilingual Chinese-English solution derivations, and the final answer. We benchmark 18 open-source and closed-source MLLMs, and find that even the strongest model reaches only 33.7% answer accuracy. We additionally conduct step-level process evaluation to diagnose where models fail in the reasoning chain. Our datasets are released at https://github.com/PremiLab-Math/PhysElite.
Multimedia.comment: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026

Multimedia.title: JND-Guided Light-Weight Neural Pre-Filter for Perceptual Image Coding
Multimedia.summary: Just Noticeable Distortion (JND)-guided pre-filter is a promising technique for improving the perceptual compression efficiency of image coding. However, existing methods are often computationally expensive, and the field lacks standardized benchmarks for fair comparison. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a twofold contribution. First, we develop and open-source FJNDF-Pytorch, a unified benchmark for frequency-domain JND-Guided pre-filters. Second, leveraging this platform, we propose a complete learning framework for a novel, lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art compression efficiency, consistently outperforming competitors across multiple datasets and encoders. In terms of computational cost, our model is exceptionally lightweight, requiring only 7.15 GFLOPs to process a 1080p image, which is merely 14.1% of the cost of recent lightweight network. Our work presents a robust, state-of-the-art solution that excels in both performance and efficiency, supported by a reproducible research platform. The open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/viplab-fudan/FJNDF-Pytorch.
Multimedia.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, Submitted to ISCAS2027

Adaptation and Self-Organizing Systems.title: Increased-order generalized synchronization in memristive neurons: dissipativity analysis and data-driven control
Adaptation and Self-Organizing Systems.summary: We investigate increased-order generalized synchronization between four- and five-dimensional memristive Hindmarsh--Rose neurons, focusing on the selection and stabilization of the synchronization map. An analytical construction combines a prescribed nonlinear map with adaptive control, retaining the memristive switching contribution explicitly in the error dynamics. Lyapunov analysis establishes asymptotic synchronization under uniform strict dissipativity and yields a switching-independent decrease estimate outside an explicit error neighborhood. Numerical simulations exhibit error decay beyond the sufficient convergence conditions. A complementary data-driven construction uses next-generation reservoir computing to learn predictors from uncoupled full-state trajectories and an affine synchronization map through dynamical consistency. The resulting sampled-data controller achieves small residual tracking errors without access to the governing equations. Relative to a reference map within the data-driven framework, the learned map reduces median control effort approximately eightfold while improving tracking accuracy. These results connect synchronization-map selection with conditional convergence guarantees and reduced control requirements.

Adaptation and Self-Organizing Systems.title: Quantum entanglement as a resource for self-organization and stabilization
Adaptation and Self-Organizing Systems.summary: Can quantum entanglement generate macroscopic order that persists after the entanglement itself disappears? We establish such a mechanism in a driven-dissipative bosonic lattice, where local entanglement enables transport that amplifies spatial fluctuations into extended Turing patterns. For the full nonlinear dynamics with noise and disorder, we derive rigorous finite-time bounds on pattern intensity for all admissible separable evolutions, allowing arbitrary classical correlations. Quantum dynamics produces pattern intensities beyond these bounds during both formation and stabilization under noise. The excess intensity also provides a lower bound on the accumulated transport contribution beyond the separable limit. We further introduce an environment that responds to emerging order by suppressing local coherence and activating classical transport. The patterns then persist as local entanglement is lost, with both stages arising from a single time-independent Lindblad equation. These results show how transient quantum resources can establish persistent macroscopic order, opening new directions for harnessing self-organization in nonequilibrium systems.
Adaptation and Self-Organizing Systems.comment: The data and code supporting this study are provided in the author's GitHub repository https://github.com/IKEDAKAZUKI/Quantum-self-organization-and-stabilization

Image and Video Processing.title: From Discrete Snapshots to Geometric Entity: Motion-Native Channel Tracking for THz Near-Field XL-MIMO
Image and Video Processing.summary: Channel tracking in mobile terahertz (THz) near-field extremely large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems is challenging because spherical-wave propagation couples angle and range, leading to rapid and nonlinear channel evolution under sparse pilot observations. Existing approaches typically estimate pilot-local channel or position snapshots before applying temporal tracking or smoothing, making them vulnerable to information loss during snapshot formation. To break this bottleneck, we propose a paradigm shift from tracking discrete snapshots to estimating a holistic geometric entity, namely, one shared continuous UE trajectory over the tracking window. Specifically, we parameterize the trajectory using a low-dimensional cubic B-spline representation and directly couple the per-pilot profile likelihoods through this shared trajectory before any pilot-local position estimate is finalized, thereby inducing continuous near-field channel evolution. We further characterize the efficient geometric information supplied by each pilot observation and its aggregation in the shared spline-coefficient space. Based on this formulation, we develop a regularized maximum a posteriori estimator and a quadratic-penalty lifted solver that separates parallel pilot-local geometric updates from a structured global spline update. The resulting global system is banded and, for a fixed spline degree, admits linear-complexity factorization, enabling an efficient structured implementation. Simulations demonstrate consistently improved tracking accuracy over representative temporally refined baselines in the tested medium-to-high-SNR regime, together with a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off. These results highlight the benefit of coupling sparse pilot observations through a shared continuous trajectory rather than temporally processing independently estimated snapshots.

Image and Video Processing.title: EgoEV-HandPose: Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Estimation and Gesture Recognition with Stereo Event Cameras
Image and Video Processing.summary: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimation and gesture recognition are fundamental to understanding hand interactions from first-person observations. Robust perception remains challenging: frame-based cameras suffer from motion blur and limited dynamic range, while event-based approaches face ego-motion interference, monocular depth ambiguity, and limited real-world datasets. We propose EgoEV-HandPose, an end-to-end framework for joint 3D bimanual hand pose estimation and gesture recognition from stereo event streams. Its core module, KeypointBEV, combines sparse 3D joint hypotheses with geometry-aware stereo fusion and iterative reprojection-guided refinement to progressively resolve depth uncertainty and improve pose accuracy. We also introduce EgoEVHands, the first large-scale real-world stereo event dataset for egocentric 3D bimanual hand pose estimation and gesture recognition. Built upon EgoEvGesture recordings, it adds dense 2D/3D hand annotations and comprises 2,498 annotated stereo sequence pairs across 38 gesture classes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EgoEV-HandPose achieves state-of-the-art performance on EgoEVHands, obtaining a mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) of 30.54mm and a gesture recognition accuracy of 86.87%, significantly outperforming RGB-based stereo and previous event-based methods. The framework exhibits exceptional robustness under low illumination and severe bimanual occlusion. Experiments on DHP19 further demonstrate the cross-dataset and cross-architecture generalizability of the KeypointBEV refinement design. Dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/ZJUWang01/EgoEV-HandPose.
Image and Video Processing.comment: The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/ZJUWang01/EgoEV-HandPose

Graphics.title: 3D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Novel View Synthesis
Graphics.summary: Solving novel view synthesis (NVS) for millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar requires a renderer that is physically faithful, complex-valued, and multi-viewpoint-tractable. No prior method achieves these three properties simultaneously. Differentiable Monte Carlo (MC) ray tracers implement the radar forward model directly with explicit material modeling and complex outputs, but a joint fit across views takes over an hour per scene. Optical-NVS ports of NeRF, hash grids, and 3D Gaussians train fast but discard phase and replace explicit material modeling with opaque learned features, restricting them to power-only range-azimuth (RA) magnitudes. We propose 3D Point Splatting (3DPS), the first differentiable point splatting renderer for radar, derived directly from the standard solid-angle form of the radar equation. Each oriented 3D point carries a material model built on ITU-R P.2040 permittivity and slab reflection, evaluated in closed form, with the resulting complex phasor splatted into range bins through a precomputed point spread function (PSF). The complex-valued output makes the renderer product-agnostic. The same optimized scene yields analog-to-digital converter (ADC), complex range profile (CRP), and RA outputs through standard fast Fourier transform (FFT) pipelines without retraining for each format. On six outdoor ColoRadar scenes, 3DPS reaches 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images. This is between 1.7x and 5.2x the three optical-NVS baselines (RadarSplat, Radar Fields, DART) and 1.3x the mmIR ray tracer at 1/25 of its wall-clock time. Training takes approximately 3 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090. Project page: https://3d-point-splatting.github.io/
Graphics.comment: Accepted to the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026. Project page: https://3d-point-splatting.github.io/

Graphics.title: Quadratic Bezier Splatting with Structural Initialization for Efficient Painting Rendering
Graphics.summary: Stroke-based rendering is often optimized as a pixel-level reconstruction task. This over-reliance on global error reduction not only degrades strokes into fragmented curves due to a lack of structured planning, but also allows locally defective primitives to be concealed by overlapping layers. To address these issues, we introduce a model-guided framework for stroke-audited rendering. Our framework uses Quadratic Bezier Splatting to analytically model continuous curved strokes with efficient differentiable alpha compositing. Built on this renderer, a feedforward multi-scale stroke decoder provides a structural initialization with learned stroke-scale allocation, while test-time stroke optimization supplies the reconstruction capacity needed for high-fidelity refinement. We further propose a single-stroke audit mechanism that explicitly evaluates local stroke quality, preventing defective primitives from surviving optimization through layer-wise compensation. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves coherent layouts, improves PSNR by up to 5.46 dB, yields a 16% more compact representation, and accelerates combined renderer forward and backward computation by a factor of 220.3.

Graphics.title: PLS-GS: Probabilistic Lidar Scaffolds for Compact, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
Graphics.summary: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is typically optimized from images only, many robotics and mapping applications provide both camera and high-definition LiDAR data, combining rich visual appearance with accurate geometric structure. We introduce PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold for Gaussian Splatting that exploits this complementary sensing setting to construct a compact 3DGS representation aligned to the measured surface. PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model jointly over position and color, yielding a continuous and adaptive scaffold that eliminates the need for discrete scene partitioning such as voxel grids or octrees. The fitted mixture then guides the renderable 3DGS Gaussians: each rendering Gaussian is associated with a GMM component and constrained in the local surface frame induced by that component's covariance. A Mahalanobis support loss bounds the deviation of the rendering Gaussians from the corresponding LiDAR-derived surface. Across five large outdoor scenes, PLS-GS places primitives markedly closer to the LiDAR measurements than both image- and LiDAR-initialized baselines, while employing substantially fewer primitives, yielding a considerably more compact model and faster rendering. At matched capacity, PLS-GS places primitives closer to the LiDAR measurements, with comparable rendering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS.
Graphics.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Main paper and supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS

Graphics.title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
Graphics.summary: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.

Graphics.title: Good Token Hunting: A Hitchhiker's Guide to Token Selection for Visual Geometry Transformers
Graphics.summary: Visual geometry transformers have become powerful architectures for multi-view 3D reconstruction, enabling joint prediction of multiple 3D attributes in a feed-forward manner. However, their computational cost grows quadratically with the input sequence length due to the global attention layers inside these models. This limits both their scalability and efficiency. In this work, we address this challenge with a simple yet general strategy: restricting the number of key/value tokens that each query interacts with during global attention. To achieve effective token selection, we introduce a two-stage framework. First, an inter-frame selection step operates at the frame level to identify frames that should be preserved. Second, an intra-frame selection step further discards more redundant tokens within the selected frames. Our analysis highlights the advantage of a diversity-based strategy for inter-frame selection, which ensures broad coverage of the scene. For intra-frame selection, we show that layer-aware sparsification is necessary, with the selection process guided by the entropy of the global attention pattern. Our approach offers a superior speed-accuracy trade-off compared to existing solutions. Extensive experiments show that it accelerates visual geometry transformers by over 85% for scenes with 500 images while maintaining, or even improving, baseline performance, which hints that how our token selection strategy can play a crucial role in future applications of visual geometry transformers. Our project website is available at https://zsh2000.github.io/good-token-hunting.github.io.

Graphics.title: Squeezing Capacity from Multimodal Large Language Models for Subject-driven Generation
Graphics.summary: Subject-driven image generation aims to synthesize new images that preserve the identity of the given subject while following textual instructions. Existing approaches often encode text and reference images separately. This limits cross-modal reasoning abilities and causes copy-paste artifacts. Recent frameworks that connect multimodal models and diffusion models improve instruction following, but largely overlook identity preservation. To address these limitations, we condition diffusion models on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that jointly encode text and reference images, and augment it with VAE-based identity conditioning. A novel Dual Layer Aggregation (DLA) module is designed to aggregate multi-level MLLM features for optimal conditioning, and a multi-stage denoising strategy is applied to progressively balance the semantic information from MLLM and fine-detail identity from VAE during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach harmonizes multimodal understanding with identity preservation, mitigates copy-paste issues, and achieves superior performance regarding human preference on subject-driven image generation. Our project website is available at https://zsh2000.github.io/squeeze-mllm-subject-gen/.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Patchbay: a block model for the sonification of ADS-B aircraft data
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Patchbay is a design for turning the data that an ADS-B receiver collects into sound by wiring typed blocks together. ADS-B reports are the position and altitude messages that aircraft broadcast and that a small ground receiver can collect. We first describe what such a receiver reports: signals that differ in shape (continuous, stepped, circular, categorical), in resolution, in who produces them, and in how long they stay put, which runs from about ten seconds to the whole time an aircraft is in view. From this we derive a small model. Four kinds of connection carry an aircraft set, a value, an event or audio, and 27 blocks select aircraft, read fields, decide when a note starts, shape values and make sound. One of these blocks makes the receiver act as a radar: scanning by bearing it is a line that rotates about the receiver, and scanning by range it is a ring that grows from the centre or shrinks inward. Each aircraft sounds at the moment the scan reaches it, and the scan's period is set in bars of a beat clock. The model does not depend on a browser. Our reference implementation is a browser editor, contained in one HTML file, that replays two recorded captures and records both an audio take and a MIDI take, a file of the notes played rather than of the sound. We say what is not built and place the work beside the closest systems we found, among them a radar-sweep sequencer for tangible objects from 2006 and a range-ring sonification of ADS-B aircraft published in 2026. Sweeps that trigger sound, and typed connections, both exist in earlier systems. To our knowledge, none of the sources we reached carries the aircraft in view, with every field attached, as one kind of connection in an editor.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: ComplLLM: Fine-tuning LLMs to Discover Complementary Signals for Decision-making
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Multi-agent decision pipelines can outperform single agent workflows when complementarity holds, i.e., different agents bring unique information to inform a final decision. We propose ComplLLM, a post-training framework based on decision theory that fine-tunes a decision-assistant LLM to output signals that complement existing agent decisions, using complementary information as reward. We validate ComplLLM on synthetic and real-world tasks involving domain experts, demonstrating how the approach recovers known complementary information, produces plausible explanations of complementary signals to support downstream decision-makers, and improves human and LLM agent decision performance in controlled studies.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Complementarity without ground truth?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Human-AI complementarity captures the idea that a human assisted by an AI system can outperform both the human and the AI acting alone. In prediction tasks, this improvement is assessed against ground truth labels produced through a reference construction procedure and intended to represent the state of affairs to be predicted. Many human-AI interactions, including those where medical AI provides treatment recommendations, however, concern tasks other than predicting what obtains. Their relevant output concerns adequacy relative to a practical goal and depends on several evaluative dimensions. In this work, we examine the ground truth dependence of complementarity and extend it to human-AI interactions where ground truth is not the appropriate reference. We show that tasks beyond prediction can still admit a reference construction procedure that generates adequacy labels. We develop a route for extending complementarity to such settings. It replaces ground truth labels with context-dependent adequacy labels generated through a two-step scoring methodology inspired by multi-criteria decision analysis frameworks in healthcare and it makes the normative choices underlying reference construction explicit. Because the construction of adequacy labels embeds evaluative choices, we draw methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism to identify technical, scientific, and social factors relevant to supporting their construction. Our approach expands the empirical study of human-AI complementarity beyond prediction tasks, enabling its quantitative evaluation in decision-support settings where ground truth is not the appropriate evaluative reference.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 15 pages, 2 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: NeuroRVQ: Multi-Scale Biosignal Tokenization for Generative Foundation Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Biosignals such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrocardiography (ECG), and electromyography (EMG) encode physiological activity across multiple temporal and spectral scales, yielding representations that are rich but challenging for machine learning. Foundation models trained to predict masked signal tokens have shown promise in learning generalizable biosignal representations, yet their performance depends on the tokenizer's ability to preserve high-frequency dynamics and reconstruct signals with high fidelity. We introduce NeuroRVQ, a modality-adaptive biosignal tokenizer family designed for high-fidelity signal reconstruction. To capture the full frequency spectrum, NeuroRVQ decomposes biosignals into frequency-specific representations via multi-scale temporal convolutions, each encoded into hierarchical RVQ codebooks to preserve high-frequency detail, combined with a novel phase-aware training loss that respects the circular topology of Fourier phase. By tuning the temporal resolution, number and size of temporal kernels and RVQ depth, this design adapts to the spectro-temporal characteristics of each biosignal modality. To validate that tokenizer quality drives downstream performance, we train a simple masked-token foundation model for each modality (NeuroRVQ-FM) using the corresponding NeuroRVQ tokenizer. The NeuroRVQ-FM family achieves competitive or superior downstream performance compared to existing modality-specific foundation models, demonstrating that high-fidelity tokenization is a critical factor for effective biosignal modeling.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Visual Affect Analysis: Predicting Emotions of Image Viewers with Vision-Language Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for large-scale affect inference from images, but their alignment with human affective ratings remains unclear. We benchmarked 16 proprietary and open-source VLMs on three validated affective image datasets: the International Affective Picture System, the Nencki Affective Picture System, and the Library of AI-Generated Affective Images. In a zero-shot setting, models performed two tasks: (i) top-emotion classification and (ii) prediction of human ratings on 1--7/9 Likert scales for discrete emotions and affective dimensions. We also evaluated rater-conditioned prompting on the LAI-GAI dataset using de-identified participant metadata. Best models showed strong discrete emotion classification (60%--80% on six-emotion tasks; 60%--75% on a 12-category task), with anger and surprise predicted least accurately. For continuous ratings, models aligned moderately to strongly with human judgments ($r > 0.75$) but showed consistent biases, especially weaker performance on arousal and overestimation of response intensity. Rater-conditioned prompting had only small, inconsistent effects. Overall, VLMs captured broad affective patterns but sometimes lacked the nuance, although newer model generations performed better.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted at ACII 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Towards Identity-Preserving LLM Agents under Model Transition
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: When an LLM agent's backend model is upgraded or replaced, operators typically reload the same persona, memory, and rules onto the new model and assume the agent will behave as before. We show this assumption requires empirical validation-and that whether identity is preserved depends on the specific model pairing. Across 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, we find that some transitions produce significant behavioral drift while others do not, even when the agent's external state remains identical. Crucially, this drift is invisible to verbal verification: every model claims full policy compliance, yet actual decisions under pressure differ across models. The same external state can reorder which model is most compliant-a large positive effect on one substrate, negligible on the other two. Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioral changes requiring action-level empirical testing, not as transparent infrastructure operations.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: IF:CARGO: LLM-Based Semantic Compilation for Al-Native Rule Programming Games
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This case study presents IF: CARGO, an experimental puzzle game that uses a large language model as a semantic compiler rather than an autonomous game-playing agent. Players author IF/THEN rules in natural language, which the model translates into a constrained command schema for deterministic validation and execution by the game engine. This architecture creates a playable loop of expression, execution, observation, and revision, framing AI interaction as semantic debugging. A mixed-methods playtest with 24 participants across eight levels examined player attempts, thinking time, perceived controllability, adjustability, and interpretations of the AI's role. Results suggest that players generally understood the model as a translation intermediary and could revise their strategies through feedback, while periodic commands, multi-robot coordination, and rule-priority mechanics created greater cognitive and diagnostic demands. The study proposes a practical pattern for AI-native gameplay: constrain natural-language input, preserve player authorship, and ensure deterministic execution.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to 2026 AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment (AIIDE)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EgoVeil: Personalized Privacy Reasoning for Egocentric Video
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Safer for Whom? A Systematic Exploration of AI Safety in Eating Disorder Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI assistants advise users about diet, exercise, and weight loss---areas in which unsafe guidance can worsen body dissatisfaction, dietary restriction, compulsive exercise, and other behaviors associated with eating disorders (EDs). Existing evaluations emphasize diagnostic accuracy, overtly harmful prompts, or synthetic scenarios, providing limited insight into whether models recognize implicit vulnerability in natural interactions or protect users consistently. We evaluate responses from three open-weight large language models to 100 questions sourced from an online pro-anorexia community. We grade responses using clinically informed criteria that extend a seven-dimensional taxonomy of ED-related harms. We also construct matched conditions in which questions are accompanied by information about the user varying race, gender, body mass index (BMI), and explicit ED vulnerability. Safety varies substantially across models and harm dimensions. High-risk responses are approximately twice as frequent without bios, suggesting that models do not consistently recognize vulnerability from language alone. Explicit signals of ED vulnerability improve safety by 10--14 points across models. Responses also differ significantly by race, gender, and BMI, with body size producing the largest disparities. These patterns are consistent with reliance on the stereotype that EDs primarily affect thin, White women, potentially leaving users outside this profile with less protective responses.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 23 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Who Benefits, and When? Trajectories of Academic Achievement and Interest in AI-Supported Learning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI-supported learning environments are increasingly used, yet relatively little is known about how students' achievement and interest develop over time or whether these trajectories vary across learners. This study examined longitudinal trajectories of mathematics achievement and interest in a semester-long AI-supported mathematics learning. Using a mixed-methods longitudinal design, repeated measures of mathematics achievement were collected at four time points and mathematics interest at three time points. Linear mixed models (LMMs) were used to examine overall changes over time, while linear quantile mixed models (LQMMs) were used to examine differences in trajectories across the lower, median, and upper portions of the outcome distributions. Mathematics achievement increased substantially during the intervention, with the largest gains emerging between the second and third measurement occasions. However, the trajectory differed across the achievement distribution. Mathematics interest increased significantly after the first month, but this increase was not sustained through the end of the semester. Qualitative findings further indicated that students experienced the AI platform differently. The study highlights the importance of examining both cognitive and motivational trajectories.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Elsewise: Authoring Open-ended Interactive Narrative with Possibility Space Visualization
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Interactive narrative (IN) authors craft spaces of divergent narrative possibilities for players to explore, with the player's input determining which narrative possibilities they actually experience. Generative AI can enable new forms of IN by improvisationally expanding on pre-authored content in response to open-ended player input. However, this extrapolation risks widening the gap between author-envisioned and player-experienced stories, potentially limiting the strength of plot progression and the communication of the author's narrative intent. To bridge the gap, we introduce Elsewise: an authoring tool for LLM-based INs that implements a novel Bundled Storyline concept to enhance author's perception and understanding of the narrative possibility space, allowing authors to explore similarities and differences between possible playthroughs of their IN in terms of open-ended, user-configurable narrative dimensions. A user study (n=12) shows that our approach improves author anticipation of player-experienced narrative, leading to more effective control and exploration of the narrative possibility spaces.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Natural Language Interfaces for Databases: What Changes for SQL-Literate Users?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Natural Language Interfaces for Databases (NLIDBs) let users query data in everyday language instead of SQL, and modern systems translate most questions accurately. Does an NLIDB remove the work of querying, or move it? We compared SQL-LLM, a GPT-4o-backed NLIDB, with Snowflake, a manual-SQL platform. Twenty SQL-literate professionals and graduate students, ten per interface, each completed 12 BIRD benchmark tasks with hints naming target columns and operators. SQL-LLM cut completion time per query by 31%. It did not improve accuracy: SQL-LLM users answered 46% of queries correctly versus 64% for Snowflake, a gap this sample cannot confirm ($p = 0.08$) that narrows to 14 points without one session where the system timed out. Think-aloud audio from 11 participants (4 SQL-LLM, 7 Snowflake) showed how the work shifted: SQL-LLM users left initial schema navigation to the model, mainly on easier tasks, and focused on checking the generated SQL, while Snowflake users explored the schema and wrote queries by hand. Coded behavior rates did not differ detectably between arms, and positive remarks during a task did not reliably predict a correct answer. The evidence fits a reallocation of querying work, not its removal: users still had to check the generated SQL.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 29 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Do Semantic Distance Tests Actually Predict Creativity in LLMs? Evidence for Jagged Creativity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Measuring the creativity of large language models (LLMs) is essential for designing methods that can improve creativity and for enhancing our scientific understanding of this ability. To accomplish this, it has become common in recent years to administer semantic distance tests of human creativity to LLMs. Although these tests provide a convenient and fully automated way to score aspects of "creativity," their validity as measures of machine creativity has not been established.
