Signal Processing.summary: Repeatable test setups support the development and evaluation of integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) hardware and algorithms. Commercial radar target simulators are expensive, while sub-6 GHz ISAC experiments often need only tens of megahertz of bandwidth within their available spectrum allocation. This makes simpler, low-cost test hardware attractive. We present a low-cost, open-source radar target simulator based on an ADALM-Pluto without hardware modification, supporting four independently configurable targets and analog bandwidths up to 56 MHz. The FPGA generates echoes with independent delays, Doppler shifts and gains, using fractional-delay filters for sub-sample adjustment. For motion-consistent echoes, delay and carrier phase are updated together to reproduce both changing range and frequency-dependent Doppler shifts. Over-the-air measurements demonstrate simultaneous echoes, sub-sample delay adjustment, and smooth target motion between sample positions. The FPGA source, firmware and on-device web interface are publicly available.

Signal Processing.title: Joint Discrete Pinching-Antenna Activation and Beamforming Design for Efficient PASS-ISAC
Signal Processing.summary: Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) offer flexible radiation points for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), but existing designs largely assume continuous antenna placement, which may be impractical with pre-installed hardware. We investigate a discrete-activation multi-waveguide PASS-ISAC system that selects sparse transmit and receive pinching antennas (TPAs/RPAs) from predefined locations. We formulate a communication-rate maximization problem by jointly optimizing beamforming and TPA/RPA activation under transmit-power, activation, and sensing signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) constraints. To solve this nonconvex problem, we develop a low-complexity joint discrete pinching-antenna activation and beamforming optimization (JDPABO) algorithm based on alternating optimization, successive convex approximation, and reweighted $\ell_1$ minimization. Simulations show that JDPABO approaches continuous-placement performance at low sensing SNR requirements and outperforms fixed activation schemes with sparse PA activation.
Signal Processing.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in the proceeding of the IEEE CCNC-2027

Signal Processing.title: Physics-Informed Generative Augmentation for Open-Set UAV Classification
Signal Processing.summary: Open-set recognition of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) from passive 5G radar micro-Doppler signatures is challenging because unknown drone types cannot be anticipated at training time. We propose a physics-informed generative adversarial network (PI-GAN) that conditions spectrogram synthesis on rotor kinematics, forcing the classifier's feature space to encode physically meaningful structure. We compare PI-GAN augmentation against a vanilla conditional GAN (CGAN) and basic data augmentation across three held-out configurations with 1, 2, and 3 unknown classes. Vanilla CGAN augmentation collapses open-set clustering, reducing the adjusted Rand index (ARI) from 0.97 to 0.01, whereas PI-GAN preserves it at 0.97. In a controlled held-out sweep with two unknown classes, PI-GAN achieves an ARI of 0.92 compared to 0.07 for vanilla CGAN. The physics-informed features enable unsupervised separation of mechanically distinct unknown drones without retraining, demonstrating that physics-conditioned generation is the key enabler of open-set capability.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted by ICT Express

Signal Processing.title: Set-Theoretic PAPR Reduction in Multi-Antenna Systems
Signal Processing.summary: In this study, we propose an optimization framework for PAPR reduction in multi-antenna systems with beamforming. Unlike previous techniques, the proposed approach permits full control over the distorted symbol constellation via arbitrary (convex) constraints on the frequency domain symbols, while minimizing the PAPR at each individual transmit antenna. We propose an iterative algorithm based on an extrapolated alternating projection method, which relies on an iterative soft-thresholding subroutine to compute projections onto sublevel sets of the objective function, and we compare its performance to optimal solutions obtained with general-purpose convex solvers.
Signal Processing.comment: Submitted to IEEE WCNC 2027 for possible publication

Signal Processing.title: A Proof-of-Concept Study of Wi-Fi Channel State Information-Based Fall Detection Using ESP32 Devices
Signal Processing.summary: This paper reports a small-scale proof-of-concept study of contactless fall detection using Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) collected with two ESP32 devices. One device acts as the transmitter and the other as the receiver, with a separation of 3.5~m. The evaluated signal-processing pipeline uses CSI amplitude, second-level discrete wavelet transform (DWT) denoising with a Symlet-10 wavelet, z-score normalization, and fixed-length segmentation. Wavelet-scattering coefficients are used as features, and MATLAB's automated classifier-selection workflow identifies a LogitBoost ensemble with a minimum leaf size of four and a learning rate of 0.022052. The proposed classifier achieved an accuracy of 93.10%, with a precision of 100%, recall of 87.50%, and F1-score of 93.33%. These results demonstrate the potential of Wi-Fi CSI-based sensing for contactless fall detection using low-cost ESP32 hardware.

Signal Processing.title: Over-the-Air Computation for Imperfectly Synchronized Multi-View Semantic Communication
Signal Processing.summary: Compared to classical task-agnostic communication systems, which focus on reliable transmission of a message, semantic communication (SemCom) focuses on transmitting the task-relevant meaning behind the message. In this paper, we design a SemCom system for a distributed multi-view scenario, where multiple semantic devices observe a scene and collaborate through a single semantic receiver to execute a task. We propose adopting an Over-the-Air Computation (AirComp) channel for efficient use of resources, as AirComp uses a superposition of signals to directly compute a function, which in SemCom is decoding the semantic variable. However, AirComp relies heavily on perfect time and phase synchronization, which is not practical in real-world communication. We show that timing offsets of standards like 5G cause negligible degradation, and that larger timing offsets can be compensated by training. Nevertheless, the system cannot deal with the encountered levels of phase synchronization errors, even when trained with those levels of synchronization errors. Therefore, we propose integrating existing phase synchronization algorithms into the AirComp SemCom system training. Simulation results show that the proposed system can approach the task execution performance of a perfectly synchronized SemCom system.

Signal Processing.title: A Tutorial on Infrastructure Self-Calibration for Radio-Based Indoor Positioning
Signal Processing.summary: Radio positioning needs the positions of its anchors, access points, base stations, or reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, and manual surveying is costly and error-prone. Calibrating this infrastructure from its own measurements is one estimation problem, studied in at least four communities as self-calibration, auto-positioning, anchor self-localization, network localization, or radio simultaneous localization and mapping. This tutorial teaches the problem through one factor graph. The measurement topology sets its factors, the reference information enters as priors, and other measurement models add nuisance states. The tutorial shows what ranges can identify, from rigidity to the motion a mobile device must contribute, and presents multidimensional scaling, nonlinear least squares, recursive filters, and convex relaxations as inference engines over this graph. One session of a ten-anchor ultra-wideband deployment is carried through every step, and recordings from a second, harsher deployment and a public partial mesh serve as contrasts. The examples illustrate three lessons. On a full mesh, choose a robust loss and set its scale first, and calibrate with the engine of the positioning system, since the engines then reach similar errors. On thinned or partial meshes, test the result at surveyed check points, because the start decides which minimum a solver reaches. On a line-of-sight deployment, estimate range offsets, which lower the error floor that a systematic ranging bias sets and a robust loss cannot remove. A decision tree and a table of their effects turn them into deployment guidance. Code and result tables are openly released, and the data are published separately.

Signal Processing.title: Geometry-based Efficient Airy Beam Training for Quasi-LoS in Terahertz Near-field Communications
Signal Processing.summary: With enlarged antenna apertures in Terahertz (THz) communications, near-field propagation becomes increasingly dominant, highlighting quasi-line-of-sight (quasi-LoS) scenarios with partial blockage. Airy beams offer a promising solution through their curved trajectories, but existing training methods for unknown blockage rely on computationally intensive parameter searches or learning-based approaches. In this paper, we propose an efficient geometry-based Airy beam training framework for uniform linear array (ULA) and uniform planar array (UPA) systems. First, theoretical feasibility bounds under finite apertures are derived to eliminate infeasible codewords. A performance-oriented Slope-Depth Geometric Codebook (SDGC) is then developed using bending-direction probing and geometric sampling. To further reduce training overhead, a latency-oriented Bijective 1D Geometric Codebook (B1GC) is proposed by mapping blockage-avoidance waypoints to receiver targets, enabling one-dimensional search. For UPA systems, a hybrid focusing--Airy mode is introduced, using four probe beams to identify the blockage-avoidance dimension and bending direction, followed by Airy beam training and orthogonal near-field focusing. Simulations show that SDGC achieves 14.8 bit/s/Hz average spectral efficiency with 40.9\% lower training overhead than the hierarchical focusing--Airy codebook (HFAC), while B1GC reduces overhead by 87.1\% with comparable performance. The UPA results further demonstrate effectiveness under two-dimensional blockage.

Signal Processing.title: VR-Net: Subarray-Level Inter-Cell Coordination for Multi-Cell XL-MIMO under Near-Field Spatial Non-Stationarity
Signal Processing.summary: Spatial non-stationarity in multi-cell extremely large-scale MIMO (XL-MIMO) confines each user to a visibility region (VR) of each array. VR-Net exploits these regions for subarray-level coordinated beamforming. A base-station (BS)-indexed conflict graph identifies overlapping VRs; gain-based association and a masked multi-cell weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) iteration restrict beam design and channel state information (CSI) uploads to the relevant subarray blocks. We establish conditions for exact per-cell decoupling, derive the expected CSI loads, bound the loss of designing on the VR-gated channel and the loss of the support constraint, and characterize single-edge visibility contrast through a closed-form Fresnel transition width. Simulations use a 3GPP TR 38.901 Release-19-based near-field UMi channel with modular facade arrays and pre-registered criteria. At a 30 dB threshold, VR-Net retains at least 99.6% of the full-aperture WMMSE sum rate in every tested setting while uploading 10-39% fewer complex CSI entries. It gains up to 3.5 bit/s/Hz over an all-user adaptation of the multi-cell scheme of Pérez-Adán et al. at moderate power and dense load, and inter-cell coordination adds up to 33% over per-cell design.

Signal Processing.title: Deep Learning-Assisted Optimization of Large Domino-Tiled Phased Arrays for Dual-Band LEO Satellite Communications
Signal Processing.summary: Irregular domino tiling reduces the number of transmit/receive modules (TRMs) of large phased arrays, but its design requires repeated pattern evaluations whose cost grows rapidly with aperture size. This paper presents a hybrid deep learning and optimization framework for large domino-tiled arrays. A local-flip Markov chain generator, about $5.2\times$ faster than a randomized greedy baseline, produces balanced tilings with nearly equal numbers of horizontal and vertical dominoes, and a Tabu Search engine reaches a sidelobe level (SLL) about $0.8$~dB lower than a genetic algorithm, simulated annealing, and iterated local search at comparable directivity. These tools build the dataset on which a convolutional neural network (CNN) surrogate is trained to predict, from the tiling structure alone, whether a candidate yields a favorable multi-angle SLL. Gating the Tabu Search with the surrogate removes $60.6$--$70.6\%$ of the full evaluations and speeds up the search by $2.56$--$3.80$ times for apertures from $20\times20$ to $100\times100$ elements, without degrading the solution quality. A convex amplitude--phase optimization of the fixed tilings then gives equal or higher directivity than two state-of-the-art methods at a comparable SLL, with more than an order of magnitude shorter computation time. Finally, the framework is applied to a $36\times36$ dual-band circularly polarized array for low Earth orbit (LEO) terminals at $11.2$ and $14.0$~GHz, whose bands are a factor of $1.25$ apart, using $648$ dominoes and a common element spacing selected from a sweep. The array scans to $50^\circ$ with no grating lobe and, compared with a reference irregular array, gives higher directivity over most of the scan range, a lower SLL at large scan angles, and a spacing that is more practical for the lower band.
Signal Processing.comment: 13pages, 19 figures

Signal Processing.title: Multimodal Semantic Communication using Shared and Unique Representation Decomposition
Signal Processing.summary: Semantic communication (SemCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm for bandwidth-constrained mobile and vehicular networks. This paper proposes a unified representation learning framework for multimodal SemCom (MSC), which encodes heterogeneous data into a compact semantic space for efficient transmission and source recovery. The framework addresses the multimodal semantic representation gap, which arises when at least one modality contains semantic information that cannot be fully inferred from the other. To preserve this information for reconstruction, the framework decomposes each representation into shared and modality-specific components. We formulate a mutual information objective for source reconstruction, cross-modal alignment of the shared components, and decoupling of the shared and modality-specific components. To enhance transmission efficiency, we introduce a shared knowledge base implemented as a compact codebook of semantic vectors learned during training. The shared components are transmitted digitally as codebook indices, while the modality-specific components are sent in analog form. We apply knowledge distillation during training, using a pretrained vision foundation model to guide the learning of quantized shared features. On image--text pairs over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Extended Vehicular A (EVA) channels, the proposed framework improves image reconstruction over conventional separate source-channel coding (SSCC) and representative multimodal and unimodal SemCom systems. Further evaluations show gradual degradation under channel-estimation mismatch, complementary effects of alignment, decoupling, and knowledge distillation on the shared representation, and alignment of shared features across modalities with separation of the modality-specific features.
Signal Processing.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Signal Processing.title: Equation-Free Digital Twins for Nonlinear Structural Dynamics
Signal Processing.summary:
Monitoring floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) under stochastic excitation and sensor failure requires computationally efficient and physically interpretable estimators. This paper introduces an equation-free, output-only digital twin framework combining Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel-DMD), sparse-sensor reconstruction, and a stochastic Kalman extension. A sufficient identifiability condition is derived for modal amplitudes recovered from delay-embedded measurements, while Tikhonov regularization addresses ill-conditioned sensor layouts. Correlation-domain identification improves damping estimates under stochastic forcing and distinguishes structural modes from rotor harmonics.
  The framework is validated using OpenFAST simulations of an NREL 5-MW spar turbine and experimental basin-test measurements from a 1:70-scale IEA 15-MW semi-submersible. In simulations, the identified tower modes agree with established operational modal analysis methods (MAC at least 0.99), while the Kalman estimator achieves R-squared values of 0.91 to 0.99 under severe sensor sparsity. Experimental results identify tower modes at 0.430 and 0.415 Hz with MAC of 1.00 against SSI-COV and reconstruct tower-base bending moments on unseen runs with R-squared values of 0.83 to 0.89 using three of four sensors. The framework provides a computationally efficient, sensor-failure-resilient structural-state estimation layer for digital twins.
Signal Processing.comment: Added more details of the theory as well as real experimental validation also included in the results. Now the manuscript is more defensible

Signal Processing.title: Analytical Characterization of Radial Resolution at Oblique Angles for Near-Field Communications
Signal Processing.summary: Exploiting radial resolvability in near-field communications requires analytical expressions that directly map physical beam parameters to resolution-controllable focal regions. However, beam characterization at oblique angles produces complex algebraic expressions that mask these critical interactions. In this work, we introduce an electromagnetic-aware analytical model built upon a tight upper bound of the spatial power density. This approach yields compact, closed-form solutions for the peak intensity position and radial focal extent, enabling the design of contiguous multi-user focal regions with controlled radial resolution. Performance evaluations confirm that the framework closely tracks exact solutions while facilitating system dimensioning and inter-beam interference management across varying steering angles.
Signal Processing.comment: 6 pages, 8 figures

Signal Processing.title: Multi-Label Classification with Constrained Search for Inverse Design of a 16x16 Reconfigurable Pixel Antenna
Signal Processing.summary: In this paper, an inverse design method is presented for a 16x16 reconfigurable pixel antenna with 480 binary switches, giving 2480 possible patterns, far beyond what full-wave simulation can explore. Given a target frequency between 1 and 6 GHz, the method searches for a switch configuration whose simulated resonance lies close to the target. A forward surrogate model is trained on 22,152 full- wave simulated patterns to predict where a given switch pattern resonates. The forward task is formulated as multi-label classification over 100 frequency bins rather than reflection-coefficient regression, because a curve-fitting objective is dominated by the flat baseline around the narrow resonances of this structure. The inverse design is a simulated annealing search over the switch state, with a connectivity constraint maintained at every step so that every pattern generated is a valid antenna. The proposed methodology combines resonance-focused surrogate modelling with connectivity-constrained discrete optimization, enabling candidate generation without full-wave solver calls during the search. The pipeline is verified in CST Microwave Studio by simulating 220 predicted candidates, ten for each of 22 target frequencies. For each request, the best of the ten candidates reached a median frequency error of 23 MHz across the 22 targets, compared with 35 MHz for a solver-guided search using 200 simulations for each target. The proposed methodology therefore enables automatic switch configuration to achieve a requested resonant frequency, eliminating solver calls during the search and manual redesign of the antenna geometry.

Signal Processing.title: Multi-Band Indoor MIMO Channel Measurements Across Sub-6 GHz, Mid-Band and mmWave: Comparing 2.55 GHz, 12.75 GHz and 25.5 GHz
Signal Processing.summary: Future wireless systems for indoor applications are expected to extend their operating frequencies from sub-6 GHz to mid-band and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies to support higher data rates. To characterize the frequency-dependent propagation behavior across these bands, multi-band channel measurements are essential. In this work, we conduct double-directional multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channel measurements in an indoor environment to enable a consistent comparison across three frequency bands. Measurements are performed using a 16x16 MIMO configuration at center frequencies of 2.55 GHz, 12.75 GHz and 25.5 GHz, covering both line-of-sight (LOS) and obstructed line-of-sight (OLOS) conditions. The measured channels are processed using the space-alternating generalized expectation maximization (SAGE) algorithm to extract multipath parameters, which are subsequently used to characterize the angular power distributions across the three frequency bands. The results show substantial angular-domain similarity across all three bands in both LOS and OLOS conditions, while also highlighting frequency-dependent variations.
Signal Processing.comment: Submitted to the 21th European Conference on Antennas and Propagation (EuCAP), 2027

Signal Processing.title: A Diffusive T-Matrix Unifying the Electric and Magnetic Polarizability Tensors in Conducting Layered Media
Signal Processing.summary: Electromagnetic induction is used to detect and classify buried and submerged objects, such as unexploded ordnance in soil and on the seabed. A small object is commonly described by its magnetic polarizability tensor (MPT), which is independent of its position and of the sensor. The MPT assumes that the surrounding medium does not conduct. In seawater at extremely low frequency, or in clay at kilohertz frequencies, this assumption fails at depths comparable to the skin depth. The object then also diverts the current induced in the medium, a galvanic response that the MPT omits. We describe the object instead by its transition matrix (T-matrix), which keeps the independence from position and sensor and includes both responses. It is computed once per medium and frequency from a single finite element problem, for any shape and materials. Its inductive block reduces to the MPT when the medium conducts weakly, and its galvanic block reduces to the electric polarizability tensor in the static limit. We test the model against full finite element solutions for a conducting box, non-magnetic and permeable, in a layered sea and in clay over bedrock. Two orders beyond the dipole, it is accurate to within 1.4% over two decades of frequency and for sizes up to 0.7 of the depth, whereas the error of the MPT carried into the conducting medium reaches 91%. Blocks coupling the two responses, contained in neither tensor, contribute up to 13%.
Signal Processing.comment: 30 pages, 4 figures

Signal Processing.title: Reduced-Complexity WMMSE Approach for Cell-Free Massive MIMO Systems With Finite-Capacity Fronthaul Links
Signal Processing.summary: We propose a reduced-complexity weighted minimum mean squared error (R-WMMSE) framework for cell-free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO) systems with finite-capacity fronthaul links. To maximize the system capacity, we need to jointly design beamforming vectors at distributed access points (APs) and fronthaul quantization noise covariances. Such a task would be addressed using conventional WMMSE algorithms and their variants. However, existing WMMSE-based methods either assume ideal infinite-capacity fronthaul links or incur high computational complexity when jointly optimizing the network-wide beamforming and fronthaul compression variables. To this end, the proposed method jointly optimizes beamforming and fronthaul compression by leveraging a sequential per-AP optimization strategy. Since each subproblem is efficiently solved via Lagrangian duality with closed-form updates, the overall computational complexity can be significantly reduced compared to the conventional WMMSE method. To further reduce hardware cost, we extend the R-WMMSE framework to hybrid analog-digital beamforming systems, tackling the joint design of digital beamforming, fronthaul compression, and analog beamforming. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme achieves performance nearly identical to that of the conventional WMMSE while reducing the runtime by over 99%.

Signal Processing.title: Affine Frequency Division Multiplexing With Pre-Chirp Spreading Index Modulation: A CSI-Driven Secure Transmission Framework
Signal Processing.summary: The flexible configurability of pre-chirp parameters in affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) provides new degrees of freedom for designing covert communication mechanisms. Leveraging this property, this paper proposes a covert AFDM pre-chirp spreading index modulation (IM) framework referred to as AFDM-PCS-IM, tailored for high-mobility scenarios. Specifically, an orthogonal pre-chirp parameter codebook is constructed by exploiting the tunability of the pre-chirp parameters. To enhance covertness, the legitimate channel state information (CSI) is utilized to generate controlled perturbations that encrypt the codebook, thereby tightly coupling the modulation structure with instantaneous channel characteristics. The encrypted pre-chirp codebook is then employed as an IM dimension for information transmission, where the index bits are conveyed through the selection of pre-chirp parameter sequences. Since eavesdroppers cannot obtain consistent CSI, they are unable to reconstruct the encrypted codebook and thus cannot reliably recover any useful information. Moreover, to address channel estimation errors inherent in practical communication environments, a noise-aware CSI quantizer is further introduced to improve robustness under imperfect CSI conditions. Finally, a low-complexity two-layer message passing detector with Walsh code constraints (TLMP-WC) is developed to enable efficient large-scale data detection while simultaneously enhancing the detection reliability. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed AFDM-PCS-IM framework with the TLMP-WC detector achieves superior covertness, improved bit error rate (BER) performance, and reduced computational complexity compared with the state-of-the-art schemes.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications (JSAC)

Signal Processing.title: Full-Duplex Communication for Pinching Antenna Systems
Signal Processing.summary: This paper investigates multiuser full-duplex (FD) communication assisted by a multiwaveguide pinching-antenna system (PASS) where each dielectric waveguide can be dynamically configured to operate in either downlink transmission or uplink reception mode. We develop a channel model that accounts for in-waveguide power attenuation and cumulative pinching antenna (PA)-induced phase shift. Building on this model, we jointly optimize the waveguide modes, PA locations, PA radiation/collection coefficients, downlink beamformers, uplink receive combiners, and uplink transmit powers to maximize the downlink weighted sum-rate (WSR) subject to uplink quality-of-service (QoS) requirements and power constraints. To tackle the resulting mixed-integer nonconvex resource allocation problem, we propose a low-complexity hierarchical block coordinate descent algorithm that capitalizes on weighted minimum mean-square error, fractional programming, majorization-minimization, and the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to obtain a high-quality suboptimal solution. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed FD-PASS outperforms an FD base station equipped with fixed antennas and exhibits greater robustness against residual self-interference. Moreover, ignoring cumulative PA-induced phase shifts can produce QoS-infeasible designs.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Delegating Authorization to Misaligned Agents: Coalitional Alignment and Safe Control
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Long-running AI agents create a control problem: each action they take changes the state, which in turn affects the trajectory of future actions. If the agent is not fully aligned, then guaranteeing safety requires approving consequential actions before allowing them to be executed. But requiring human approval at every step makes attention a bottleneck. Delegating review to other AI agents raises the same alignment problem: the reviewers may themselves be misaligned. We identify a condition on a reviewing panel that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient for a guarantee that the principal fares at least as well in expectation as under a designated baseline policy.
  Each reviewer agent reports whether an action proposal made by a proposer agent improves its own utility relative to the baseline. We show that a threshold rule tolerating $k$ disapprovals is safe exactly when, after any $k$ reviewers are removed, the principal's utility can be written as a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers' utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. We call this property $k$-robust coalitional alignment. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted MDP with an arbitrary proposer agent, safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve on the baseline.
  When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe under the unanimous approval rule; in contrast, more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even when reviewers are individually aligned.
  Experiments with existing reviewer models show that collective review can remain sound without an aligned individual, even when some disapprovals are tolerated.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Before AI Agents Negotiate for Us: A Competitive Tournament of Rule-Based, Search, Optimization, Learned, and Language-Model Negotiators Under Scarcity
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Automated bilateral negotiation underlies two-sided matching markets such as freight brokering, where many shippers and carriers negotiate price before a matching mechanism decides who is paired with whom. Prior strategy comparisons typically use isolated one-on-one duels or a single fixed market, so they cannot show how a strategy behaves against several live rivals under a changing balance of supply and demand. We built nine negotiation architectures spanning rule-based, search-based, optimization-based, imitation-learning, and reinforcement-learning families, and ran all nine simultaneously on both sides of a Gale-Shapley matching market under a balanced condition and two scarcity conditions rotated across all 36 exclusion pairs. In the balanced carrier market, an imitation-learned engine (ML2), a reinforcement-learning policy trained only on isolated negotiations (RL), and an expected-utility optimization engine (OPT) formed a statistically tied top group, and no architecture led in every condition and role. RL beat all eight carrier rivals when carriers were scarce, but its match rate collapsed from 62% to 16% when shippers were scarce and it had to compete with the other carrier agents for demand. A second reinforcement-learning policy trained against rival agents (RL2) kept its match rate above 91% in every condition, yet lost on realized payoff to all eight shipper-side rivals in two of the three conditions, traced to a confirmed train/deployment feature mismatch. We also tested nine large language models (LLMs), from 1 to 72 billion parameters, under the same protocol: they lost significantly to the two strongest engines (OPT2 and ML2) in 32 of 36 comparisons and won none. These results show that isolated or single-condition evaluation can hide failure modes that a many-sided, scarcity-varying, statistically corrected tournament exposes directly.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Code, data and trained models: https://github.com/AILabFr8tech/wehaveadeal (archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.24122038)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Coverage-Aware Routing with Approximate Equilibrium Guarantees for Location-Diversity Vehicular Crowdsensing
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Vehicular crowdsensing uses the sensors of everyday vehicles to monitor cities, but traffic concentrates on few roads, leaving much of the network unsensed. Location-diversity incentives pay vehicles more to travel where few others go, but our earlier mechanism sets how far each vehicle deviates without optimizing collective coverage in route selection. We add this step in two stages. First, a non-cooperative game with diversity-weighted rewards yields each vehicle's equilibrium deviation. Second, the platform recommends to each vehicle a feasible route whose deviation is within a tolerance of this value, chosen to improve coverage. The coverage gain is monotone submodular, so a greedy router with local search attains at least half of the optimal gain over generated candidates. If every active vehicle has a candidate within a tolerance that is small relative to the aggregate deviation, the recommended routes form an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium, with $\varepsilon$ first order in the tolerance, or second order under a stronger condition. On London and Monaco road networks, the router achieves 99.4% and 98.9% of the optimal reduction in the coverage penalty on small instances and exceeds closest-length selection by up to 27.9 points. Under heterogeneous costs, uniform deviation needs compensation averaging 42% of the budget to give every vehicle nonnegative utility; the equilibrium targets need almost none. They also yield more coverage per unit of added travel in most settings and up to 22.6 more points at small budgets, an advantage that depends on placement and reverses at large budgets, where detour limits bind.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Improved Metric Distortion Bounds for Deterministic Weighted-Tournament Voting Rules
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study deterministic weighted-tournament voting rules, also known as C2 rules, which use only the fraction of voters who prefer one candidate to another for each pair of candidates. Voters and candidates lie in a common but unknown metric space, and voters rank candidates by distance. The goal is to select a candidate minimizing the sum of distances to the voters, and distortion measures the worst-case approximation ratio relative to an optimal candidate. Charikar et al.~[EC 2025] introduced the Unblanketed Set rule with distortion at most $3.9312$ and proved a lower bound of $3.1128$ for deterministic C2 rules. We extend their rule to the Path-Unblanketed Set rule, which runs in polynomial time and achieves distortion at most $1+2\sqrt{2}\approx3.8284$. The rule uses paths between candidates to combine pairwise comparisons without increasing the approximation loss with the path length. With computer assistance, we prove a better upper bound of $3.3346$ for five or six candidates and a general lower bound of $3.1828$ using a construction with 17 candidates.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Beyond Worst-Case Online Algorithms via Input Subsampling
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study whether classical competitive ratios survive input subsampling, when both the online algorithm and the offline optimum are evaluated on the same subsampled input. We consider the canonical problems of prophet inequalities and ski-rental. In these settings, for any single subsampling rate, the classical worst-case ratios remain unchanged. We ask a stronger question: can one adversarial input remain worst-case at two distinct rates $p>q$?
  For prophet inequalities, in the model where the policy knows the sampling rate and learns item survival online, every instance has competitive ratio strictly below $2$ at one of the two rates, and we determine the tight simultaneous guarantee. For ski rental, in the fluid model where sampling scales the horizon, the answer depends on $q/p$. Against adversarial distributions over horizons, one unrestricted randomized algorithm achieves a strict simultaneous improvement over $e/(e-1)$ for every distribution exactly when $q/p$ is below approximately $0.34$. Requiring the algorithm to buy by the breakeven time lowers this threshold to approximately $0.31$, showing that unlike classical ski-rental algorithms, buying later can provably help in this setting.
  Our results therefore reveal a new form of beyond-worst-case fragility under input subsampling: instances that are worst-case at one rate need not remain hard at two rates simultaneously.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted to ITCS 2027

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Golden Ratio: EF1 and Ordinal-MMS for Additive Goods
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Every complete allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1) guarantees each of the $n$ agents her $1$-out-of-$(2n-1)$ maximin share. Can we construct allocations that satisfy EF1 together with stronger ordinal maximin share guarantees? For additive valuations, we prove that there always exists a complete allocation that is simultaneously EF1 and ($1$-out-of-$\lfloor\varphi n\rfloor$)-MMS, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$ is the golden ratio. For bivalued valuations, where each agent may have her own two non-negative values for the goods, we obtain a complete allocation that is simultaneously envy-free up to any good (EFX) and ($1$-out-of-$\lceil(7n-1)/6\rceil$)-MMS.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: GT-HarmBench: Benchmarking AI Safety Risks Through the Lens of Game Theory
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Frontier AI systems are increasingly capable and deployed in high-stakes multi-agent environments. However, existing AI safety benchmarks largely evaluate single agents, leaving multi-agent risks such as coordination failure and conflict poorly understood. We introduce GT-HarmBench, a benchmark of 1,535 high-stakes scenarios spanning game-theoretic structures such as the Prisoner's Dilemma, Stag Hunt and Chicken. Scenarios are drawn from realistic AI risk contexts in the MIT AI Risk Repository. Across 15 frontier models, agents fail to choose socially beneficial actions in 39% of high-stakes cases, such as military escalation, election manipulation, and medical malpractice. We measure sensitivity to game-theoretic prompt framing and ordering, and analyze reasoning patterns driving failures. We further show that game-theoretic interventions improve socially beneficial outcomes by up to 31%. Our results highlight substantial reliability gaps and provide a broad standardized testbed for studying alignment in multi-agent environments. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/Flecart/gt-harmbench.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Main Conference

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategically Robust Linear Quadratic Dynamic Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study linear quadratic dynamic games where players are uncertain about each other's control policies or goals and consequently seek to be strategically robust. Building on recent work on strategically robust and risk-averse game theory, we first formalize the problem of strategically robust linear quadratic dynamic games. We show that these can be rewritten as simple transformations of linear quadratic games in which each player chooses a controller in a fictitious game in which they are faced with an adversary who is penalized for deviating from the other players' policies. This formulation naturally induces a novel notion of dynamic equilibrium, which we call a strategically robust dynamic equilibrium. We establish existence and uniqueness (in the subgame-perfect sense) of such equilibria and show that the equilibrium policies are Markovian, linear, and can be efficiently computed via coupled backward Riccati equations. Through numerical simulations, including experiments in a network game, we illustrate the benefits of strategic robustness in designing robust and resilient decentralized control schemes. Our experiments also expose a "free-lunch" phenomenon in games in which robustness does not incur a corresponding loss in performance but can yield improvements in players' utilities and social welfare.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Who Moved the Frontier? Paying Open Frontier Challenges with Free Identities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free? Rank prizes can be gamed: on a replay of one track of a recent challenge, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize. We consider a prediction-market rule, proposed for machine-learning contests, that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds; with exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only these resist splitting and merging, and extra identities gain nothing. With noisy scores and independent normal runs, we prove that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something, on average, to a change that does nothing. We propose a fee per submission, at least what luck pays per attempt, that removes each attempt's expected profit if verifiers are honest and no submission is noisier than planned; nothing enforces that bound, and under noise the rule does not cap the total paid. If crediting another and faking credit to one's second account look the same, a rule that neither rewards fakes nor punishes honesty pays for credit at most what lying costs. We introduce a royalty on how much a later gain falls without the earlier change, which needs no claims but needs removable changes. For five public challenges, we name the rule our results would support.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 20 pages, 7 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Peer Prediction for Learning Agents
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Peer prediction refers to a collection of mechanisms for eliciting information from human agents when direct verification of the obtained information is unavailable. They are designed to have a game-theoretic equilibrium where everyone reveals their private information truthfully. This result holds under the assumption that agents are Bayesian and they each adopt a fixed strategy across all tasks. Human agents however are observed in many domains to exhibit learning behavior in sequential settings. In this paper, we explore the dynamics of sequential peer prediction mechanisms when participants are learning agents. We first show that the notion of no regret alone for the agents' learning algorithms cannot guarantee convergence to the truthful strategy. We then focus on a family of learning algorithms where strategy updates only depend on agents' cumulative rewards and prove that agents' strategies in the popular Correlated Agreement (CA) mechanism converge to truthful reporting when they use algorithms from this family satisfying an additional condition on full exploitation. This family of algorithms is not necessarily no-regret, but includes fixed-parameter versions of familiar online learning algorithms (e.g multiplicative weight update and Follow the Perturbed Leader) as special cases. Simulation of several algorithms in this family as well as the $ε$-greedy algorithm, which is outside of this family, illustrates their finite-horizon behavior in the CA mechanism.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 38 pages, 9 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Price of Anarchy in Markets for Lemons
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations. Equilibria in such settings are typically complex, as proposed prices can convey private information held by the proposer. Such equilibria suffer lost gains from trade both due to the inefficiency introduced by screening (as in independent private value settings) and due to adverse selection. We identify broad conditions under which, nevertheless, sequential equilibria are guaranteed to achieve a constant fraction of the first-best gains from trade. Our bounds quantify the central role of rare pessimistic seller signals and rare optimistic buyer signals. The results apply to seller-proposer, buyer-proposer, and random-proposer mechanisms. The key idea in our analysis is to relate equilibrium gains from trade to proposer profits in an auxiliary market with independent private values.

Computational Complexity.title: The Ultimate Karp-Lipton Collapse
Computational Complexity.summary: Karp and Lipton proved that if $NP\subseteq P/poly$, then $PH$ collapses. A long line of work pushed the collapse to smaller classes. In particular, Chakaravarthy and Roy obtained two such collapses, to (apparently) incomparable classes $O_2^P$ and $P^{prMA}$. We united them earlier by a collapse to the input-oblivious version $P^{prOMA}$ of $P^{prMA}$, which is contained in both; and, jointly with Williams, to a slightly smaller class. Two other deepest known collapses are to $ZPP^{ONP}$ (following from Köbler and Watanabe) and to $OL_2^P$ (proved in this paper). We unite the three collapses by a collapse to a class contained in all of them. We use a three-stage computational model OGTD (oblivious generator-tester-decoder): a polynomial-time generator with an oracle computes an advice string from $1^n$, a tester certifies it, and a polynomial-time decoder uses it (it is the only one that sees the actual input). Let $OM$ be the class of OGTD languages defined by a restricted version of $prOMA$ as the generator's oracle, by a co-$ONP$ tester, and a $P$ decoder. We show that it is contained in the three collapse classes above and prove that $PH$ collapses to $OM$ under $NP\subseteq P/poly$. The collapse also holds for an unambiguous version of $OM$. All these input-oblivious collapse classes lie in $P^{prSBP}$, and so do even the non-input-oblivious versions $P^{prMA}$, $L_2^P$ and $S_2^P$: we prove that $P^{prS_2^P}\subseteq P^{prSBP}$. This strengthens the containment $S_2^P\subseteq P^{prAM}$ of Chakaravarthy and Roy and our earlier containment $L_2^P\subseteq P^{prSBP}$. The proof unites the Goldreich-Wigderson-type procedure of Chakaravarthy and Roy with our earlier approximate-counting technique. Its input-oblivious counterpart concerns $O_2^P$, the first collapse class of Chakaravarthy and Roy: every language in $O_2^P$ has polynomial-size circuits constructible in $FP^{prSBP}$.

Computational Complexity.title: The multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier
Computational Complexity.summary: We prove that the multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier is six, giving a structural, enumeration-free lower-bound proof valid against unrestricted nonlinear reuse in Boolean XOR-AND circuits. The value was previously established by SAT searches of the second author. An explicit six-AND circuit supplies the upper bound. The lower bound combines derivatives, quadratic products, complementary minors, and extraction modulo a Boolean ideal. Independent finite checks accompany the arguments. $\mathrm{MC}(M_3)=6$ is fully formalized in Lean 4. The kernel-checked proof uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
Computational Complexity.comment: 21 pages, 1 table. Lean formalization and verification artifacts: https://github.com/bishara74/lowhalf-mul3

Computational Complexity.title: Statistical-to-computational gaps in central limit theorems for high-dimensional tensors
Computational Complexity.summary: We study high-dimensional central limit theorems (CLTs) as hypothesis testing problems, comparing the number of summands needed for statistical and computational indistinguishability of the normalized sum from the limiting Gaussian distribution as the dimension and number of summands grow together. For the off-diagonal entries of sums of i.i.d. rank-one tensors formed from standard Gaussian vectors (equivalently, the problem of distinguishing Wigner from Wishart tensors), we prove total variation bounds sharpening previous estimates of Mikulincer (2020) and give matching polynomial-time tests. This shows that the statistical and computational thresholds coincide for this CLT, contrary to a proposal by Kunisky, Moore, and Wein (2024). On the other hand, we also show that, for tensors of order at least three, sufficient Gaussian dilution of the summands by adding independent Gaussian noise and rescaling gives a CLT model with a statistical-to-computational gap (in the above setting and ones with more general rank-one summand distributions). To the best of our knowledge, such a phenomenon has not been observed before in any high-dimensional CLT. In particular, in the relevant parameter regimes, we show that a brute-force search achieves strong detection, while polynomials of degree up to $n^{Ω(1)}$ cannot achieve strong separation. The latter lower bounds control low-degree $χ^2$-divergences by a novel method based on cumulant generating functions, and we further illustrate the use of these tools by applying them to masked tensor CLT models where only a prescribed subset of tensor entries is revealed.

Computational Complexity.title: Small Maximum Likelihood on Fixed Cavender-Farris-Neyman Trees: An Approximation Scheme and Limits to Fully Polynomial Approximation
Computational Complexity.summary: Small Maximum Likelihood fits the edge substitution probabilities of a given phylogenetic tree to an observed alignment, summing over the unobserved ancestral states. For the binary Cavender--Farris--Neyman model, we assume a uniform root and an edge-specific substitution probability $p_e\in[0,\tfrac12]$ for each edge $e$, shared across all alignment sites. We give a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme. The algorithm achieves a factor of $1+\varepsilon$ for both the negative log likelihood and the loss after subtracting the uniform-root contribution. Its main step fixes ancestral sequences at one periodically spaced class of depths while summing over all remaining ancestors. A posterior entropy bound controls the cost of this restriction, and dynamic programming optimizes the resulting components over a finite parameter grid. We also give a randomized reduction from Clique showing that an FPTAS returning feasible rational edge probabilities would imply $RP=NP$. These results separate fixed-accuracy approximation from fully polynomial approximation for the same fixed-tree model.

Computational Complexity.title: Geometric Interpretation of 3-SAT and Phase Transition
Computational Complexity.summary: Interpretation of 3-SAT as a volume filling problem, and its use to explore the SAT/UNSAT phase transition.

Computational Complexity.title: Asymptotic Rank of Weighted Graph Tensors via Completely Positive Bounds
Computational Complexity.summary:
We give a conic upper bound on the asymptotic rank of every weighted graph tensor over every field. If $W$ is the logarithmic edge-weight matrix of its dimension matrix $Q$, then $$ \operatorname{MaxCut}(W)\le\log_2\operatorname{\widetilde R}_{\mathbb F}(\mathsf{WT}(Q))\le U_{\operatorname{CP}}^Δ(W). $$ Here $U_{\operatorname{CP}}^Δ(W)$ maximizes $\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}W_{i,j}P_{i,j}$ over nonnegative symmetric zero-diagonal matrices $P$ such that $J-2P$ is copositive and $P_{i,j}\le P_{i,k}+P_{k,j}$ for all distinct vertices. The matrix $J$ is all-one, and copositivity means nonnegativity of the quadratic form on nonnegative vectors.
  Our starting point extends OpenAI's polynomial multiplication method and its subsequent arbitrary-field developments from three tensor legs to arbitrary order. We prove $$ \left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor\le\log_2\operatorname{\widetilde R}_{\mathbb F}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))\le\frac{n^2}{4}. $$ The edge exponent is at most $n/(2(n-1))$ and tends to the optimal value $1/2$, improving the previous Coppersmith--Winograd bounds and answering Question 1.3.1 of Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam. The bounds coincide for every even $n$.
  For every odd $m\ge3$, the theorem gives $\log_2\widetilde R_{\mathbb F}(\mathsf{GT}_2(C_m))\le m-1+1/(m+1)$, improving the previous cycle bound with a gap of only $1/(m+1)$ above the maximum cut. On weighted triangles, the program recovers the rectangular matrix multiplication curve of Uzna'nski and Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam. The CP and semidefinite programs, with or without path constraints, all have value $9/4$ on the unweighted triangle, giving this upper bound a natural conic interpretation. Further applications give explicit bounds for complete multipartite graphs, split graphs, and wheels, including new cases of maximum-cut equality.
Computational Complexity.comment: 82 pages, 5 figures, abstract shortened to meet arXiv requirements

Computational Complexity.title: Combining Determinism and Indeterminism
Computational Complexity.summary:
Our goal is to construct mathematical operations that combine indeterminism measured from quantum randomness with computational determinism so that non-mechanistic behavior is preserved in the computation. Formally, some results about operations applied to computably enumerable (c.e.) and bi-immune sets are proven here, where the objective is for the operations to preserve bi-immunity. While developing rearrangement operations on the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$, we discovered that the bi-immune rearrangements generate an uncountable subgroup of the infinite symmetric group (Sym$(\mathbb{N})$) on the natural numbers.
  This new uncountable subgroup is called the bi-immune symmetric group. The bi-immune symmetric group contains the finitary symmetric group on the natural numbers, and consequently is highly transitive. Furthermore, the bi-immune symmetric group is dense in Sym$(\mathbb{N})$ with respect to the pointwise convergence topology. Moreover, the bi-immune symmetric group contains permutations that are a single infinite cycle on all of $(\mathbb{N})$, even though every one of its generators has only finite orbits. Using an invariant called the {\it crossing number}, we also prove that the bi-immune symmetric group is a meager subset and a proper subgroup of Sym$(\mathbb{N})$.
Computational Complexity.comment: 33 pages. A new section 6 titled, "Bi-Immune Infinite Cycles", has been added that proves the bi-immune subgroup contains infinite cycles. Another new section 10, titled "Density of Bi-Immune Permutations" has also been added. Section 11 proves that the bi-immune subgroup is a proper subgroup of Sym$(\mathbb{N})$

Computational Complexity.title: An even simpler hard variant of Not-All-Equal 3-SAT
Computational Complexity.summary:
We investigate Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat under a strong structural restriction and delineate a sharp tractability threshold. In particular, we consider the restriction of Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat to instances that simultaneously satisfy the following properties: (i) the clauses can be decomposed into a disjoint union of $k$ partitions of the variable set, and (ii) the collection of clauses is linear, that is, each pair of distinct clauses shares at most one variable.
  We show that, under these conditions, Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat remains NP-complete for any fixed $k \geq 4$. On the positive side, we prove that for $k \leq 3$, the problem is in P and, notably, all such instances are not-all-equal-satisfiable. Our results do not only show robustness of NP-completeness despite the strong structure imposed but also have implications for hypergraph coloring.
  In particular, by the well-known correspondence between Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat and hypergraph coloring, we obtain the following corollary of our results: For $k\geq 4$, Bicolorability is NP-complete for linear 3-uniform $k$-regular hypergraphs even if the edges are given as a decomposition into $k$ perfect matchings; with the same restrictions, for $k \leq 3$ Bicolorability is in P, and all such hypergraphs are bicolorable.
  In addition, we show that loosening the restriction to 3-clauses by also allowing 2-clauses shifts the above-mentioned tractability threshold. Moreover, we deduce that every instance of Positive Planar Not-All-Equal Sat with at least three distinct variables per clause is nae-satisfiable. Besides, for Linear Not-All-Equal 3-Sat we derive a computational complexity dichotomy with respect to the number of variable appearances.

Computational Complexity.title: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps
Computational Complexity.summary:
Reed-Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations. For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius.
  We prove smaller error bounds using affine combiners, which combine two received words $f,g$ as $f(x)+(α+βx)g(x)$, where $α,β$ are independent uniform elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$. For output degree bound $d=ρn$, fixed $ρ\in(0,1)$ and $0<η<1-\sqrtρ$, and sufficiently large block length $n$, we prove mutual correlated agreement (MCA) with one coordinate of agreement loss at threshold $A=\lceil(\sqrtρ+η)n\rceil$, with error $O_{ρ,η}\left(\frac{1}{q}+\frac{n^2}{q^2}\right)$. The result holds over arbitrary evaluation domains in every finite field, including prime and binary extension fields. The agreement threshold can approach the Johnson threshold, beyond unique decoding.
  For $q\ge n^2$, our error is $O_{ρ,η}(1/q)$, an asymptotic factor-$n$ separation from scalar combiners: we prove that their worst-case MCA error is $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ at the same agreement threshold and with the same one-coordinate loss. We also prove that affine combiners incur worst-case error $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ when no agreement loss is allowed. Thus one coordinate of agreement loss is necessary for our guarantee; this relaxation of standard MCA reduces the guaranteed common agreement fraction by at most $1/n$. We also extend the result to $k$-variate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids, obtaining MCA error $O_{ρ,η,k}(q^{-k})$ for fixed $ρ,η,k$, sufficiently large $n$, and $q\ge n^{k+1}$, with agreement loss $n^{1-1/k}$.

Computational Complexity.title: Tokenization: Hardness and Bicriteria Approximation Algorithms
Computational Complexity.summary: We study Binary Tokenization: given a corpus of binary strings over $\{0,1\}$ and a vocabulary budget $K$, select at most $K$ substrings (called vocabulary) to minimize the total number of tokens needed to represent the corpus. The primitive symbols $0$ and $1$ are always available, and each document must be segmented separately. Letting $n$ denote the total corpus length and $M$ for the maximum document length, we prove that, for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, Binary Tokenization problem does not have polynomial-time $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation algorithms unless $\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{NP}$. To complement the hardness result, we give a polynomial-time $(γ,γ)$-bicriteria algorithm, with $γ= \sqrt{M}\log n$: The algorithm outputs a vocabulary of size at most $γK$ with number of tokens at most $γ{\rm OPT}_K$, where ${\rm OPT}_K$ is the optimal number of tokens under the original budget $K$. We also study a storage-budget variant, in which the sum of the selected substrings' lengths is bounded by $B$. For $2\le B<n$, we obtain an $(O(\log n\log B),O(\log n\log B))$-bicriteria approximation algorithm.

Computational Complexity.title: The determinantal complexity of the 4*4 permanent is 15
Computational Complexity.summary:
The best known lower bound on the determinantal complexity of the 4x4 permanent is 10. In this short note, I prove that this value is exactly 15: the 4x4 permanent is the determinant of a 15x15 matrix of affine linear forms, and cannot be that of any smaller matrix. To do so, I must establish both a lower and upper bound. To establish the upper bound, I use Grenet's construction of size 2^n-1. Hence that construction is optimal at n=4 (and n=3). This now constitutes the first knwon exact value of the determinantal complexity of the permanent at n=4. Only the value at n=3 was exactly known, prior to this note. The general quadratic bound only gives 8 for n=4.
  To establish the lower bound, I work from a normal form at a zero of the permanent. In the first row (and column) of the normal form, the linear forms vanish on a linear space inside the singular locus of the permanent. A hessian inequality bounds the size of the matrix in terms of that space. Then, a matrix of sie 14 foces the space into any of nine corordinate types. The forcing is either up to symmetry, or else into a family that degenerates to one of them. I then rule out every case. All involved computations are exact.
  In respect of the claim, I have made all certificates public.
Computational Complexity.comment: expanded to show full proofs, unabridged, 57 pages, contains link to repository with certificates

Computational Complexity.title: A proof of P != NP (New symmetric encryption algorithm against any linear attacks and differential attacks)
Computational Complexity.summary: P vs NP problem is the most important unresolved problem in the field of computational complexity. Its impact has penetrated into all aspects of algorithm design, especially in the field of cryptography. The security of cryptographic algorithms based on short keys depends on whether P is equal to NP. In fact, the security requirements for cryptographic keys are much stricter than those for P$\neq$NP, the security of the key must ensure not only a sufficiently high computational complexity to crack it, but also consider the security of each bit of the key, while fully avoiding the effectiveness of various attack methods. In this paper, we innovatively propose a new encoding mechanism and develop a novel block symmetric encryption algorithm, whose encryption and decryption can be completed in linear time. The key consists of 12 variables, for the attacker, in the case when only the plaintext-ciphertext correspondence is known, the problem of cracking the key is equivalent to solving a system of equations about 12 unknown variables $(w_{1}, w_{2}, ..., w_{11}, w_{12})$ together with some implicit variables which are generated by the encryption process. In this paper, we will prove that there is no universal algorithm without brute-force searching at least one variable during the process of verifying five variables $(w_{1}$, $w_{2}$, $w_{3}$, $w_{4}$, $w_{9})$ whose computational complexity is not greater than solving the 12 variables......

Computational Complexity.title: Almost Optimal Lower Bounds under Almost ETH for Approximating Euclidean k-means
Computational Complexity.summary:
In the Euclidean $k$-means problem, we are given a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the goal is to find $k$ representative points in space so as to minimize the sum of the squared distances from each point to its closest representative. Algorithmically, de la Vega, Karpinski, Kenyon, and Rabani [STOC'03] and Kumar, Sabharwal, and Sen [JACM'10] obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for high-dimensional Euclidean $k$-means in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{O(1)}} \cdot dn^{O(1)}$, which was subsequently improved to $2^{\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)} + O(ndk)$ by Feldman, Monemizadeh, and Sohler [SoCG'07]. On the lower-bound side, a recent work of Cohen-Addad, Karthik, Saulpic, and Schwiegelshohn [SoCG'26] proposed the Exponential Time for Expanders Hypothesis (XXH), which asserts exponential-time hardness for $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximating Vertex Cover on vertex expanders, and used it to prove nearly matching running time lower bound whenever $k=\tildeω(1/\varepsilon)$.
  We observe that XXH does not hold in the parameter regime needed for the above result, and show how to repair their reduction under a more standard assumption. More precisely, we show that assuming the Almost Exponential Time Hypothesis for 3-SAT (Almost ETH), for every constant $β\in(0,1)$, Euclidean $k$-means in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{1-β}}\text{poly}(n,d)$, whenever $k=\tildeω(1/\varepsilon)$. By modifying the construction, we also obtain a similar result for approximating the Euclidean $k$-median problem.

Computation and Language.title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
Computation and Language.summary: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop TAE: Can We Trust AI Evaluation? Robustness, Causality, and Risk in Modern AI Assessment

Computation and Language.title: Show Your Work in Swahili: Reinforcement Learning for Native-Language Mathematical Reasoning
Computation and Language.summary: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.

Computation and Language.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
Computation and Language.summary: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

Computation and Language.title: When Language Overrules: Revealing Text Dominance in Multimodal Large Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a diverse range of multimodal tasks. However, these models suffer from a core problem known as text dominance: they depend heavily on text for their inference, while underutilizing other modalities. While prior work has acknowledged this phenomenon in vision-language tasks, often attributing it to data biases or model architectures. In this paper, we conduct the first systematic investigation of text dominance across diverse data modalities, including images, videos, audio, time-series, and graphs. To measure this imbalance, we propose two evaluation metrics: the Modality Dominance Index (MDI) and the Attention Efficiency Index (AEI). Our comprehensive analysis reveals that text dominance is both significant and pervasive across all tested modalities. Our in-depth analysis identifies three underlying causes: attention dilution from severe token redundancy in non-textual modalities, the influence of fusion architecture design, and task formulations that implicitly favor textual inputs. Furthermore, we propose a simple token compression method that effectively rebalances model attention. Applying this method to LLaVA-7B, for instance, drastically reduces its MDI from 10.23 to a well-balanced value of 0.86. Our analysis and methodological framework offer a foundation for the development of more equitable and comprehensive multimodal language models.

Computation and Language.title: Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models
Computation and Language.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.

Computation and Language.title: NotAI.AI: An Interactive Explainable System for AI-Generated Text Detection
Computation and Language.summary: We present NotAI[dot]AI, an explainable AI-generated text detection system. Instead of returning only a binary label or confidence score, the system shows which signals influenced the prediction and lets users inspect an attribution-based sensitivity estimate obtained by subtracting selected local contributions. NotAI[dot]AI combines sentence-level conditional probability curvature, a neural detector score, and interpretable stylometric and readability features in an XGBoost meta-classifier. It explains predictions with TreeSHAP feature contributions and can turn the resulting evidence into a concise natural-language explanation. We evaluate the system on a category-balanced subset of RAID containing human-written, clean AI-generated, and attacked AI-generated texts. The full model outperforms variants based on individual feature families, reaching 0.9685 F1 on the held-out within-subset test split. In an automatic evaluation, two model judges rate 94.5-98.6% of generated explanations as faithful to the supplied detector evidence.

Computation and Language.title: Human-Likeness and Conversational Preference Diverge for Synthesized Agent Speech in Customer-Service Calls
Computation and Language.summary: Listeners can judge an agent's speech on how human it sounds (human-likeness) and on how much they would want to talk to it (conversational preference). Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between the two judgments is unclear. We compared them in paired-choice tests on 120 turns that actors improvised as customer-service representatives. On each trial, two agents spoke the same turn. In Study 1, both agents came from six commercial text-to-speech systems, each with eight voices. In Study 2, one was the actor's original recording and the other a system. Some systems ranked higher on human-likeness, and others on conversational preference. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials (and 49% for the most preferred system). On both judgments, variation among a system's voices was about three-quarters of that between systems. Of three automatic naturalness scores, two predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted conversational preference. In this setting, listeners tended to favor faster speech and fewer pauses between clauses on both judgments, and more pitch variation for conversational preference.
